AI, Tariffs & a New FedEx CFO: November Supply Chain Moves

on Google
Jamere Jackson will be joining FedEx on November 30.
FedEx hires AutoZone’s CFO, Maersk bets on customs expertise as tariffs bite and Danone names a new US president to oversee operations
Jamere Jackson, FedEx
Jamere Jackson will be starting his new role at FedEx, joining the company as EVP and CFO, effective November 30. Throughout his career, he has used strong financial management and precise capital allocation in order to develop business growth. Upon joining the global logistics company, Jamere will be working to support FedEx's profitable growth strategy and deliver long-term value.
I am pleased to welcome Jamere to FedEx and the executive leadership team. Jamere brings a deep understanding of how disciplined financial strategy translates into strong operational performance.
Raj Subramaniam, President and Chief Executive Officer of FedEx Corporation
Paul Duffy, Viatris
Paul Duffy has come out of retirement to join Viatris
Paul has come out of retirement to join Viatris, leading the company's global supply organisation. He is bringing more than 35 years of experience across global supply chain management, which will be used in advancing operational excellent at the company. In this role, Paul will be working alongside his colleagues to further the culture of quality, compliance, safety and integrity.
Throughout my career, one thing has always remained constant: people make the difference. What attracted me to Viatris is the opportunity to join an organisation committed to helping millions of patients around the world.
Paul Duffy, Chief Supply Officer at Viatris
Kevin Shoemaker
Kevin Shoemaker has joined A.P. Moller - Maersk as Regional Head of Global Trade and Customs Consulting (GTCC) NAM
Kevin is joining Maersk, bringing more than 20 years of experience to the job. In this role, he will be making use of his knowledge in customs and trade tech products, alongside tariff management, optimisation and upstream trade compliance. Kevin has a strong understanding of supply chain risk, global trade management and AI.
Today, I'm excited to share the next step in my journey: I'm joining A.P. Moller - Maersk as Regional Head of Global Trade & Customs Consulting (GTCC) for North America. The timing couldn't be better. Tariffs and shifting trade regulations have turned customs from a back-office function into a board-level issue. Importers are facing higher and less predictable duties, more complex rules of origin and growing enforcement risk.
Kevin Shoemaker, Regional Head of Global Trade and Customs Consulting (GTCC) NAM at A.P. Moller - Maersk
Francois Lacombe, Danone
Francois Lacombe has taken on the role of President of Danone USA
Francois has spent his almost 30-year career at Danone working in various countries around the world, including Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and Amsterdam. Now, he is returning to the US as President of Danone USA. He will be bringing his rich career experience of operating with trusted brands and innovative strategies in order to lead the US branch of the company.
I’m ready to hit the ground running alongside our US teams, to listen and learn from our consumers and customers, and to keep growing a business that can make a real difference to people’s health.
Francois Lacombe, President of Danone USA
Ralf Finzel, ADM
Ralf Finzel is joining ADM in a new career move
Ralf Finzel has joined ADM, a global agricultural supply chain manager and processor, empowering across beverages, biofuels, home care and pet treats. Ralf is joining from his four-year career at IFF, and brings more than 23 years of experience working within the supply chain at Honeywell. In his new role, he is leading the nutrition team and working to strengthen ADM's end-to-end supply chain capabilities.
I am honored to be part of the Nutrition leadership team and look forward to working with colleagues across the global business to strengthen our end-to-end supply chain capabilities, support growth, and create value for our customers and stakeholders.
Ralf Finzel, President, Nutrition E2E Supply Chain at ADM
Julie Tracy Lockwood, Genpact
Julie Tracy Lockwood has joined the team at Genpact
Julie is bringing her 15+ years of experience to Genpact, following an extensive career history of driving global go-to-market strategies, operational transformation and leadership. Much of her focus is on bringing data maturity, AI and generative AI to business processes, working as a Professor in Emerging Technologies at the University of Colorado. In her new role at Genpact, Julie will be leveraging AI and ensuring seamless collaboration between humans and technology.
I’m happy to share that I’m starting a new position as VP and Partner Supply Chain, Order Management LifeSciences at Genpact!
Julie Tracy Lockwood, VP and Partner Supply Chain, Order Management LifeSciences at Genpact
Zara Ward, Baringa
Zara Ward, Manager at Baringa
Following a six-year career at Deecon, Zara is bringing her experience to the supply chain and procurement team at Baringa. Her experience focuses on programme delivery, procurement and commercial strategy, overseeing the end-to-end delivery of complex projects. With an emphasis on relationship building and trust across cross-functional teams, Zara has led many effective transformation initiatives.
I'm looking forward to combining my existing procurement and commercial experience with new perspectives, new challenges and opportunities to create meaningful impact for clients.
Zara Ward, Manager at Baringa
Ian A. Arroyo, Accenture
Ian A. Arroyo, Managing Director at Accenture
For more than 20 years, Ian has worked within global logistics, technology and corporate growth leading strategy. In his roles, he has helped enterprise leaders as they scale and unlock measurable operating outcomes through complex strategies. In his new role at Accenture, Ian is leading Logistics, Transportation & Fulfillment (LTF) transformation, partnering with C-suite and senior supply chain leaders to scale next-generation supply chain networks.
I’m happy to share that I’m starting a new position as Managing Director, Logistics, Transportation, and Fulfillment at Accenture!

title: QuantumScape launches open platform for sulphide-based solid-state batteries - electrive.com
content:
The Volkswagen partner has unveiled an open platform for sulphide-based solid-state batteries. It aims to create new licensing and co-development opportunities for existing customers - and allow the integration of third-party components.
Symbolic image: A cell developed by QuantumScape with the company logo.
Image: QuantumScape
QuantumScape has introduced its new open platform for the next generation of solid-state batteries under the name ‘Osprey’. The platform builds on the company’s existing QSE platform and incorporates the ceramic separator developed by QuantumScape over the past years, as well as its established anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode. The US company’s primary goal with the new platform is to enable “new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulphide-based all-solid-state batteries.”.
The background is that the battery industry has long been working on solid-state batteries based on sulfide electrolytes, yet no commercially viable technology has emerged so far. QuantumScape explains: “Sulfide-based solid-state battery approaches are widely popular across the battery industry. Their popularity is due to the high ionic conductivity of sulfide electrolytes and the relative simplicity of processing them. However, sulfide still face several significant limitations, including the need for high applied pressure, as well as poor cycle life and incompatibility with lithium metal.” Although significant progress has been made along the entire value chain, “these efforts have been somewhat fragmented, and they have all run against the same fundamental limitations of sulphides as separators.”
The Osprey platform is thus designed to address this issue, and serve as a new open foundation. QuantumScape states that it is already working with partners from the automotive industry on development projects based on the new platform, with collaboration beginning in the early stages of cell development. QuantumScape elaborates: “Whereas our QSE platform is currently being scaled up to mass production as a full-stack technology solution, Osprey presents a fundamentally collaborative model for all-solid-state battery development.” Customers who prefer a sulphide-based cathode can either utilise QuantumScape’s proprietary sulphide-based cathode technology or integrate their own cathode into the Osprey platform, which “allows them to leverage their own cathode technology, materials and supply chain while gaining the benefits of the QS ceramic separator.”
QuantumScape is now referring to its ‘Osprey’ cells, which have reportedly achieved 1,000 full charge cycles with approximately 80% capacity retention and fast charging from 10% to 80% in five minutes during initial testing. This has been demonstrated under demanding standard conditions, the company says. Specific parameters include charge/discharge rates of 1C/1C, a cathode loading of >5 mAh/cm², a 100% depth of discharge at room temperature – all at a pressure of 1 atmosphere. Furthermore, the platform enables the use of high-loading cathodes, allowing for an energy density at the cell level of up to approximately 1,100 Wh/L.
The compatibility of the cathodes has reportedly been demonstrated with both QuantumScape’s own solid cathodes and third-party solid cathodes. Dr Siva Sivaram, President and CEO of QS, summarises: “Osprey is the result of years of frontier R&D efforts, and we’re excited to share it publicly for the first time. The industry has invested heavily in sulphide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations. We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development.”
However, there are still technical challenges to address before Osprey is ready for mass production. According to the US company, automotive industry customers generally prefer larger prismatic cells that offer higher capacity than the existing QSE-5 design. The aforementioned results, however, primarily come from two-layer test cells. While these have the same footprint as the QSE-5 cell design, “larger cells will likely require both more layers and more area per layer,” the company states. Additionally, much development work remains on the production process, as it has so far only been demonstrated on a laboratory scale.
Looking back at the company’s history: QuantumScape is one of the most promising solid-state battery developers in the US and is primarily supported by Volkswagen. At the end of 2025, the company announced that it had completed the installation of key equipment for the pilot production of its aforementioned QSE-5 solid-state cells in San Jose, California,
as reported here
. In February 2026, the pilot line was inaugurated. This so-called Eagle Line is an automated line for building QuantumScape battery cells, intended to serve as the foundation for future mass production. However, QuantumScape does not aim to manufacture its own cells at scale but instead plans to implement GWh-scale projects primarily through licensing agreements with partners.
In October 2025, the US company
reported
that it had begun delivering B1 samples of the QSE-5 cell. The company did not specify who received the new samples, but Volkswagen is likely among the recipients, as the ties between QuantumScape and the Wolfsburg-based automaker are strong and were further strengthened in the summer of 2025
as reported here
. The focus of their joint programme is the
Ducati V21L motorcycle
, which is equipped with solid-state batteries and undergoing extensive testing. Additionally,
has been publicly listed as a prominent development partner since mid-2025.
What is clear is that
the QSE-5 cell
is set to become QuantumScape’s first commercial product, and features a capacity of 5 Ah, an energy density of over 844 Wh/l, and a charging time of 12.2 minutes from 10 to 80 per cent SoC (State of Charge). In October 2024, the manufacturer stated that it had launched small-scale production and delivery of B-sample cells for testing by automotive customers.
QuantumScape specifically describes the QSE-5 as an 84.5 mm x 65.6 mm x 4.6 mm solid-state battery cell. The cell is also designed to function at low temperatures down to -30 degrees Celsius. The QSE-5 was preceded by two cell prototypes at QuantumScape: ‘A0’ cell samples were delivered to automakers for testing
just before Christmas 2022
, followed by the so-called
“Alpha-2” cells
in March 2024.

title: QS Unveils Osprey Platform for Solid-State Battery Development
content:
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Materials
Battery News
Battery Manufacturing
QuantumScape’s new all-solid-state battery platform combines its ceramic separator with sulfide cathodes for collaborative development and laboratory-scale validation.
November 11, 2026
3 Min Read
QuantumScape researcher at the lab.
QuantumScape
QuantumScape has introduced
as a new platform for all-solid-state battery development, placing it at the center of a longer-term strategy beyond its existing QSE platform. According to QS, Osprey is “an open solid-state platform for all-solid-state battery development” that combines the company’s ceramic separator with cathodes that use solid sulfide catholytes. The company says Osprey cells are all-solid-state, are anode-free as manufactured, and store energy as pure lithium metal.
The announcement is notable because of how the company is framing the platform. Rather than presenting Osprey as a closed battery product that customers must adopt in full, the company is describing it as a technology base that can support work with outside partners. That makes Osprey important both as a technical development and as a collaborative model for future battery programs.
What Osprey is
According to QS, Osprey is “an open solid-state platform for all-solid-state battery development.” An all-solid-state battery is a battery cell built with solid components rather than the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. The platform consists of three parts: the ceramic separator, the solid cathode with sulfide catholyte, and the process used to assemble those components into an all-solid-state cell.
Related:
How 587 Cells Redefine Utility-Scale Battery Storage Efficiency
The company says this system is intended to address challenges such as interfacial resistance between solid materials and the instability that can arise when sulfide systems interact with lithium metal. QuantumScape argues that this approach could help
overcome limitations
that have slowed the commercial progress of sulfide-based designs.
QS solid-state battery Vs Conventional lithium-ion battery. Courtesy of QuantumScape.
Performance claims and technical relevance
QuantumScape says Osprey cells have demonstrated 1,000 cycles to 80% capacity retention under what it calls “gold-standard testing conditions.” According to QS, those conditions include 1C/1C cycling, 100% depth of discharge, room temperature, one atmosphere of pressure, and a two-layer unit cell with commercially relevant area and cathode loading.
One of the more specific claims in the announcement concerns pressure. According to QS, Osprey cells have shown stable cycling at about one atmosphere of applied pressure, which the company says removes the need for complex pressure application devices at the system level. QuantumScape adds that “to the best of our knowledge, no other sulfide-based solid-state cell has ever demonstrated this capability.”
An open and collaborative model
A central part of the Osprey announcement is that QuantumScape is not presenting the platform as a closed system with only one allowed configuration. According to QS, customers may choose to use the company’s sulfide-based cathode technology or bring their own cathode materials, supply chains, and related development work to the platform. This approach is different from a fully closed, single-supplier battery model.
Related:
Growing Role of LFP Batteries in Global Energy Transition
That openness may matter because many battery developers and automotive companies have already invested time and resources in sulfide cathode research. Osprey, according to QS, lets those companies build on that work while using QuantumScape’s separator technology to address the separator and anode side of the system.
What the announcement indicates
The Osprey announcement shows that QuantumScape is presenting both a technical platform and a partnership model. According to QS, Osprey combines the QS ceramic separator, sulfide-based solid cathodes, and an anode-free architecture in a system that has shown defined results in laboratory-scale testing. At the same time, the company says the platform is open and collaborative, and in its conclusion describes Osprey as “a pathway for broad cooperation in the highly competitive race to develop commercial ASSB technology.”

Q&A: Standardized Imaging Framework Enhances Battery Research Reliability

title: McKinsey & Company on LFP Growth Driving Battery Materials Demand
content:
Materials
Batteries
EV Batteries
Market Analysis
Industry Trends
McKinsey’s Marcelo Azevedo discusses LFP growth, battery materials demand, supply-chain risks, US capacity gaps, and recycling’s expanding role worldwide today.
November 11, 2026
5 Min Read
As LFP adoption accelerates, the shift is beginning to reshape demand for battery materials.
AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
The growing role of
Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries
in the global energy transition is now gaining momentum as performance improvements make them increasingly attractive for a wider range of mobility and stationary storage applications. As adoption accelerates, the shift is beginning to reshape demand for battery materials, supply-chain priorities, regional manufacturing strategies, and the long-term outlook for recycling. In this interview,
Battery Technology
speaks with Marcelo Azevedo, Associate Partner at
McKinsey & Company
and leader of McKinsey MineSpans, about the forces driving the battery materials market today.
What is driving the battery materials market right now?
Marcelo Azevedo, Associate Partner at McKinsey & Company and leader of McKinsey MineSpans:
Battery demand growth remains the main driver of the battery materials market, led by electric mobility and increasingly supported by battery energy storage systems (BESS). Mobility still accounts for the largest share of battery raw materials demand globally, at approximately 80% in 2026, while BESS is an emerging segment, with demand estimated at more than 15% this year.
Related:
Sodium-Ion Batteries Gain Ground in Australia’s Energy Storage Market
Meanwhile, the shift in battery chemistry is reshaping demand for specific materials. In particular, the growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries is increasing demand for phosphate-based materials, creating new opportunities across the supply chain.
Where are the biggest supply-chain risks for lithium-ion batteries today?
Azevedo:
One of the biggest supply-chain considerations remains the geographic concentration of battery materials and component production, particularly in China. This is especially pronounced for graphite anode materials and LFP cathode materials, where China accounts for more than 90% and 95%, respectively, of global nameplate capacity today. Moreover, as seen in our
Global Materials Perspective 2026
, the share of refined production from top 3 countries has either increased or remained at the previous high levels between 2020 and 2025 for cobalt, manganese, nickel, natural graphite and lithium.
At the same time, significant imbalances remain between local battery cell production capacity and demand across regions, particularly by battery chemistry. By 2030, available NMC cell capacity is expected to exceed local demand by approximately 30% in Europe and approximately 130% in North America, while LFP capacity is projected to fall short of demand by approximately 45% and approximately 20%, respectively.
Related:
ExxonMobil on Building a Competitive & Resilient North American Graphite Supply Chain
These imbalances become particularly important as LFP adoption accelerates outside China, highlighting the growing mismatch between available production capacity and evolving battery chemistry needs, and reinforcing the importance of assessing regional supply options.
How strong is the US battery supply chain right now?
Azevedo:
The US battery supply chain is strengthening, particularly in cell manufacturing, but significant gaps remain further upstream in cathode and anode materials.
Across North America, announced cell capacity could increase significantly, potentially shifting the region from a cell deficit to a surplus, if projects come online as planned. However, there is still a mismatch in battery chemistry today. Most US cell capacity was focused on nickel-based chemistries in 2025, while LFP capacity, which is particularly important for energy storage, is beginning to scale from approximately 20 GWh in 2025 to a projected nameplate capacity of approximately 260 GWh by 2030.
The larger challenge remains upstream. With China expected to account for most of global cathode and anode material capacity in 2030, North America is expected to remain reliant on imported materials, even as local cell manufacturing expands. That said, if one were to take into account a high supply scenario, based on announced capacity, North America could increase its sufficiency in lithium, nickel and natural graphite by 2035, according to our
Global Materials Perspective 2026
Related:
SPE Names Three Finalists for EV Innovation Award
Is recycling starting to play a bigger role in battery materials?
Azevedo:
Recycling is expected to play an increasingly important role in battery materials supply, particularly after 2030, as more batteries reach the end of their useful lives.
Today, recycling is still largely driven by manufacturing scrap, which is estimated to account for more than 55% of black mass supply in 2026. However, this balance is expected to shift as the first major generations of EV batteries reach end of life. By 2030, end-of-life batteries are projected to account for more than 70% of black mass supply, overtaking production scrap as the main source.
This transition could be an important development for the recycling industry, expanding the availability of recoverable materials and increasing recycling's potential contribution to battery material supply.
What is the one market trend everyone should be paying attention to right now?
Azevedo:
An important trend to watch is the accelerating adoption of LFP batteries beyond China, supported by ongoing technological improvements and growing demand in both electric mobility and battery energy storage systems (BESS).
LFP is already the leading chemistry for BESS, driven by its cost competitiveness, safety, and cycle life. At the same time, advances in 4
- and emerging 5th-generation LFP materials are improving energy density and performance, narrowing the gap with nickel-based chemistries and making LFP increasingly attractive for electric vehicles.
As this chemistry shift accelerates, battery manufacturers and automotive OEMs are increasingly reassessing their production strategies, including how to build greater flexibility into manufacturing footprints and investment decisions to accommodate evolving demand across LFP and nickel-based chemistries.
This shift also has broader implications for battery materials demand and recycling, given LFP's lower recoverable metal value.

title: Evergreen Builds Suez Canal Momentum After Transit
content:
Evergreen Builds Suez Canal Momentum After Transit
Prioritise Us
on Google
Container traffic via the Suez Canal has now surpassed 50% of pre-conflict levels, as Evergreen eyes rerouting loops after a successful transit (Credit: Getty)
Evergreen plans to send more vessels via the Suez Canal, adding to the number of line operators routing container vessels through the Canal
Evergreen successfully dispatched a container vessel via the Suez Canal route on 8 November. Taiwan-based liner operator Evergreen’s 16,556 TEU container vessel, Ever Eon, transited through the canal on 8 November, according to Osama Rabie, the Chairman of the Suez Canal Authority (SCA).
Evergreen has indicated that it intends to send more shipments through the Canal. Evergreen joins a number of ship operators to have rerouted scheduled services via the Suez Canal or to have trialled sailings.
Two other members of the Premier Alliance (the Singapore-based ONE and Yang Ming) have also announced the beginning of scheduled services via the Suez Canal in November.
Maersk and
Hapag-Lloyd
were the first operators to resume sailings via the Suez Canal in early July 2026, when they announced AE15/SE3 Asia-Mediterranean service would return to the Suez Canal. Since then, the return to normal routings has accelerated.
Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have also added a further service (ME1) to the list of routes passing through the Suez Canal, rather than around the Cape of Good Hope. Its ME1 service connects the Middle East and India with Europe, meaning the trans-Suez route is the optimal one for efficiency.
The SCA notes that
, MSC and COSCO have also increased the proportion of their shipments passing through the Suez Canal.
Evergreen sent a container vessel via the Suez Canal route on 8 November 2026 (Credit: Evergreen)
Slow resumption of service
The latest services to be routed via the Suez Canal build on the increasing volume of container shipments passing through the route.
The volume of container shipments passing through the Suez Canal has reached its strongest level since the beginning of the Red Sea crisis began in early 2024. According to data published by the Suez Canal Authority, the amount of container vessels passing through the canal has exceeded 50% of pre-February 2024 levels for the first time.
”During the first two weeks of October, weekly container ship capacity transiting the Suez Canal averaged 753,000 TEU, according to Clarksons Research, compared with 1,457,000 TEU during the same period in 2023. Since the Houthi attacks began in the Red Sea, this is the first time that transits have exceeded 50% of pre-disruption levels," says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO in a research note.
The steady normalisation of services via the
Suez Canal
remains subject to security concerns, and a flare up of security tensions could lead the steadily increasing proportion of seaborne trade flowing through the Canal to reverse.
Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO
Key facts about Suez Canal demand
10-Day Shorter Sea Transit: Reducing Asia-to-Europe voyage times from 36 days via Africa to 26 days via the Suez Canal.
1,290,000 TEU Historical Baseline: Prior to the beginning of Houthi attacks on shipping in November 2023, an average of 1,290,000 TEU of container capacity transited the Suez Canal weekly.
10% Global Capacity Adjustment: The unwinding of the Cape of Good Hope diversion is expected to lower global container shipping demand.
3,300 Nautical Miles Shaved: Shorter routes lower fuel consumption and help carriers meet international carbon reduction targets.
October 2026 Shipping Capacity Rose: Canal transit volumes have exceeded 50% of pre-disruption levels, rising from a low of 141,000 TEU earlier in 2026.
Impact of resumption of Suez Canal trade on boxship demand
The trans-Suez route is the preferred sailing route for many logistics companies and the recovery points to a gradual return to shorter, more predictable Asia-Europe routings. The Suez Canal traditionally acts as a vital maritime corridor between the East and the West, ensuring efficiency across global supply chains.
However, the unwinding of the diversion of routes via the Cape of Good Hope while directing later shipments via the Suez Canal risks creating short-lived capacity and congestion pressures at major destination hubs along the Mediterranean or the northwest European coast, such as Rotterdam or Hamburg.
"We estimate that rerouting away from the Suez Canal increased global container ship demand by about 10%. That increase is now reducing quickly. However, as the return to the Suez Canal has coincided with increased port congestion in Asia, the full effect on supply/demand has yet to be seen," says Rasmussen.
Some 12% of the world's seaborne trade transits through the Suez Canal, according to the SCA.
Strategic Maritime & Logistics Partners
Evergreen Marine Corporation (Liner Operator)
Taiwan-based container shipping line and a major global carrier. Operating a modern fleet of mega-container vessels, the company serves key trade lanes linking Asia, Europe, and the Americas, prioritising route optimization and supply chain reliability across the global maritime network.
BIMCO (International Shipping Association)
The Baltic and International Maritime Council is the world’s largest direct-membership organization for shipowners, charterers, and agents. Representing over 60% of the global merchant fleet, BIMCO provides market intelligence, security advisories, and standardised contracts to streamline international maritime commerce.
Clarksons Research (Maritime Market Intelligence)
A global leader in maritime data and shipping market intelligence. The firm tracks container carrier capacities, port congestion indices, and vessel transit volumes across critical global trade corridors, providing essential market analytics for ocean carriers, financial institutions, and logistics operators.
Suez Canal Authority (Infrastructure Owner)
The state-owned authority managing and maintaining Egypt’s Suez Canal. The SCA oversees structural maintenance, traffic orchestration, and safety protocols for the vital maritime waterway, which facilitates roughly ten percent of all global seaborne trade and links major European and Asian markets.
Port of Rotterdam (Primary Destination Hub)
Europe’s largest seaport, located in the Netherlands. Serving as the primary gateway for containerised freight entering Northwest Europe, the port coordinates massive intermodal rail, barge, and road distribution networks to handle mega-vessel arrivals and mitigate global supply chain bottlenecks.

title: Shipsy: The Role of AI in Delivery Network Planning
content:
Shipsy: The Role of AI in Delivery Network Planning
Prioritise Us
on Google
AI is transforming the logistics industry, creating more efficiency and visibility. Credit: Getty
As logistics continues to navigate disruption, Shipsy aims to close the execution cap across value chains with physical AI, explains CEO Soham Chokshi
Around the world, logistics is becoming more complex, with increasing demands for visibility and efficiency gains.
AI has become an increasingly useful tool to ensure
fleet managers can track
their vehicles at all times and can ensure the safety of their drivers.
Shipsy is an AI-native platform working to increase route optimisation and innovation throughout the logistics industry.
AI-native solutions
Since its foundation, Shipsy has been developing innovative solutions to aid with route optimisation, delivery,
transport management
and more. It has solutions for international logistics, including multi-modal, cross-border shipments, as well as real-time visibility across carriers.
AgentFleet is Shipsy’s digital workforce, with five specialist AI agents that have specific roles, allowing them to execute actions across the logistics chain:
Clara - customer communication
Astra - driver and routing operations
Atlas - control tower
Nexa - financial settlement
Vera - dispute resolution
These agents operate within a guardrailed perimeter to execute an end-to-end workflow, based on their specific roles. Rather than just flagging the issues to the human workforce, these agents can act autonomously, operating on a 24/7 basis.
In September, Shipsy beta-launched ‘Shipsy Brain’, a fine-tuned model purpose-built for logistics.
“Most logistics systems were built to record what happened. But the actual decisions still happen outside the system, in spreadsheets, emails, phone calls and people’s heads,” Shipsy CEO, Soham Chokshi explains.
Soham Chokshi, CEO of Shipsy
“That’s what we’re changing with Shipsy Brain, our fine-tuned model purpose-built for logistics. It builds on insights from more than five billion shipments, 50 billion operational events and one billion decisions processed through the Shipsy platform.”
The model combines specialised open-source models with data generated across Shipsy’s platform. This helps the agents understand the relationships between every cog in the logistics chain, including carriers, routes and financial processes.
It is a direct response to the challenges faced within logistics, using data which includes more than 50 billion operational events which have been recorded across five years, more than 100 billion GPS location pings that are connected with route outcomes and more than three billion hub scans covering shipment movements.
The brain watches live operations in order to identify manual work that can be automated and it learns when a human has corrected its actions.
At a glance
More than five billion shipments have been processed on the platform every year
It has more than 150 global customers
Shipsy operates in more than 30 countries
It has 240 carrier integrations across a connected ecosystem
Shipsy Brain is built off more than 50 billion operational events from across five years
Navigating supply chain complexity
Logistics is a complex environment, becoming more so by increased trade tensions, global disruption and the high amount of vehicles on the road. Alongside this, the demand for safer, more transparent logistics is increasing. As a result, fleet owners are looking for ways to gain full visibility across their operations and explore means of cost and emissions reduction.
Shipsy is an AI-native logistics platform that aims to make operations easier across the entire chain, from postal operations to global FMCG brands. Part of Shipsy’s driving force is using AI to handle repetitive tasks so that humans can focus on
decision-making and customer service
“The goal isn’t to remove humans from logistics,” Soham adds.
“It’s to let machines handle the repetitive investigation, cross-checking and coordination that humans cannot perform at scale.”
The logistics industry is hit by constant disruption, and that is not made easier by the fact that it runs on outdated systems. It runs on outdated systems that track shipments, with platforms adding AI as a bolt-on, rather than properly embedded into planning. The sheer size of the global logistics industry means any technology it uses need to be able to work at scale.
Shipsy combines enterprise TMS and WMS with AI co-workers, making sure that AI is built into the centre of each workflow. Its agents are in place to support the human team, taking on routine tasks and decisions to allow the team members to use their expertise to the full extent.
The goal isn’t to remove humans from logistics. It’s to let machines handle the repetitive investigation, cross-checking and coordination that humans cannot perform at scale.
Soham Chokshi, Shipsy CEO
Shipsy helps with route optimisation and helps transform the logistics industry. Credit: Getty Images
Key Partners
Shipsy is a SaaS-based logistics management platform founded in 2015, headquartered in India. The company provides AI-powered solutions for supply chain visibility, route optimization, and delivery management. Shipsy serves e-commerce, retail, and logistics companies globally, helping them streamline operations, reduce costs, and enhance customer experience through real-time tracking, automated workflows, and predictive analytics for efficient last-mile delivery operations.
DPD (Dynamic Parcel Distribution) is a European parcel delivery network founded in 1977, owned by La Poste's Geopost. Headquartered in France, DPD operates in over 50 countries with approximately 100,000 delivery experts. The company offers time-specific delivery services, parcel tracking, and flexible delivery options. Known for innovation in sustainable delivery solutions, including electric vehicles and carbon-neutral services, DPD serves both business and consumer markets.
Heinkeken
Heineken is a Dutch multinational brewing company founded in 1864 by Gerard Adriaan Heineken in Amsterdam. The world's second-largest brewer, Heineken owns over 300 beer brands across 190+ countries, with its flagship Heineken lager being one of the most recognized global beer brands. The company employs approximately 85,000 people and emphasizes sustainability, responsible drinking, and innovation in brewing technology and marketing.
Kelloggs
Kellogg's is an American multinational food manufacturing company founded in 1906 by Will Keith Kellogg in Battle Creek, Michigan. The company produces cereals, snacks, and convenience foods sold in over 180 countries. Iconic brands include Corn Flakes, Frosted Flakes, Rice Krispies, Pop-Tarts, and Pringles. In 2023, Kellogg's split into two companies: WK Kellogg Co (cereals) and Kellanova (snacks).

title: Volkswagen's new electric SUV is taking over where the ID.4 left off
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Nov 12 2026 - 7:42 am PT
Volkswagen
is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV. The new ID. Tiguan is now rolling off the assembly line and will replace the ID.4 in 2027.
Move over ID.4, here comes the VW ID. Tiguan
The ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the new ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.
Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it.
The new electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.
Volkswagen announced on Thursday that
series production
of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.
“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer said last month after unveiling the new SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”
Volkswagen begins series production of the electric ID. Tiguan (Source: Volkswagen)
The ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.
Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The new design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan (Source: Volkswagen)
Unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the new ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.
In Volkswagen’s words, the new ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan interior (Source: Volkswagen)
Inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s new infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.
Another highlight is the return of physical buttons. After listening to customer feedback from current drivers, Volkswagen added physical buttons under the center display and on the steering wheel for climate control and other vehicle functions.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan Digital Cockpit with Retro Mode (Source: Volkswagen)
To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun new Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.
Drivers can also choose from six classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.
The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:
a rear-wheel-drive version with 140 kW (190 PS) and a 58 kWh battery
a rear-wheel-drive version with 210 kW (286 PS) and a 77 kWh battery
and a 220 kW (299 PS) 4MOTION all-wheel-drive variant, also with a 77 kWh battery.
Depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “new benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).
Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.
After it launches in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.
Volkswagen said prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.
Since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.
Official US prices have not yet been announced. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

title: Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Nov 12 2026 - 6:36 am PT
A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.
The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.
What happened on the 417
OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”
According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.
Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.
Canada keeps catching them
Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:
March 17: B.C. Highway Patrol ticketed a 37-year-old woman on the Trans-Canada Highway during the morning rush: $368 for driving without due care and attention, plus $138 for speeding. She said she had “zoned out.” Police said in-car video showed she was “literally asleep at the wheel.”
July: A witness filmed a Tesla driver asleep behind large sunglasses on the mountain stretch between Golden and Revelstoke, with two kids in the back.
We broke down how Tesla’s driver monitoring missed it
. Revelstoke RCMP followed up with the owner.
August 11: B.C. Highway Patrol ticketed a 45-year-old woman allegedly asleep in a Model Y on Highway 1 in North Vancouver ($368).
August 27: Another driver allegedly asleep in a Tesla on Highway 1 in Langley got the same $368 ticket, plus $81 for not producing a licence.
This isn’t new in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and
criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h
with dangerous driving.
The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas
, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.
And in October, a driver
told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car
in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.
Better FSD, sleepier drivers
A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.
Now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.
Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.
Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.
Tesla’s driver monitoring is too easy to beat
Since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”
In other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.
The penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.
And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.
Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.
The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.
Electrek’s Take
We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.
But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.
The fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.
NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

title: Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?
content:
Electric Motorcycles
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Nov 12 2026 - 4:28 am PT
Honda has been steadily
expanding its electric motorcycle lineup
, but one of its most interesting new models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.
Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year
when the company announced plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.
But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.
Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.
There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.
And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.
So why can’t Americans have nice things?
The UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However,
recent reports
That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.
But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t announced any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.
And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.
In much of Southeast Asia,
scooters are everyday transportation
, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.
Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.
That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.
It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.
Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

title: Spanish IPP deploys automated solar installation platform at 457 MW Texas project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Matrix Renewables is using Terabase Energy’s Terafab V2 automated construction platform at its 457 MW Tormes Solar project in Navarro County, Texas. The system combines robotic module assembly, automated quality inspection, autonomous transport vehicles and digital construction management tools.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
12 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
United States
Utility-scale
The Terafab platform
Spain-based independent power producer (IPP)
Matrix Renewables
is deploying Terafab V2, an automated solar construction platform developed by US-based Terabase Energy, at part of its 457 MW Tormes Solar project in Navarro County, Texas. California-based Solv Energy is serving as an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor on the project.
Terafab V2 combines robotic assembly, AI-assisted quality inspection and autonomous vehicles to streamline module assembly and transportation, shifting labor-intensive construction activities from the solar field to an automated production line installed on-site.
According to Matrix Renewables, PV modules and structural components are delivered to the on-site assembly line, where robotic equipment mounts the modules onto tracker torque tubes. The completed assemblies then pass through an integrated quality inspection system before being transported to their installation locations.
The modular “factory” is designed for rapid deployment and relocation within a construction site. Terabase says the latest version can be moved and set up in approximately four hours, allowing the assembly line to be repositioned as construction progresses.
Following inspection, robotic equipment loads the completed assemblies onto autonomous vehicles, known as rovers, which transport them to designated locations in the solar field. Workers then unload the assemblies and install them onto prepositioned tracker supports.
Terafab V2 incorporates a manufacturing execution system (MES) to coordinate assembly operations, material flows, quality inspections and transportation.
The platform also integrates construction planning, inventory management and logistics software with a digital twin of the project site. AI-assisted tools support workflow optimization and the coordination of automated equipment.
The system’s modular architecture allows multiple assembly lines to operate at a single project, increasing production capacity according to construction requirements.
Terabase says Terafab V2 is designed for continuous operation, with a production cycle of approximately two minutes per assembly. According to the company, each line could achieve an output of around 20 MW per week under continuous operating conditions.
The company claims its automated construction approach can double labor productivity compared with conventional utility-scale PV installation methods. Actual output depends on project configuration, equipment utilization and site conditions.
Terabase has been developing its automated solar construction technology for several years.
pv magazine
reported in August 2022
, the company raised $44 million in a Series B financing round to support its digital and robotic construction platforms. Earlier that year, it had deployed its technology to install 10 MW of capacity at a 400 MW solar project in central Texas.
May 2023
, Terabase announced the launch of its Terafab automated installation system and opened a manufacturing facility in Woodland, California. The company described the plant as a “factory to make factories.”
Later that year, Terabase completed its
first commercial Terafab installation
, using the system to build 17 MW of a 225 MW solar project in Arizona developed by Leeward Renewable Energy, with RES serving as the construction contractor.
The V2 platform represents a further step in the company’s automation strategy. In
April 2026, Terabase told
pv magazine
that the upgraded system had completed field testing and was ready for commercial deployment.
The new version features a more compact factory design, increased automation and faster assembly operations. It is currently optimized for First Solar Series 7 modules and Nextpower trackers, although Terabase plans to expand compatibility with other module and tracker technologies.
Terabase said the first-generation Terafab platform had been used to install approximately 40 MW of tracker-mounted solar capacity across several US projects.
While the current system automates module assembly, inspection, loading and transportation, the final installation of the assembled PV tables onto tracker supports still requires workers. Terabase has said it is developing additional robotics to automate this step in a future version of the platform.

title: Octopus aims to mobilize $600 million for Asian renewables - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Octopus Energy has launched an Asia fund whose first investment backs a Manila developer targeting 450 MW of solar and 350 MWh of battery storage by 2030.
Brian Publicover
12 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
UK-based Octopus Energy has launched the Octopus Asia Electrification Fund, which aims to mobilize $600 million from institutional investors for clean energy projects across Asia.
The fund, managed by
Octopus Energy Generation
, is backed by $50 million from Japanese investors, the company said, without naming them. Octopus announced the fund on Nov. 10 at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, but did not disclose its structure or a target closing date.
Its first investment is in Octali Energy Development, a Manila-based solar and storage developer. Octopus said it will help Octali develop a targeted 450 MW of solar and 350 MWh of battery storage, which it said could supply more than 300,000 Philippine homes a year by 2030. The investment is Octopus’ first in the Philippines, where the company said coal still accounts for more than 60% of electricity. It did not disclose the size of the investment, its stake in Octali or the locations of the projects.
“We’re now combining our experience in renewable energy across the region with capital to help ambitious local developers scale, bring more clean power to consumers, and help build Asia’s clean energy future,” said Zoisa North-Bond, chief executive of Octopus Energy Generation.
Asian pipeline
Beyond the Philippines, the fund will target Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam, investing in solar, onshore wind and storage, as well as microgrids and electric vehicle charging, according to Octopus.
Octopus Energy Generation said it already manages 2 GW of clean energy projects in development in Asia, including investments in solar developers Yotsuya Energy in Japan and Skygreen Energy in South Korea, and offshore wind developer Deep Wind Offshore, which has projects in South Korea. In May 2023, Octopus announced plans to invest GBP 1.5 billion ($1.98 billion) in renewables projects in the Asia-Pacific region by 2027.
Large-scale solar-plus-storage is gaining ground in the Philippines. Meralco PowerGen
inaugurated the first phase
MTerra Solar project
in July, after Huawei
agreed in 2024 to supply 4.5 GWh
of batteries for the project. The country’s fourth green energy auction, which included a category for integrated solar-plus-storage,
awarded 9.4 GW
in September 2025, short of its 10.6 GW goal.

title: Predicting power output from artistic BIPV pixel by pixel - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have developed a model linking artwork colors to power output and potential hot-spot risks in colored BIPV arrays. Simulations of 50 masterpieces show how selectively darkening bright pixels can improve electrical performance.
Lior Kahana
12 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Illustration of BIPV façades displaying Girl with a Pearl Earring
A South Korean research team has developed a novel model to predict power output and hot-spot risk in colored building-integrated PV (c-BIPV) systems featuring artistic images. The researchers modeled PV arrays displaying 50 masterpieces, including Johannes Vermeer’s
Girl with a Pearl Earring
and Vincent van Gogh’s
Café Terrace at Night.
“Unlike a uniformly colored module, an image-based array contains many differently colored cells. Because each color requires a different optical reflection profile, the photocurrent generated by each cell can vary across the array,” corresponding author Hyung-Jun Song told
pv magazine
. “This spatial mismatch can reduce power output and, under certain bypass-diode configurations, expose cells to reverse bias and hot-spot risk.”
The novelty of the research, Song added, lies in directly linking the visual characteristics of a candidate image to the electrical performance and reliability of the entire PV array. “For every pixel, we estimated the minimum-loss selective-reflection spectrum needed to reproduce its color and calculated the resulting photocurrent. We then used equivalent-circuit simulations to evaluate the series-connected array under different bypass-diode configurations,” he explained.
Schematic of an artwork-based colored PV array | Image: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
In its work, the group has converted each of the 50 artworks into a 36 × 36-pixel mosaic, with each of the 1,296 pixels representing an individual series-connected PV cell. They assigned each pixel the average color of its corresponding image region. For each color, they calculated an ideal dual-band selective-reflection spectrum, selecting the reflection-band parameters that most closely reproduced the target color. They then calculated the photocurrent generated from the sunlight transmitted through the colored layer, accounting for the underlying cell’s wavelength-dependent internal quantum efficiency.
Using a single-diode equivalent circuit calibrated to commercial TOPCon cells, they modeled each cell’s current-voltage characteristics at 300 K. They simulated the fully series-connected array in LTspice. The simulations compared configurations without bypass diodes and with one diode protecting between one and 36 cells, assessing maximum power output and the number of cells operating under reverse bias at the maximum power point as an indicator of potential hot-spot risk.
“One of the most surprising findings was that the overall brightness or colorfulness of an image does not necessarily determine its photovoltaic performance. Instead, the spatial distribution of brightness plays a much more important role,” Song said about the results. For example, the simulated array displaying
Café Terrace at Night
achieved 91.7% of the power output of an equivalent black reference array without bypass diodes, compared with 74.3% for
Girl with a Pearl Earring
“We found that even a small number of extremely bright pixels can limit the power output of an entire series-connected PV array,” the researcher added. “We also identified an interesting trade-off associated with bypass diodes: installing more diodes can improve power output, but it may simultaneously increase reverse-bias conditions and the associated hot-spot risk.”
Illustration of BIPV façades displaying
Café Terrace at Night
Girl with a Pearl Earring
, installing one bypass diode per cell increased normalized power from 74.3% to 84.4% of the black reference array’s output, a 13.6% relative improvement. However, 24 of the 1,296 cells entered reverse bias at the maximum power point. Selectively darkening those 24 pixels instead raised normalized power to 84.8% without bypass diodes, while avoiding reverse-biased cells under the simulated conditions.
“Based on these findings, we developed a screening framework that classifies artistic images according to their expected power performance and hot-spot risk, using only two image-derived parameters: the brightest pixel and the overall brightness variation,” the academic added. “The framework was further examined using additional images, demonstrating its potential to assess the electrical suitability of candidate artwork without requiring a full circuit-level simulation for every image.”
Concluding, Song said that his team is planning a few follow-up studies. These include incorporating measured reflectance spectra into a more realistic optical model, expanding the image database, and developing an AI-assisted tool to assess uploaded images and suggest modifications that improve power output and reduce hot-spot risks while preserving their appearance.
The article “
Prediction Model for Power Output and Hot-spot Risk in Colored Photovoltaic Arrays with Artistic Image
” has appeared in
. Researchers from South Korea’s
Seoul National University of Science and Technology
Gachon University
have participated in the study.

content:
Markets & Policy
Sweden plans to launch a voluntary database for solar inverters, battery storage systems and bidirectional EV charging equipment in 2027, replacing its existing pre-assessment system for new listings. The database will provide standardized technical documentation to support grid connection assessments by network operators.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Inverters
Sweden is preparing to replace its existing list of pre-assessed solar and battery inverters with a new digital database in 2027, according to Swedish energy industry association Energiföretagen Sverige.
The new system, called Rikta Rätt 2.0, will provide standardized technical information on inverters used in solar photovoltaic and battery energy storage installations, helping electricity distribution system operators (DSOs) assess grid connection applications.
“The basic requirements for inclusion in the new database will be limited to contact information, manufacturer name and type designation. However, inclusion will not constitute an approval or demonstrate compliance with technical requirements,” a spokesperson for Energiföretagen Sverige told
pv magazine
. “The database will provide relevant technical information and supporting documentation for each model. Manufacturers must provide supporting documentation where required, for example certificates when claiming conformity with a particular standard.”
Rikta Rätt 2.0 will not require additional product testing solely for inclusion in the database. Technical information will generally be supported by certificates, test reports and other documentation from existing testing and conformity assessment procedures.
“The approach is similar to the current Rikta Rätt process, but more transparent: the database will show technical information and supporting documentation on which the network operator can base its assessment.,” the spokesperson added. “The categories and associated requirements are still being finalized, but the documentation requirements are expected to remain close to those applied in the current Rikta Rätt.”
Inverter models already included in the current Rikta Rätt list will remain on
the PDF version of the list
CSV version
will be removed from the Energiföretagen Sverige’s website at the end of 2027.
“There will be no automatic migration to Rikta Rätt 2.0. Manufacturers and importers will need to apply for inclusion in the new database and provide the information and documentation required for the relevant categories,” the spokesperson specified.
According to Energiföretagen Sverige, the transition will not change the existing grid connection approval process for solar PV installations, as individual network operators will retain responsibility for assessing compliance.
“The final compliance assessment is already carried out by individual network operators, but we understand the concern about potentially inconsistent requirements. Grid conditions vary, and the aim is to provide a common structure while allowing requirements to be adapted to actual conditions. Compared to the current Rikta Rätt, the new approach should result in less restrictive and more appropriately targeted requirements. It will be sufficient for an inverter to meet the requirements relevant to actual grid conditions, at a level of detail manageable for manufacturers and network operators,” the spokesperson stated. “We do not expect approval times to increase significantly once the new procedure is established. Instead of checking whether a product is listed in Rikta Rätt, network operators will check a small number of relevant data points in the Rikta Rätt 2.0 database.”
Cybersecurity is not currently planned as a separate category within Rikta Rätt 2.0, although Energiföretagen Sverige may consider adding further categories as regulations evolve.
“Manufacturers and network operators are subject to an increasingly extensive cybersecurity regulatory framework. Cybersecurity is already part of the requirements relevant to CE marking, with requirements will become more extensive in the coming years. Verifying actual compliance as part of a product assessment remains challenging, particularly where conformity can be demonstrated through manufacturer self-assessment,” the spokesperson added. “We will continue to follow regulatory developments and consider whether additional categories should be incorporated into the Rikta Rätt 2.0 database in the future.”
The voluntary Rikta Rätt 2.0 database is scheduled to open in early 2027, while new listings under the existing system will cease in September 2027.

title: Chasing the sun: Feasible CO₂ supply as a gateway to low-cost e-fuel production - pv magazine Global
content:
Chasing the sun: Feasible CO₂ supply as a gateway to low-cost e-fuel production
Producing fuels from captured CO2 requires large amounts of renewable electricity, yet major carbon sources and the best wind or solar sites are often far apart. This creates a supply chain dilemma: should e-fuel producers build facilities next to the carbon source, or transport the molecular CO2 or possibly biomass to regions where renewable electricity is lower in cost?
For e-methanol, produced with hydrogen from renewable electricity and reacted with CO2, the answer comes down to logistics. Recent modeling from LUT University reveals how to best combine these ingredients by comparing transport options, production locations, and alternative carbon sources. Three research articles are presented in more detail, focusing on relative infrastructure options, transport options for CO2 also in dependence of renewable energy resources, and transporting biomass instead of biogenic CO2.
Bringing carbon to affordable electricity
Finland is a region rich in both wind energy and biogenic as well as industrial CO2 sources. Yet these resources are on the opposite sides of the country. In a comparison of transport options connecting Finnish pulp and paper mills with the best wind resources 370-590 km away, moving CO2 by pipeline results in the lowest methanol costs. Conversely, moving hydrogen or electricity from wind-rich regions directly to the CO2 source makes methanol 5-15% more expensive. Savings from producing hydrogen and methanol at sites with best renewable resources outweigh the cost of transporting CO2.
For longer distances, besides pipelines, shipping also opens access to sunnier regions with even lower renewable electricity costs. In another recent analysis, researchers compared using 2.24 million metric tons of CO2 annually from the Finnish pulp and paper industry to produce methanol locally in Finland versus methanol production in solar-rich Spain.
In 2050, methanol produced in Spain with Finnish CO2 costs about €63 /MWh, compared to €75 /MWh in Finland, including capture, conditioning, transport, electricity costs, and fuel production. Spain’s cost advantage, driven entirely by low-cost solar PV, which might supply most electricity for e-fuel synthesis in 2030, grows from about 7% in 2030 to 16% in 2050. The massive reduction in costs for solar electricity and subsequently hydrogen can easily compensate for the expenses associated with transporting CO2 from Finland.
For these long-range routes, shipping is the cheapest option, avoiding the high capital investments needed for pipelines. On land, existing railways can compete with pipelines if the rail infrastructure is present, while trucks become cost-prohibitive at large volumes.
Modeled CO2 routes from Finland to fuel-production sites. Image: LUT University
Sequestration synergies
These same industrial CO2 sources can also supply carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) projects in Norway or Iceland. For example, Norway’s shorter transport distance offsets its higher injection costs in the modeled chains. Permanently sequestrating CO2 from biogenic sources can provide carbon dioxide removal (CDR) if the stored volumes exceed the supply chain’s emissions. Conversely, producing methanol would qualify as carbon capture and utilization (CCU): the carbon eventually returns to the atmosphere when the fuel is used. Methanol is expected to evolve as a valuable platform carrier service demands in the maritime industry, chemical industry, and maybe food supply, so that methanol-to-X routes as part of a Power-to-X Economy raise attention.
Moving biomass instead of CO2
What if we move biomass and capture the CO2 at the destination for e-methanol synthesis? A recent study compared importing wood pellets from Finland to Germany or Spain, to transporting molecular CO2. e-Methanol produced from transported CO2 or transported and combusted biomass is then compared to e-methanol produced with CO2 from direct air capture in Finland, Germany, and Spain. Biomass imported from Finland can be used to supply power plants, combined heat and power plants, or cement plants. Pellets carry both usable energy and carbon. Transporting them to Spain in 2050 costs about €18 /tCO2 captured at the destination, drastically undercutting the €73 /tCO2 transportation chain.
However, final methanol costs completely reverse this advantage. In the 2050 Spanish scenario, using imported pellets used in power or combined heat and power plants with subsequent CO2 capture yields methanol at €88-93 /MWh, compared to just €65 /MWh using transported CO2. The combined costs of pellet purchase, conversion, and carbon capture outweigh the cheaper transport, even when factoring in revenue from the generated electricity and heat.
Cement production offers a unique cost advantage because the imported pellets supply both kiln heat and carbon for methanol. This setup lowers methanol costs, provided pellet and kiln costs are charged to the cement side, while methanol only covers pellet transport, its share of capture costs, and final methanol synthesis. In Spain, the cost of e-methanol produced from the cement plant’s biogenic CO2 falls from €86 /MWh in 2030 to €55 /MWh in 2050. For comparison, the 2050 cost is €65 /MWh with CO2 shipped directly from Finland, €93 /MWh when CO2 is captured from imported pellets burned in a power plant, and €88 /MWh via a combined heat and power plant. Because the kiln also releases mineral CO2 from limestone, emissions are strictly separated: only the biogenic CO2 from the pellets counts towards e-methanol, while the limestone CO2 is assigned to sequestration.
How does this compare to direct air capture in solar-rich regions?
Direct air capture offers a geographically independent option. Assuming projected technology improvements and cost reductions, methanol produced using locally captured atmospheric CO2 reaches about €63 /MWh in Spain in 2050, which competes with the €65 /MWh cost of methanol produced from imported Finnish industrial CO2. Background on the energy transition dynamics is related in more detail for analyzes for Spain and Finland, and the detailed industrial CO2 availability from Southeast Finland.
The primary takeaway for the PV sector is clear: low-cost solar PV justifies moving molecular or embedded CO2 over long distances. Determining the optimal supply route requires evaluating the entire fuel production cost, while accounting for reliable industrial CO2 supplies, sustainable biomass, and local demand for useful heat. By connecting these dots, regions with different energy profiles can share the economic opportunities of renewable fuel production.
Authors: Sina Namdarpour Naghani, Tansu Galimova, Dominik Keiner, and Christian Breyer
This article is part of a monthly column by the LUT University.
Research at LUT University encompasses various analyses related to power, heat, transport, industry, desalination, and carbon dioxide removal options. Power-to-X research is a core topic at the university, integrated into the focus areas of Planetary Resources, Business and Society, Digital Revolution, and Energy Transition. Solar energy plays a key role in all research aspects.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own, and do not necessarily reflect those held by pv magazine.

title: Viessmann launches propane ground-source heat pump compatible with PVT systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy uses R290 refrigerant and delivers heating capacities ranging from 6 kW to 16 kW, with a maximum flow temperature of 70 C and a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of up to 5.5.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy (ie) heat pump
German heating specialist
Viessmann
has launched the Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy (ie), a new inverter-driven brine-to-water heat pump designed for indoor installation in new and existing residential buildings.
The system uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and features an integrated active safety system for refrigerant management.
The heat pump is available in three versions, designated 06, 12 and 16, with modulating heating capacity ranges of 1.8 kW to 9.3 kW, 3.2 kW to 12.2 kW, and 3.2 kW to 15.6 kW, respectively. Their nominal heating outputs at a brine inlet temperature of 0 C and a heating water temperature of 35 C (B0/W35) are 3.25 kW, 5.26 kW and 6.16 kW, with corresponding coefficients of performance (COPs) of 4.7, 5.0 and 5.0.
All three models measure 1,018 mm × 600 mm × 680 mm. The smallest version weighs 167 kg, while the two larger models weigh 185 kg each. The floor-standing units require an installation footprint of approximately 0.5 m2.
Viessmann said the system achieves an SCOP of up to 5.5 in low-temperature applications, with seasonal space-heating efficiency of up to 212% and an A+++ energy efficiency rating.
The heat pump delivers flow temperatures of up to 70 C, making it suitable for heating system retrofits as well as new installations, according to the manufacturer. The smallest model has a sound power level of 34 dB(A) under European Union Energy-related Products (ErP) testing conditions.
The system can also be connected to photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) collectors, which can serve as an alternative heat source to conventional geothermal boreholes while simultaneously generating electricity. Existing boreholes can be reused when replacing older ground-source heat pumps.
Viessmann said up to four units can be connected in a cascade configuration, providing a combined heating capacity of up to 64 kW. A single universal controller manages the entire cascade.
The heat pump incorporates the company’s One Base Intelligence control platform, which enables integration with photovoltaic systems, battery storage, electric vehicle charging equipment and compatible third-party devices. Its integrated energy management system supports weather-based optimization and dynamic electricity tariffs, while the ViCare app enables remote monitoring and control.
An optional natural cooling function uses the relatively low ground temperature to provide indoor cooling during summer. According to Viessmann, the feature can reduce indoor temperatures by up to 3 C.
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy is available for order, with deliveries scheduled to begin on Nov. 30, 2026. A compact version with an integrated domestic hot water storage tank is expected to become available in April 2027.
