Markets & Policy
Politicians in the Netherlands have supported calls for a framework covering the connection of balcony solar systems to be drafted before the spring of next year.
Patrick Jowett
12 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Netherlands
Residential
The House of Representatives in the Netherlands, the country’s lower house of parliament, has passed a motion requiring the government to develop a framework for balcony solar by the spring of next year.
, raised by Democrats 66 (D66) politician Felix Klos, says that while 35% of Dutch households have now installed solar panels, permitting balcony solar would offer more households the opportunity to generate their own electricity and reduce their energy bills.
It calls on the government to develop a framework that allows for the safe connection of balcony solar and to identify which relevant standards and regulations would need to be amended to facilitate the move.
The motion received broad cross-party support, with representatives from 12 political groups voting in favour.
There are 17 parliamentary groups represented in the Netherlands’ House of Representatives in total, with D66 holding the most seats. The party leads a minority government alongside the People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) and Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA).
Klos’ motion cited Germany as an example of a country that permits balcony solar. Around
of PV capacity added in Germany last year came from new plug-in systems.
The United Kingdom became one of the latest countries to
legalise balcony solar
in August for customers in England, Scotland and Wales. A month later, Greece
permitted plug-in balcony solar
solar up to 800 W and standalone batteries for the first time.
Last month, a group of Green Party politicians in Norway, who do not form part of the ruling government, put forward a proposal to make it possible to
connect plug-in solar and batteries
that meet established safety requirements by the end of 2027.

Markets & Policy
Kazakhstan is proposing a new mechanism allowing renewable energy generators to sell electricity to the country’s single buyer after at least 36 months under bilateral contracts. The measure aims to reduce offtake risks, improve revenue certainty and make projects more attractive to investors and lenders.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Utility-scale
Kazahkstan’s Minister of Energy Erlan Qūdaibergenūly Aqkenjenov
Kazakhstan
is working to improve its regulatory framework for renewable energy power purchase agreements (PPAs) in a bid to attract more investors and lenders. The proposed changes aim to increase contractual certainty, reduce investment risks and facilitate financing for new wind and solar projects.
Under the proposed amendments, power generation facilities that have supplied electricity under bilateral contracts for at least 36 months would be eligible to switch to selling their output to the country’s single electricity purchaser, the Financial Settlement Center for Renewable Energy Support (RFC), a subsidiary of Kazakhstan’s national grid operator, Kegoc JSC.
The mechanism would provide generators with an alternative offtake arrangement if their existing bilateral PPAs expire or their buyers stop purchasing electricity. By reducing counterparty and electricity sales risks, the proposed framework aims to improve revenue predictability, boost investor confidence and facilitate project financing.
However, the proposed provisions do not specify the pricing arrangements, contract duration or other terms governing electricity sales to RFC. These details will be critical in determining whether the mechanism improves project bankability.
The government is also preparing to introduce competitive auctions for energy storage capacity.
The planned auction framework is expected to provide greater clarity for private investment in energy storage. However, key details such as procurement volumes, contract structures, technical requirements and implementation timelines, have yet to be confirmed.
Kazakhstan’s pipeline of large-scale solar projects reached around
900 MW at the end of October
, according to government figures.
The country’s installed solar capacity reached
in April, when total renewable energy capacity exceeded 3.7 GW. Renewables currently account for 8.5% of Kazakhstan’s electricity mix, according to government figures.
Kazakhstan aims to install at least 8.4 GW of new renewable energy capacity by 2035, including approximately 1.8 GW of solar.

Markets & Policy
Japan has published its last application deadlines for feed-in tariff (FIT) and feed-in premium (FIP) support before ground-mounted commercial solar closes to new projects.
Brian Publicover
12 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Japan’s Agency for Natural Resources and Energy (ANRE) has set Dec. 11 as the deadline for new and amended FIT and FIP certification applications for solar of 10 kW and above, wind, hydro, and geothermal projects seeking approval in fiscal 2026, which ends March 31, 2027.
The agency said that, following a review by the Procurement Price Calculation Committee in fiscal 2025, ground-mounted solar of 10 kW and above will be excluded from FIT and FIP support from fiscal 2027, making this the final year for new certification in the category.
Applicants must submit grid-connection agreement documents with their applications, and projects without a connection agreement by the deadline cannot be certified this fiscal year. The agency noted that utilities take a standard eight to nine months to respond to connection studies and contract applications for high-voltage and extra-high-voltage connections.
Projects subject to environmental impact assessment can apply without proof that the scoping procedure has begun, provided they consult their regional economy bureau first and submit that proof by Jan. 29, 2027. Changes to the operator name, equipment category, output, or site after an application is filed require withdrawal and reapplication, subject to the same deadline.
Applications to
move existing FIT projects to FIP
are not bound by the deadline, and projects in FIP auctions, which cover solar of 250 kW and above, follow the auction schedule instead.
The deadline for solar below 10 kW is Jan. 5, 2027, and for biomass Nov. 27. The Japan Photovoltaic Energy Association (JPEA) published the notice on Nov. 9, saying it expects more applications than usual because this is the category’s final year.
signaled in December 2025
that it could end FIT and FIP support for large ground-mounted solar. The agency has since
proposed four categories of non-rooftop solar
that would keep priority support, including solar on government-owned land and solar carports, with rules due to take effect April 1, 2027.
Larger ground-mounted projects compete for FIP support through auctions. Japan’s 29th solar auction, the second round of fiscal 2026,
allocated 38.2 MW
against an auction volume of 115 MW and a ceiling price of JPY 9.60 ($0.06)/kWh. The previous round allocated 89.2 MW at an average final price of JPY 6.74/kWh.

title: Nuclear fusion reactor exhaust gets world’s first dipole divertor tech
content: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has selected OpenStar Technologies and Columbia University to design the world’s first exhaust system for a levitated dipole fusion reactor.Commercial nuclear fusion relies on trapping superheated gas—known as plasma—inside magnetic fields. However, every reactor must safely clear away heat and stray particles before they melt the machine’s interior walls. Typical fusion devices solve this using a “divertor,” which guides escaping plasma onto cooled target plates.No divertor has ever been built for a levitated dipole. Unlike conventional doughnut-shaped reactors that surround plasma with massive external magnets, a levitated dipole floats a single superconducting magnet inside a vacuum chamber. This mimics the natural magnetic fields of planets like Earth and Jupiter. Removing physical support struts eliminates a major pathway for heat to leak out, keeping the plasma stable.“The magnetic dipole is an elegant and remarkably simple fusion concept that remains largely unexplored,” said Prof. Ben Zhu, an assistant professor at Columbia Engineering. “A viable exhaust solution is among the most pressing challenges facing any fusion energy system, so what we learn here will contribute directly to the broader pursuit of commercial fusion power.”Modeling the magnetic edgeOver the next 12 months, researchers will map how heat and particles behave at the edge of a dipole’s magnetic field. This geometry creates a true magnetic field null, known as an X-point. It forces engineers to look beyond standard reactor models.To do this, Columbia will pair two advanced software tools: TokaMaker and an open-source edge-modeling code called Hermes-3. The team will test their simulations against real-world data from OpenStar’s existing New Zealand prototype, Junior. In February, OpenStar used this $10 million machine to levitate a 0.5-ton magnet inside a five-meter vacuum chamber, successfully confining plasma heated to over one million degrees Celsius.“Working together with OpenStar we will investigate how to extend our basic physics knowledge to modeling tools,” said Dr Christopher Hansen, a Columbia research scientist who leads TokaMaker’s development.To debut on TahiThe project also marks a reunion for dipole pioneers. Columbia previously ran the original Levitated Dipole Experiment with MIT, where OpenStar’s Chief Science Officer, Dr Darren Garnier, served as chief experimentalist. He will lead the new effort alongside OpenStar Principal Scientist Dr Jerome Guterl.Their final divertor design will debut on OpenStar’s next machine, Tahi. Built to achieve fusion-relevant conditions, Tahi will initially produce neutrons for medical radioisotopes, serving as a stepping stone toward grid-scale fusion power plants.“We are excited to combine Columbia’s outstanding expertise in edge plasma modeling with the lessons learned from decades of tokamak divertor research to develop power and particle exhaust solutions for Tahi and future dipoles,” concluded Guterl.The partnership is backed by the DOE’s Innovation Network for Fusion Energy (INFUSE). This year, the program is distributing $8.5 million across 28 joint projects between private companies, national laboratories, and universities. OpenStar secured the grant through its American subsidiary, OpenStar USA. The company also won a second INFUSE award this round to develop plasma diagnostics with the University of California, San Diego.

title: MIT engineers copy leaf veins to build impact-resistant materials
content: Advancement in various fields hinges on the best quality materials. Now, a new class of “scale-rich metamaterials” has been designed by introducing controlled disorder inspired by natural networks such as leaf vasculature and dragonfly wing veins. Engineers have spent decades chasing mathematical perfection when designing synthetic “metamaterials,” mimicking identical microscopic building blocks to create rigid honeycombs and lattices. A new collaboration between MIT and Northeastern University just proved that a little chaos works much better.Physical tests proved these irregular materials resist impacts better, offer tunable stiffness, and protect fragile embedded objects.This technology could advance the development of safer sports helmets and lightweight body armor. It may also enable precision acoustic lenses that control sound waves and vibrations with high accuracy.Little disorder to make synthetic materialsThe research introduces “scale-rich metamaterials.” These synthetic structures abandon uniform grids for messy, sprawling physical networks modeled after leaf vasculature, neural connections, and even the internet.Uniform metamaterials share a weak spot. When a single cell in a repeating lattice cracks or punctures, the surrounding identical cells immediately follow suit, causing a chain-reaction collapse. MIT associate professor Carlos Portela and his team wanted to cut this localized failure, so they teamed up with Northeastern physicist Albert-László Barabási, a pioneer in network science.Barabási spent his career mapping invisible webs — from social media links to financial markets — to see how networks resist collapse. Together, the researchers turned those abstract mathematical rules into tangible, physical matter.The team wrote an algorithm that generates a virtual blueprint for a material without using a single repeating pattern. The program picks a random point in space and draws a line across the entire domain. The press release explained that it then picks a second random point and draws a line that stops the moment it hits the first line or an outer edge. Repeating this process thousands of times creates a dense, web-like architecture of intersecting support beams in wildly varying sizes and thicknesses.The team developed an algorithm to virtually generate a network of beams with the constraints of a physical material. Here, the network of beams creates the MIT logo.Impact-proof metamaterialsScientists can customize a material‘s stiffness simply by adjusting two parameters in their algorithm: the thickness of the initial line and how quickly subsequent lines get thinner. After simulating these variations, the researchers 3D-printed credit-card-sized polymer samples with interconnecting beams ranging from microns to centimeters.Further, physical tests confirmed that these chaotic networks outperform usual ordered materials across the board. The scale-rich designs absorbed sudden, violent impacts without buckling, offered a massive range of tunable stiffness, and successfully cushioned delicate objects embedded deep inside them.“This is a completely new way of thinking for metamaterials,” Portela said. “Unlocking this network design for materials really frees us to think of new microstructures and mechanical benefits that haven’t been possible before.”In practical applications, manufacturers could soon use the algorithm to print next-generation sports helmets, lightweight body armor, and precision acoustic lenses that focus sound waves and vibrations with unprecedented control.The findings were published in the journal Nature.

title: Solar-powered drone with 30-hour endurance makes first flight in China
content: China’s first commercial-grade solar-powered drone has completed its maiden flight in the country’s northwest, where it took off, climbed, circled, and landed safely.The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation’s 11th Research Institute developed the aircraft, called Light Cavalry. Powered entirely by solar energy, Light Cavalry has a maximum design endurance of 30 hours. The institute developed the aircraft for commercial missions that require sustained low-altitude coverage, such as inspecting infrastructure and surveying land. The maiden flight tested its controls, avionics, and energy storage system, as well as its stability and handling.A solar aircraft built for commercial payloadsLight Cavalry measures 10.5 feet long and has a 26-foot wingspan. It has a takeoff weight of 99 pounds and a service ceiling of 23,000 feet. The aircraft can carry more than 11 pounds of equipment.Its payload can be swapped to suit different assignments. The aircraft can carry electro-optical instruments for observation, communications equipment, or detection systems. That gives operators the option to use the same airframe for jobs ranging from land surveys to ecological monitoring.The developer said all systems were functioning normally after landing. The reported tests covered the aircraft’s behavior from takeoff through landing, with 30 hours specified as its maximum design endurance.A vehicle-mounted launcher replaces the runwayThe drone uses a vehicle-mounted takeoff system and takes about 20 minutes to prepare on the ground. Launching without a fixed runway allows crews to work in places where airfields are scarce, including mountainous regions, remote coastlines and wilderness areas.The developer sees potential uses in disaster assessment, water resource monitoring and surveys of coastlines and ports. For infrastructure operators, long endurance could help crews cover more of an inspection area in a single flight. The launch system would also allow crews to choose a departure point closer to the area they need to survey.Smaller solar drones face tighter power constraintsMuch of the development work on solar-powered drones has focused on large and ultra-large aircraft. Those platforms have mainly served as research aircraft or high-altitude pseudo-satellites. Smaller aircraft could serve a wider range of commercial jobs closer to the ground, but their size complicates the task of powering them entirely with sunlight. A smaller airframe offers less surface area for solar panels, limiting how much electricity the aircraft can generate. At the same time, the structure, avionics and energy storage equipment still account for a substantial share of its weight. Improvements in materials, motors and energy storage could help narrow the gap between what the panels generate and what the aircraft needs to stay aloft. The institute expects Light Cavalry to fill a gap in the market for long-endurance, low-altitude aircraft. It sees the solar design as a way to extend flight times and reduce operational carbon emissions on missions that require sustained coverage over large areas.

title: Elephant trunk-inspired robots bend, grip, and team up for tough tasks
content: Researchers at Colorado State University have developed flexible robots inspired by elephant trunks that can bend, grip objects, and connect with other machines. The robots use a structural design called tensegrity, in which rigid rods are held together by tensioned cables rather than fixed joints.The construction allows them to collapse, bend, and change shape while using gripping claws at both ends of their tube-like bodies to manipulate objects or attach to other robots.The technology could eventually enable teams of robots to support space exploration and other complex tasks.Shape-shifting robotic teamsThe system combines a flexible body with mechanical claws, allowing individual robots to operate independently or assemble into larger configurations.The technology addresses a limitation in existing modular robots, which typically use rigid components that restrict their ability to adapt to different environments and tasks. The researchers aim to combine the flexibility of soft robots with the reconfigurability of modular robotic systems.The new machines use a structural design called tensegrity, in which rigid rods are held together by a network of tensioned cables rather than being permanently fixed to one another. This arrangement allows the robot’s body to bend, stretch, collapse, and change shape while maintaining its structural integrity.Joint-free, tentacle-like bodies feature claws at both ends to grip objects and connect with other robots.Unlike conventional robotic arms, which rely on fixed joints to control movement, the tube-like machines have flexible bodies that can deform continuously. They also feature mechanical gripping claws at both ends, allowing them to grasp objects and connect with other robots.The dual-claw arrangement is central to the system’s modular design. Individual robots can use their claws to attach, creating larger structures without relying on magnetic connections. This mechanical attachment approach also helps reduce alignment problems when multiple units connect.Once joined, the robots can form different configurations, including chains, loops, and branching structures. Each arrangement offers different possibilities for movement and manipulation, allowing the collective to adapt its physical structure to the requirements of a task.The researchers demonstrated that individual units could perform manipulation and locomotion independently, while connected groups could coordinate their movements to transport objects. The machines also demonstrated multimodal locomotion, using different movement strategies to navigate varied environments.Another capability is loco-manipulation, which combines movement and object handling. Rather than relying on separate mechanisms for navigating terrain and manipulating objects, the robots can use their flexible bodies and gripping claws to perform both functions. Their ability to bend around objects could also help them lift and carry loads of different sizes.Robots prepare for autonomyThe team tested the robots across laboratory and real-world scenarios, including natural landscapes. These experiments explored how different configurations could support coordinated object handling, transportation, and movement across challenging terrain.According to the team, developing the system required overcoming several engineering challenges, particularly in selecting motors. The actuators needed to be compact enough to fit within the robots while providing sufficient power and reliability for different movements. The team also tested multiple structural configurations to determine how the machines performed during practical trials.Despite the demonstrations, the robots are not yet fully autonomous. They currently require human piloting for most operations, although the researchers have demonstrated that two units can independently locate one another and establish a connection.Future development will focus on improving their autonomy, increasing operating speeds, and enabling them to work alongside humans with less supervision. The researchers also envision deploying larger groups of the machines, potentially involving tens or hundreds of interconnected units.Such robotic collectives could travel to a designated location before rearranging themselves into configurations suited to specific operations. Potential applications include manufacturing, space exploration and search-and-rescue missions, where robots may need to navigate unpredictable environments, manipulate objects and adapt to changing requirements.Researchers said that by combining a compliant tensegrity structure with mechanical docking mechanisms, the system offers an alternative to robots built around fixed geometries. It could provide a foundation for multifunctional robotic teams capable of changing both their physical arrangement and how they move to tackle different tasks.

title: World's largest artificial reef: SS United States sinks near Florida
content: The historic SS United States sank off the coast of Destin, Florida, on Wednesday, marking the end of its 74-year journey and the beginning of a new role as an artificial reef in the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long vessel, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, will now rest on the seabed and provide a new habitat for marine life.The sinking operation began Wednesday afternoon, with the vessel deployed at approximately 2:40 p.m. ET. The process of flooding the ship started shortly before 5 p.m. After several hours, the ocean liner finally reached the seafloor at around 10 p.m.The ship will rest at a depth of approximately 180 feet, with its upper decks about 55 feet below the water’s surface. The site is expected to become a major diving destination and is being described as the world’s largest artificial reef.Historic ocean liner completes its final voyageLaunched in 1952, the SS United States made history during its maiden voyage by setting a transatlantic speed record. The American-built ocean liner carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic during its 17 years of service before being retired in 1969.After its retirement, the vessel remained docked in Philadelphia for decades. Several owners explored plans to preserve and restore the historic ship, but maintaining the aging vessel became increasingly expensive.In 2021, port authorities increased their daily dockage fee to $1,700. The non-profit SS United States Conservancy could no longer afford the growing costs, making it difficult to continue preservation efforts.Florida county purchased ship for $1 millionIn 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa County purchased the vessel for $1 million to convert it into an artificial reef. The project aims to create an underwater habitat that can support several marine species.Officials expect the structure to attract fish such as red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel, and tuna. Its size and location could also make it an important attraction for recreational divers visiting Florida’s Gulf Coast.Before the sinking, Susan Gibbs, president and co-founder of the SS United States Conservancy, explained how the project would preserve part of the vessel’s legacy.“She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat, so that, combined with the land-based museum and visitor experience, will honor her history in a deeply moving way.”Ship’s designer had a personal connectionGibbs also has a family connection to the ocean liner. Her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the SS United States and played a major role in bringing the historic vessel to life.She recalled his deep attachment to the ship and how he followed its journeys across the Atlantic.“His relationship with the ship was, I would say, a full-bore obsession. He would joke that he loved the SS United States a thousand times more than my grandmother. He would see the ship off every time she set sail for Europe, and be one of the first to greet her on her return.”The ship’s transformation into an artificial reef will give it a new purpose after decades of uncertainty over its future. A land-based museum and visitor experience are also planned to help preserve its history for future generations.

title: 9V-powered coating uses tiny cracks to kill over 80% of bacteria
content: Researchers at Flinders University have developed an electrically activated antibacterial coating that uses microscopic cracks in its surface to help destroy dangerous bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant strains.The flexible material combines liquid gallium, a metal that melts near room temperature, with carbon nanotubes. When the coating dries, tiny cracks naturally form across its surface. Rather than weakening the material, these networks create electrical hotspots that enhance its antibacterial activity.In laboratory tests, a one-minute electrical stimulation using a standard 9-volt battery killed more than 80% of bacterial cells within three hours, according to the researchers.The findings could eventually support smart wound dressings, flexible medical devices and wearable technologies designed to help prevent infections without relying solely on antibiotics.Cracks create electrical hotspotsThe international research team, led by scientists at Flinders University’s Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory, developed the coating to generate an antibacterial response when activated by a small electrical charge.As the liquid gallium and carbon nanotube mixture dried, microscopic cracks formed naturally across its surface. The researchers found that these structures concentrated electrical activity into tiny hotspots, helping amplify the material’s ability to damage bacterial cells.Electrical stimulation increased stress inside the bacteria, contributing to cellular damage and death. The coating could also generate plasma, an energised gas that produces reactive molecules known to suppress bacterial growth.This combination of electrical and plasma-related effects gives the material its antibacterial properties. The researchers say the cracks can be deliberately incorporated into the coating rather than treated as unwanted defects.Associate Professor Vi-Khanh Truong from Flinders University’s College of Medicine and Public Health and the Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute said the findings challenge conventional engineering approaches.“Instead of seeing cracks as defects, we’ve demonstrated they can be designed into materials to create useful functions,” Truong said.Testing against resistant bacteriaThe researchers tested the coating against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Both bacteria can cause serious infections, particularly in healthcare settings and vulnerable patients.Following just one minute of electrical stimulation, more than 80% of bacterial cells were dead within three hours. Laboratory tests also indicated that the material remained compatible with human skin cells under the conditions examined.The results suggest the coating could eventually be incorporated into flexible medical devices that deliver antibacterial activity directly at the site of an infection.Potential applications include wound dressings designed to help protect difficult-to-heal injuries and wearable patches that combine infection prevention with health monitoring. The material can bend, stretch, and conduct electricity, making it potentially suitable for soft skin-mounted devices and smart textiles.Such systems could one day monitor signals such as heart or muscle activity while providing an additional layer of protection against bacterial growth.However, the technology remains at an early research stage. The laboratory findings do not establish its safety or effectiveness in patients, and further testing will be needed before it can be considered for medical use.The research was published in the journal Small Structures.

title: IBM to merge two powerful quantum chips into a 1,040-qubit system
content: IBM plans to connect two next-generation quantum processors into a single system with 1,040 qubits in 2027. The proposed system will use the company’s upcoming Nighthawk r3 architecture. Each processor will support 520 programmable qubits and execute up to 10,000 quantum operations.The announcement signals IBM’s push toward larger quantum systems capable of handling increasingly demanding computational workloads. The company also reported substantial performance gains from its existing Nighthawk r2 processor. Industry partners have already executed more than 34 billion circuits on the hardware.Nighthawk pushes performanceIBM’s current Nighthawk r2 processor has demonstrated significant improvements in quantum execution speed. Introduced in September 2026, the system can deliver up to 100,000 samples per second. It also supports computations involving more than 7,500 quantum operations across 120 qubits.Quantum applications often require millions or billions of samples to produce useful results. Faster execution allows researchers to complete demanding experiments without spending excessive time running individual circuits.Partners including German energy company E.ON, Algorithmiq, and Q-CTRL have reported improvements of up to 19 times. E.ON, for instance, achieved a 15-fold speedup in quantum machine learning for electricity grid optimization.IBM also used Nighthawk r2 to accelerate a magnetic materials simulation conducted with Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The experiment ran 12 times faster than its earlier implementation on IBM’s Heron processor.An experiment with Algorithmiq delivered another notable result. Nighthawk r2 executed circuits eight times faster than the original Heron-based experiment. The updated computations also presented a greater challenge for classical simulation methods.Connecting quantum processorsNighthawk r3 will introduce additional hardware capabilities to support larger systems. Its design includes 2,034 physical qubits, alongside 520 programmable qubits. IBM will retain the square-grid connectivity found in the previous generation.The processor will also feature 10 chip-to-chip connections called l-couplers. These components allow separate quantum processors to exchange quantum states. That capability could help IBM expand computing capacity without relying on a single increasingly large chip.IBM has already demonstrated the technology through an earlier connection between two Nighthawk r1 processors. Four l-couplers achieved 99.3% quantum state transfer fidelity. The company is working toward a target of 99.9%.Its next milestone involves connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors in 2027. The resulting 1,040-qubit system would represent another step toward larger quantum architectures.Quantum joins classical computingIBM is also changing how researchers access computing resources through its enhanced Quantum Platform. The environment now brings quantum processors and classical high-performance computing resources together.Researchers can coordinate quantum workloads with conventional computing systems. These resources help handle error correction, noise analysis, and processing after quantum measurements.Early results suggest the integration can improve research efficiency. IBM and RIKEN scientists completed an existing sample-based quantum diagonalization workflow roughly five times faster. They also performed 100 times more computations than their original study.Cleveland Clinic and RIKEN used the platform to process 608 million samples for modeling biological structures. Workflow automation helped complete the task 33 times faster.IBM’s broader roadmap targets fault-tolerant quantum computing. Reaching that goal will require increasingly capable processors and tighter integration with classical computing infrastructure.

title: Torus taps existing grid capacity to power modular data centers
content: Torus has launched a modular computing system designed to bring inference capacity online at existing commercial and industrial sites, using available grid connections instead of waiting for new data center infrastructure.The Salt Lake City-based energy and infrastructure company unveiled Foundry on November 11, alongside a $500 million funding announcement led by Magnetar. The funding will support manufacturing expansion and deployments of its energy storage and computing systems across the US.The launch comes as demand for inference computing grows. Unlike model training, which involves developing and refining models, inference runs those models to generate responses and perform tasks. McKinsey projects that data center demand for inference will grow at a compound annual rate of 35 percent through 2030, compared with 22 percent for training.Bringing compute to powerFoundry combines computing hardware, power systems, energy storage, cooling and networking in a prefabricated modular unit. Torus says each site can support between 1 and 20 megawatts of computing capacity and can move from contract to operational workloads in 12 to 16 weeks.The system is designed to operate at existing commercial and industrial sites with available electrical capacity. Rather than waiting for new grid connections or large-scale infrastructure upgrades, Torus aims to use existing interconnections and manage electricity demand through its Torus Reserve energy storage system.Reserve combines battery storage and inertial-based technology to manage peak demand, provide backup power, and adjust electricity consumption. The company says its load-management controls can help accommodate the fluctuating power requirements of computing hardware while supporting grid stability.Foundry is also designed for distributed deployment, placing computing resources closer to businesses and the workloads they serve. Torus argues this could appeal to enterprises seeking greater control over where their data is processed, alongside security and intellectual property protections.Scaling modular capacityTorus is offering Foundry through three deployment models. The Strategic option provides a powered enclosure without GPUs, while the Partner configuration includes computing hardware. Its Direct model offers dedicated, single-tenant inference capacity for enterprise customers.The company named AI infrastructure provider Hydra Host among Foundry’s first customers, alongside another unnamed cloud provider. Torus says thousands of GPUs are already deployed in Foundry units and plans to increase that number to more than 47,000 by the end of 2027.The systems are manufactured at GigaOne, Torus’s 545,000-square-foot facility in Salt Lake City, Utah. The company says its Foundry production line is designed to support 500 megawatts of IT load, with plans to expand capacity to 1 gigawatt.Torus also says Foundry uses a closed-loop, waterless cooling system that consumes 95 percent less water than evaporative cooling systems. These environmental and performance figures are company-reported claims.The $500 million financing round was led by Magnetar, with participation from ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners and Trinity Capital. The launch reflects a growing effort to address data center power constraints by distributing computing capacity across existing sites. However, Foundry’s deployment timelines, available grid capacity, and planned GPU expansion remain dependent on individual site conditions and future execution.

title: Oracle helps US utilities cut peak power demand by record 1 GW in 2026
content: Electricity demand can surge during extreme temperatures, putting additional pressure on power grids. US utilities are increasingly turning to customers themselves to help manage those peaks. Oracle says its utility programs have delivered a record 1 gigawatt (GW) of peak demand reduction across North America in 2026.The company’s Opower platform supported 73 demand response events across winter and summer. Those efforts involved 4.3 million customers across participating utilities. The total demand reduction equals the output of more than three peaker power plants in Washington state.Customers help balance grid demandOracle’s Opower platform uses behavioral demand response (BDR) and peak-time rebate (PTR) programs. These initiatives encourage households to shift electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Customers can receive personalized messages explaining when and how to reduce their usage.The approach also expands virtual power plants (VPPs) beyond households with connected devices. Utilities can draw on participating customers’ flexible electricity consumption to reduce pressure on the grid. Some programs also offer financial rewards for reducing usage during designated peak periods.Oracle reported that utilities conducted 73 events in 2026, compared with 49 last year. That represents an increase of nearly 50%. Average peak demand savings reached 16,592 kilowatts per event, equivalent to the peak electricity needs of approximately 4,150 homes.Customer participation also climbed significantly. The programs reached 4.3 million customers, up from 3.3 million in 2025.Utilities expand demand responsePuget Sound Energy (PSE) has incorporated Oracle’s BDR program into its virtual power plant strategy. Its Flex Events initiative uses customer communications to encourage temporary reductions in electricity consumption.The program combines text messages, interactive voice calls, and email outreach. PSE reported peak load reductions of up to 16.6 megawatts (MW) during individual events across three consecutive deployment seasons.Earlier in 2026, PSE introduced performance-based incentives to encourage greater participation. Customers can now receive a $0.50-per-kilowatt-hour bill credit for reducing electricity consumption during qualifying events.“We’re excited to continue partnering with Oracle to design customer-focused solutions that are easy to participate in,” said Tom Smith, PSE’s supervisor for demand response.CPS Energy also reported strong participation across its service area in San Antonio, Texas. More than 350,000 customers joined its behavioral demand response programs. That represents over one-third of its customer base.The utility conducted 12 demand response events during summer. Participation helped deliver nearly 19 MW of peak demand reduction during August.Programs target winter peaksOracle has also expanded its demand response offerings to support year-round events. Utilities can now use these programs during winter storms and other periods of elevated electricity consumption.The expansion addresses changing electricity demand patterns across the United States. Some regions increasingly experience their highest grid demand during winter. Flexible customer participation gives utilities another way to manage those seasonal pressures.Opower also allows utilities to target different customer groups with tailored messages. This gives households more relevant guidance based on their participation and energy programs.Behavioral demand response and peak-time rebates are becoming important tools for managing electricity consumption. Their growing reach could help utilities access flexible capacity across more households. That capacity may prove increasingly useful as US electricity demand puts greater pressure on existing grid infrastructure.

title: AlphaGenome 2 finds nearly 2x more disease-linked DNA variants
content: Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaGenome 2, an upgraded DNA sequence model that predicts how genetic variants affect different human cell types, helping researchers investigate the genetic mechanisms underlying disease.The model builds on the original AlphaGenome, which maps molecular activity across a broad range of tissues and covers both coding and non-coding regions of the genome. This provides a unified approach to assessing the potential effects of genetic variants.Earlier this year, the company introduced the AlphaGenome Atlas, a separate predictive resource mapping the effects of every possible single-letter DNA change in the human genome.From tissues to cellsAccording to the company, AlphaGenome 2 moves beyond broad tissue-level averages to analyse individual cell types and states. This allows researchers to examine how genetic variants affect disease-relevant cells and how their effects may differ across cellular conditions.The model was trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from human and mouse samples spanning 68 tissues. Unlike its predecessor, which generated predictions across multiple tissues in parallel, the updated model takes a specific biological condition alongside a DNA sequence as input.Researchers can select a cell type from a reference catalogue or use their own single-cell data to examine a previously unseen cellular state. The model can also estimate missing experimental measurements, such as chromatin accessibility, from other available data.Nearly twice as many variantsIn a benchmark using TenK10K, a single-cell dataset covering 28 primary immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 identified 30% of causal variants, compared with 16% for the original model fine-tuned on single-cell data and other specialised tools, according to Google DeepMind.The model also improved its ability to determine the direction of a variant’s effect on gene activity. It correctly identified whether a variant increased or decreased gene expression in 43% of cases, compared with 23% for the earlier model and comparison tools.The results suggest the updated system could help researchers narrow down which genetic changes are most likely to influence disease-related processes in particular cell types.Testing disease-linked variantsGoogle DeepMind also demonstrated the model’s ability to examine genetic effects in cellular conditions it had not previously encountered.In one example, researchers used single-cell data from a study of people receiving a COVID-19 mRNA vaccine. AlphaGenome 2 distinguished activated immune T cells from resting ones and found that a variant associated with severe COVID-19 had a stronger effect on gene activity in the activated cells.The company also used the model to reproduce computationally a finding involving inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The variant, located in a distant regulatory region of DNA, was shown to increase activity of the ETS2 gene in gut macrophages, a type of immune cell. The model predicted that this effect was concentrated in those cells rather than occurring broadly across other cell types.These examples illustrate how cell-specific predictions could help researchers connect genetic variants with the cells and biological processes involved in disease. However, computational predictions still need experimental validation.AlphaGenome 2 is available for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API, while commercial researchers can access it through a private preview. Google DeepMind said the model is intended for research use and has not been validated or approved for clinical or diagnostic purposes.

title: Nvidia board weighs ousting Jensen Huang after second alleged affair
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could lose control of the chipmaking giant as mounting personal controversies threaten his leadership. The company’s board is reportedly preparing to discuss his future following revelations about two alleged extramarital relationships.The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board could meet as soon as November 12. Directors will reportedly consider whether Huang should remain CEO. The controversy involves his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working with Beijing’s intelligence services. A separate report has also linked him to a senior Nvidia executive.Nvidia shares dropped approximately 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. The latest selloff adds to a turbulent week for the world’s most valuable semiconductor company.Two relationships under scrutinyReports emerged on Wednesday that Huang maintained an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell. She serves as Nvidia’s vice president of health care and reports within the company’s executive structure.Five people familiar with Nvidia described the relationship to the newspaper. Two former company insiders also claimed they witnessed Huang and Powell behaving affectionately at a San Jose hotel. The encounter reportedly occurred during Nvidia’s annual GTC developer conference in March.Three people briefed on the incident described another development. Huang’s security team allegedly confronted a bystander who recorded the interaction. The team reportedly offered the individual a nondisclosure agreement.Both Huang and Powell are married to other people. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and gradually advanced through its leadership ranks. She became senior director of artificial intelligence business development in 2016. Nvidia appointed her vice president of health care in 2017.Her responsibilities include expanding applications for Nvidia technology across medical imaging and higher education. She also represents the company at international technology conferences.Nvidia’s employee code of conduct addresses potential conflicts involving personal relationships. It also requires the company to investigate reported misconduct. However, Nvidia has not publicly confirmed any investigation involving Powell.Chinese spy allegations escalateHuang’s reported relationship with Powell adds another complication to an existing controversy. It was previously reported that his relationship with Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly identified the Chinese businesswoman as an intelligence asset.She allegedly helped facilitate shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. Beijing has denied the espionage allegations. Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment.Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into the Chinese connection earlier this month. Law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is overseeing the inquiry. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an internal employee memo.He accepted responsibility without disclosing further details about the relationship. The board initially expressed confidence in his leadership following the announcement.Republican leaders from three influential House committees have also requested a closed-door briefing. They want Huang to explain his interactions with Alice Huang. He could face a congressional subpoena if he fails to cooperate.Leadership uncertainty growsThe allegations now place Nvidia’s leadership under unprecedented scrutiny. Jensen Huang co-founded the company in 1993 alongside Curtis Priem and Chris Malachowsky. He transformed its graphics processor business into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips.Nvidia now sits at the center of the global computing boom. Its technology also plays an increasingly important role in U.S.-China technological competition.Losing Huang would create significant uncertainty for the roughly $4 trillion semiconductor giant. His departure could disrupt leadership continuity during a critical period for the industry.When approached by The New York Times about Powell, Huang declined to discuss the relationship. He reportedly told the newspaper, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He subsequently ended the call.Nvidia declined to comment on the latest allegations. Powell also did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The board’s reported deliberations could determine whether Huang remains at the helm of the company he spent three decades building.

title: China's military drone uses medicine darts to treat wounded troops
content: China has demonstrated a new battlefield rescue capability that could change how military medics reach injured soldiers. The country’s Air Force Medical University has developed a drone that can locate casualties and deliver emergency medication remotely.The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can inject medicine directly into a wounded person’s muscle using a dart-like projectile. Researchers say the technology could provide critical initial treatment when conventional rescue teams cannot safely reach casualties.The development points to a growing role for unmanned systems in military medicine. Chinese researchers are also exploring ways to evacuate wounded personnel using aerial and ground-based robotic platforms.Drones bring battlefield medicineWang Jianqi, a representative of Air Force Medical University, described the system in a report on Wednesday. State broadcaster CCTV quoted him saying the university had developed China’s military’s first casualty-search drone.Wang said the aircraft could deliver emergency medication from considerable distances. Its injection capability could help stabilize wounded soldiers before medical teams reach them.Chinese drone shooting medicine darts in demonstration. Credit – CCTV“Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle,” Wang said. He added that the approach could buy valuable time for further treatment.Footage accompanying the report showed a UAV releasing a dart toward a soldier lying on the ground. The demonstration illustrated how an aircraft could administer medication without requiring a medic’s immediate presence.Military commentator Song Zhongping told the Global Times that modern warfare complicates battlefield medical evacuations. He pointed to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, where attacks increasingly affect areas beyond conventional front lines.“One of the biggest problems in modern warfare is that it has blurred the concept of the front lines and the rear,” Song said. He argued that casualties can now emerge across much wider areas.Rescuing troops under fireMedical personnel traditionally face significant danger when approaching wounded soldiers in contested territory. Drones could reduce that exposure by delivering initial treatment before rescuers enter dangerous locations.Song said some casualties require pain relief before evacuation. Medical teams must also stabilize injured personnel to prevent further complications during transportation.The technology could eventually support broader medical evacuation operations. However, researchers still face considerable engineering challenges before unmanned aircraft can transport wounded personnel.Wang said air-ground unmanned treatment remains experimental. One major obstacle involves retrieving injured soldiers and loading them onto drones for evacuation.Robotic systems expand rescueOther Chinese military medical units have also tested robotic equipment during battlefield rescue exercises. The PLA Joint Logistic Support Force’s 967th Hospital conducted one such drill, according to the PLA Daily in October.During the exercise, a thermal-imaging drone searched for simulated casualties. Smaller cargo drones transported emergency medical supplies into areas inaccessible to conventional rescue vehicles.Robotic dogs also entered narrow passages to locate casualties and relay information about surrounding conditions. These machines could help rescuers assess dangerous locations before sending personnel inside.The technology could also have applications beyond military operations. Song suggested drones could assist civilian rescue teams during landslides, road collapses and floods.Such emergencies can isolate survivors behind damaged infrastructure or inaccessible terrain. Unmanned aircraft could deliver essential medication without requiring helicopters and their crews to enter equally dangerous conditions.China’s latest demonstration remains an early step toward remotely operated battlefield medicine. Its eventual effectiveness will depend on reliable delivery, accurate casualty detection, and safe evacuation capabilities.

title: US to add 300 MW of solar power with four new Florida projects by 2028
content: Scaling America’s clean energy solutions, Duke Energy Florida has proposed four new utility-scale solar sites with a combined generating capacity of 300 megawatts (MW).The plan to expand the renewable energy portfolio of the Southern state was announced Tuesday, November 10, as electricity demand continues to grow across the state.The American energy company has filed plans with the Florida Public Service Commission (PSC) to construct the four solar facilities, which are expected to enter service by mid-2028. Together, the projects will add 300 MW of emissions-free electricity generation to Florida’s power grid.Four solar sites across FloridaThe planned facilities include solar energy sites in Orange and Sumter Counties, with a tentative online date of June 2028.The Orange County facilities include Nova Renewable Energy Center, Bull Creek Renewable Energy Center, and Wewahootee Renewable Energy Center. The construction of the former two are expected to begin early next year. Construction for the third is slated to begin in May 2027.Hogeye Renewable Energy Center is the only one planned in the Sumter County.According to Duke Energy Florida, the new projects are part of its long-term strategy to meet rising electricity demand while increasing the share of renewable energy in its generation mix.“Our strategy is centered on delivering cleaner energy while maintaining reliable and affordable service for our customers,” Melissa Seixas, Duke Energy Florida state president, said in a statement.Each facility will generate electricity using photovoltaic solar panels connected to Duke Energy Florida’s transmission network. Once operational, the projects will collectively provide enough renewable generation to strengthen the utility’s growing solar portfolio.However, the company has not yet revealed the individual capacity of the four proposed solar sites.Clean energy expansionThe latest filing is part of the company’s plan to expand the state’s battery system to store excess energy when power demand is low.Through these new systems, the company hopes to provide customers with clean solar energy even during the period of no sunlight.“These solar energy sites are just one example of how we’re planning for the future and strengthening our system to continue providing safe, reliable power, at the lowest possible price, for years to come,” Seixas added.Over the next decade, it plans to build over 1 gigawatt of battery storage, the company said in a statement expanding on the long-term impact of the proposed solar utility sites.The utility noted that the four projects are also projected to deliver approximately $1 billion in customer savings over their operating lifetimes through reduced fuel costs, although the primary focus of the proposal is to add new renewable generating capacity to Florida’s electric grid.Beyond providing cost-effective fuel to power the American grid, the new facilities would also provide emission-free energy to the U.S. homes. According to the company, about 1.1 million cubic feet of natural gas, 12,000 barrels of fuel oil, and 9,000 tons of coal are saved annually at each solar energy site.The company currently owns, operates, and maintains 25 solar energy sites that contribute 1,850 MW to the grid. Each energy site holds the capacity to power nearly 15,000 homes, it said.

title: US ally installs seabed sensors for 100M-ton CO₂ storage project
content: The UK has installed the first monitoring systems for its first commercial-scale offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS) project, a major breakthrough toward developing a facility expected to permanently store up to 100 million tons of carbon dioxide over 25 years beneath the North Sea.The system comprising a six seabed landers has been deployed at the Endurance CO₂ store, around 93 miles (150 kilometers) off the coast of Teesside, before carbon dioxide injection begins. According to the team, the new system will establish baseline environmental and seismic conditions and enable engineers to verify that injected CO₂ remains safely contained underground throughout the project’s lifetime.It is deployed under the Northern Endurance Partnership (NEP) project, a joint venture between BP, Equinor, and TotalEnergies. The partnership is developing the transportation and storage infrastructure for the UK’s East Coast Cluster, one of the country’s flagship industrial decarbonization initiatives.CO₂ injection is scheduled to begin in 2028, making Endurance the UK’s first operational commercial-scale offshore CCS project.Baseline before carbon storageThe monitoring campaign combines three autonomous environmental monitoring landers built by Sonardyne, now part of Kraken Robotics, with three co-located TIAMAT passive seismic monitoring systems developed by Germany’s K.U.M.Newly deployed systems are collecting baseline measurements of seawater chemistry, ocean currents, seabed conditions, and natural seismic activity before any carbon dioxide is injected into these storage systems. These measurements will provide a reference against which future changes can be compared once storage operations begin.Beneath the seabed, the reservoir lies approximately 3,280 feet (1,000 meters) deep. At these depths, porous rock formations are expected to permanently contain captured industrial emissions transported from Teesside and the Humber.Under the project’s measurement, monitoring, and verification (MMV) program, the monitoring equipment is designed to demonstrate that stored carbon dioxide remains securely trapped in the geological reservoir over decades.Continuous monitoring without retrievalSonardyne’s landers are designed for long-term autonomous operation on the seabed, without the need for regular recovery.Onboard power management, edge data processing, and wireless underwater acoustic communications help to operate the system remotely and periodically transmit information to the sea surface.This allows engineers to collect data over extended periods without repeatedly retrieving the instruments, reducing operational costs while maintaining continuous oversight of the storage site.“Confidence in offshore CO₂ storage starts with good data,” said Stephen Auld, Business Development Manager for Custom Projects at Sonardyne.He said reliable environmental and micro-seismic monitoring throughout the storage lifecycle, not just at a single point in time, is essential for demonstrating the integrity of offshore carbon storage.UK’s decarbonization goalsNEP said establishing environmental and seismic baselines before operations begin is a critical step in proving the long-term safety of offshore carbon storage.“The deployment of these monitoring systems is a great example of the expertise and innovation that is helping to deliver CCS in the UK,” said Mike Stephen, Head of Technical at NEP.He added that the data collected will help verify the safe and secure storage of carbon dioxide over time while supporting the infrastructure needed to decarbonize heavy industry across Teesside, the Humber, and surrounding regions.Once operational, the Endurance project will provide the offshore storage component for the East Coast Cluster, transporting captured carbon emissions from industrial facilities to the North Sea for permanent underground storage. Over its first 25 years of operation, the site is expected to sequester up to 100 million tons of CO₂, making it one of Europe’s largest planned offshore carbon storage projects.

title: Google unveils Gemini Decisions API to handle 1,000 questions at once
content: Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint powered by its Gemini Decision 1 model that helps AI agents make fast, predefined decisions without generating lengthy text responses.The interface allows developers to evaluate up to 1,000 independent questions against a shared multimodal input containing text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. Instead of generating responses token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores predefined options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores with an end-to-end latency of 150–250 milliseconds.Google said the model is built for bounded tasks such as selecting tools, checking policy compliance, routing queries to the right models, and grading context. Developers can submit yes-or-no checks, multiple-choice questions with up to 255 options, or scoring requests based on predefined rubrics in a single API call.Faster decisions at lower costsAccording to Google, the API delivers a median model computation time of 50–100 milliseconds, with performance remaining nearly unchanged when processing between one and 100 questions per request. The model supports a context window of up to 256,000 tokens and can process multiple types of data simultaneously. This allows developers to combine inputs such as audio recordings, images and documents without relying on separate processing systems.Google also claims the model outperforms competing systems across benchmarks covering agent routing, reasoning, ranking and multimodal understanding, while achieving the lowest calibration error.The company said Gemini Decision 1 is nearly five times cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite using the Interactions API across its shared benchmark suite.The launch comes amid growing competition in specialized AI decision-making tools. OpenAI introduced its Decisions API in October, powered by its GPT-6 Luna model. The company said the service can deliver decisions up to 10 times faster than its Responses API and supports up to 400 questions per request. Like Google’s offering, it provides probability-based checks, multiple-choice selections and rubric-based scoring, with pricing starting at $0.10 per million input tokens.The Decisions API costs $0.10 per million input tokens, with no charges for output tokens. Developers are billed only once for shared input data, regardless of how many questions are evaluated, although each question adds instruction and criteria tokens.Powering real-world AI applicationsGoogle is already deploying the technology across several of its products, proving how specialized decision-making models can improve the speed and efficiency of automated systems.In Gemini Notebook, the API routes incoming queries to appropriate model tiers and reasoning levels. According to Google, this approach can reduce latency for everyday queries by up to 40 percent while reserving more powerful reasoning models for complex tasks.The technology also powers rapid design experiments in Google’s Stitch platform, allowing users to generate interactive product wireframes and make changes through voice commands or touch inputs.Meanwhile, Google’s CC assistant uses the API to select emoji reactions from more than 200 options in a fraction of a second.Google Search is also using the technology as a safety layer to detect adversarial behavior involving Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools.Beyond these applications, the API could help developers build systems that automatically select appropriate tools, assess incoming information and determine when human intervention is necessary.The Decisions API is now available through Google AI Studio, including a free tier for prototyping. Google is also rolling out integrations with developer platforms such as OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, and Pydantic AI.

title: 3D model could slash energy losses in US green hydrogen production
content: Researchers in the US have developed a three-dimensional (3D) computer model that could make green hydrogen production far more efficient, by revealing how bubbles waste energy during water electrolysis.The computational tool was created by scientists at New York’s Cornell University and their colleagues at City University of Hong Kong. It reveals how tiny bubbles, formed during water electrolysis, can disrupt hydrogen production, and increase electricity consumption.At the same time, the team identified a critical bubble size beyond which energy losses rise. Their simulations suggest that keeping bubbles below this threshold could limit the additional voltage required due to an individual bubble to within three percent.The 3D model also uses a computational method that reduces the effort needed to run simulations by approximately 1,000 times, without actually compromising numerical accuracy. The scientists hope the findings could make green hydrogen much cheaper to produce.Why bubble size mattersGreen hydrogen is a clean energy fuel made by splitting water (H2) into hydrogen and oxygen through water electrolysis powered entirely by renewable sources like solar or wind energy. It emits zero carbon dioxide (CO2) during production, which means it could provide a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels in industries including steelmaking and chemical manufacturing.However, the hydrogen and oxygen bubbles that form during the process pose a significant challenge. As electricity passes through an electrolyzer, these bubbles develop on the electrodes where chemical reactions take place. They can, therefore, block the active reaction sites, keep water from reaching the electrode surfaces, or interfere with the movement of the charged particles. This causes the electrolyzer to use more electricity to produce hydrogen. To address this problem, research teams have long experimented with changing electrode shapes, adjusting liquid flows, and modifying surface properties to help the bubbles detach easily. Yet, calculating the precise amount of energy lost due to individual bubbles has remained difficult. “Experimentally it’s really challenging to isolate the impact of bubbles on each individual scale,” Lenan Zhang, PhD, an assistant professor at Cornell University’s Sibley School of Mechanical and one of the study’s lead authors, pointed out.A revolutionary approachFor the project, the team built a 3D mathematical model that simulates processes across eight orders of magnitude in length. As per Weihong Li, PhD, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at City University of Hong Kong, and second lead study author, it works like a digital twin of an electrolyzer. It can reproduce real electrode shapes, materials, and operating conditions, while revealing microscopic processes that are difficult to observe experimentally. With the model, the researchers were able to examine individual hydrogen bubbles on an electrode in an alkaline electrolyzer.They figured out that bubbles cause the greatest energy losses when they block active electrode surfaces. What’s more, they managed to identify a critical bubble radius. Once a bubble exceeds this size, the extra voltage needed for electrolysis rises exponentially.Under certain simulated conditions, this extra voltage could exceed 50 percent of the voltage required without bubbles. Moreover, the scientists confirmed that the critical size depends on electrode geometry and how easily liquid spreads across its surface.They believe they could improve the efficiency by creating electrodes that release bubbles before they become too large. The team now plans to expand the model to test how multiple bubbles grow, merge, and interact. They also aim to combine the technology with computational optimization and 3D printing to develop more efficient electrode designs.The study has been published in the journal EES Catalysis.

title: Scientists develop 200-nanometer diamond pillars for quantum computers
content: Scientists in Germany have launched a manufacturing platform that can carve diamonds at the nanoscale while embedding individual atomic-scale defects. The system aims to turn one of nature’s hardest gems into a reliable building block for next-generation quantum computers, ultra-secure communication links, and high-sensitivity quantum sensors.The initiative is led by the Joint Lab Diamond Nanophotonics, a partnership between the Ferdinand-Braun-Institut (FBH) and Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin.Diamond is a natural candidate for quantum hardware. Inside its rigid crystal structure, tiny missing carbon atoms or foreign elements form defects called color centers. These flaws behave much like trapped single atoms. Physicists can read and alter their spin states with laser light, creating stable bits of quantum information.Yet building practical quantum microchips out of diamond has proved notoriously difficult. The global semiconductor industry spent decades perfecting the mass production of silicon circuits. Diamond processing, by contrast, is still in its infancy. Diamond is brittle, chemically stubborn, and prone to microscopic damage during handling.Precision fabrication for future integrationThe Berlin team tackled this hurdle by designing an industrial-grade fabrication pipeline built around three core stages.The first stage focuses on surface cleanup. “Mechanical polishing can leave strain and damage near the surface, potentially introducing unwanted noise in quantum applications,” said the research team in a press release. To eliminate this issue, engineers use oxygen- and chlorine-based plasma etching. The technique strips away up to 20 micrometers of damaged material, leaving behind an exceptionally flat surface with an average roughness of only half a nanometer.The second stage introduces functional quantum defects on demand. Engineers fire beams of selected ions directly into high-purity synthetic diamonds. The facility can insert atoms of nitrogen, silicon, germanium, tin, or carbon. Because the host diamond is virtually free of impurities, the implanted color centers retain long coherence times and remain shielded from surrounding electromagnetic interference.“Finally, FBH can structure the diamond into nanoscale pillars,” added the press release. The researchers use electron-beam lithography to carve the diamond into nanoscale pillars. These tiny pillars act like built-in optical antennas. When a single defect center inside the pillar emits a photon, the pillar channels the light upward instead of letting it scatter inside the crystal. This design sharply boosts the collection efficiency of single photons, a vital requirement for quantum networks that transmit secret cryptographic keys.Adaptable to various defect types“With our diamond processing capabilities, we are establishing a technology platform that brings together precise nanofabrication and quantum optical functionality,” said Prof. Dr. Tim Schröder, who heads the joint lab. He noted that the processes are adaptable to various defect types and can support research teams and industrial clients alike.Moving forward, the team plans to fuse these diamond pillars directly into standard photonic circuits, clearing the path toward compact quantum light sources and scalable quantum repeaters.“This allows us to develop and refine processes for different color centers and make them available for research and application-oriented development,” concluded Dr. Schröder.

title: US Marines drill with deadly 12-mile-reach strike drones in California
content: The US Marine Corps is continuing to integrate small first-person-view (FPV) attack drones into infantry training, with Marines recently operating the Neros Archer system during a battalion field exercise at Twentynine Palms, California.Official imagery released through the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) on November 8 shows Marines from the 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, 1st Marine Division, inspecting and preparing the small unmanned aircraft during training held on October 20. The exercise placed the drones within a broader infantry training environment, where Marines practiced making tactical decisions against an opposing force.The latest activity follows a series of live-fire demonstrations and training events in the Indo-Pacific, as the Marine Corps works to give smaller units an additional precision-strike capability without relying exclusively on artillery, aircraft, or other supporting weapons.A small drone designed for infantry strike missionsThe Neros Archer is a compact FPV aircraft controlled by an operator using a live video feed from the drone. Unlike conventional reconnaissance quadcopters, the Archer is designed to carry modular payloads, including explosive warheads, for one-way attack missions.Its intended role is to give infantry formations the ability to engage targets beyond the range of many weapons normally available to small units. The aircraft can be used against vehicles, equipment, and personnel, depending on its payload configuration.The Marine Corps demonstrated the system’s reach at its Air-Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms in March 2025. According to the service, the Archer conducted a ground strike at a distance exceeding 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) and an aerial interception at 10 kilometers (6.2 miles). The aircraft also integrated real-time video and position data during the demonstration.Those figures illustrate the potential reach of the platform, rather than establishing the effective range of every mission or payload configuration.The Marine Corps has since expanded its practical employment of the drone. In August 2026, Marines from the 4th Marine Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, completed the service’s first series of live-fire FPV attack-drone flights in South Korea. The exercises involved the 3rd Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion and the 3rd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, which used Archer drones for precision anti-armor and antipersonnel strikes.The Marine Corps described the system as a way to extend precision fires down to small-unit formations, potentially allowing Marines to engage targets while remaining farther from hostile positions.From operator training to distributed strike capabilitiesThe Archer is also being incorporated into more complex employment concepts. During an October 20 exercise at Camp Fuji, Japan, Marines from Battalion Landing Team 1/1, 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit, conducted two live-fire drone missions. One scenario simulated an anti-armor ambush, while another tested the aircraft against ground communications infrastructure.The exercise was designed around the Marine Corps’ hunter-killer team concept, in which reconnaissance assets identify and track targets before passing information to an FPV drone operator for engagement.This approach connects surveillance and strike capabilities within smaller formations, potentially reducing the time between detecting a target and engaging it. It also gives infantry commanders another option when larger supporting weapons are unavailable or unsuitable.The service is building a standardized training structure to support this expansion. A December 2025 Marine Corps directive established pilot courses and certification requirements for small unmanned aircraft operators, including personnel employing attack drones such as the Neros Archer. The framework is intended to develop operator skills, safety procedures, and consistent training across different units.The effort reflects lessons from conflicts such as the war in Ukraine, where inexpensive FPV drones have become widely used for reconnaissance and attacks against vehicles, personnel, and defensive positions. Their battlefield effectiveness has also highlighted vulnerabilities to electronic warfare, communications disruption, and air defenses.For the Marine Corps, the challenge is not simply acquiring drones but developing the personnel, tactics, and logistics needed to use them in conventional infantry operations. The latest training at Twentynine Palms is another step in that process, as the service works to make small unmanned strike systems a more routine part of its ground combat capabilities.
