title: Wind-powered 30 MW plant produces first green hydrogen molecule
content: The first molecule of green hydrogen was produced by a 30-megawatt (MW) German energy plant powered by a 50MW wind farm, according to an announcement on Tuesday, November 10.​The latest milestone marks the start of integrated system testing, with all major components now operating together ahead of the plant’s full commissioning in 2027.​Calling it “an important milestone,” Holger Kreetz, COO of Uniper, one of the companies leading the project, said, “the hydrogen economy needs more than electrolyzers…it is crucial that the entire process chain functions reliably in operation.”Wind-powered electrolysis​The system uses renewable electricity from the connected wind farm to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, a process called electrolysis. The process is carried out in a pressure-alkali electrolyzer comprising three modules, each with a capacity of 10 MW. The electrochemical conversion of water into hydrogen and oxygen takes place inside the stacks, two of which are present in each module.​According to the company, the green hydrogen produced as a part of this project will be fed into Central Germany’s industrial hydrogen pipeline network, supplying chemical manufacturers and, in the future, supporting hydrogen-powered urban transportation.​Green hydrogen was produced more than three years after construction began at the Bad Lauchstädt Energy Park near Leipzig. The plant is expected to become fully operational next year.​Upon completion, the project is expected to produce up to 3,000 tons of green hydrogen per year. Almost 75 percent of the annual green hydrogen production from the fully operational plant would be supplied via a 15-mile (25-kilometer) pipeline to TotalEnergies, a refining and petrochemical facility at the Leuna Chemical Complex.​”With the production of the first hydrogen, we are getting closer to our common goal of transferring renewable energy into an industrially usable energy source,” said Konstantin von Oldenburg, Managing Director of VNG H&V.​However, two partner energy companies, Uniper and VNG Handel & Vertrieb (VNG H&V), which are leading the project, have not revealed a firm timeline for reaching the plant’s full production capacity.Future direction​With the plant now producing its first hydrogen, engineers will focus on fine-tuning the integrated system before it enters commercial operation.​The next phase will focus on optimizing how electricity generation, electrolysis, gas treatment, and hydrogen transport work together under real-world operating conditions while coordinating the plant’s technical processes.​Moving forward, the pipeline infrastructure is expected to connect the wider hydrogen core network of Germany, spread across nearly 5600 miles (9000 kilometers). According to the statement, for this wide-scale expansion, salt cavern storage could be added to the site in the later phase of the project.​Besides the German plant, advances in green hydrogen technology are also underway in the Middle East, with Saudi Arabia set to become a world leader in clean energy technology. In September this year, the construction of the world’s largest green hydrogen facility was completed in the country. NEOM Green Hydrogen and Ammonia project is one of the most ambitious green-hydrogen developments ever undertaken.​Once operational, the facility will produce up to 600 tons per day of carbon-free hydrogen, converted into green ammonia for global export, providing a practical blueprint for green hydrogen at scale.

title: This $10,000-a-Pound Spice Could Help Save Colorado Farmers
content:
Saffron is the world’s most expensive spice, prized for its vibrant crimson color, distinctive flavor, and delicate aroma. Harvested by hand from the tiny stigmas of purple Crocus sativus flowers, saffron requires extraordinary labor to produce. Credit: Shutterstock
Beneath Denver’s solar panels, a spice nicknamed “red gold” is yielding a promising harvest that could help Colorado farmers earn more with less water.
Colorado State University Spur
, horticulture graduate student Reece Bailey is investigating whether saffron could become a profitable addition to the state’s farms. His experiments in the campus’s urban gardens and
green roof research areas
are testing how the crop handles Colorado’s climate, how much water it needs, and whether growing it beneath solar panels improves production.
The appeal starts with its extraordinary value. A pound of saffron typically costs between $600 and $5,000, with some varieties reaching $10,000. Vanilla, the second most expensive spice, sells for roughly $90 to $225 a pound. Those prices caught Bailey’s attention, but the research must establish whether the potential earnings justify the work.
These tiny purple saffron flowers have been a prized crop for thousands of years. Credit: Colorado State University
Why Saffron Could Suit Colorado
Colorado may seem an unlikely home for a spice closely associated with the Middle East. Yet Iran, which produces roughly 85% of the world’s saffron, has mountainous, semiarid conditions that resemble parts of the state. Bailey sees that overlap as a reason to investigate whether “red gold” could find a foothold on Colorado’s high plains.
The crop also offers an unusual combination of low water demand and late production. Saffron typically blooms in November, potentially bringing farmers income after other harvests have ended. Under suitable conditions, Bailey said, it could provide that additional crop without requiring extra irrigation.
“One thing that’s always been interesting to me is new ideas and novel ways of integrating crops into our environments,” said Bailey, who grew up in Aurora and has worked on Spur’s green roof for three years.
The Work Behind “Red Gold”
The world’s most expensive spice comes from a remarkably small harvest: the three slender red stigmas inside each purple saffron flower. Collecting enough to produce a pound of dried spice requires roughly 75,000 flowers.
That harvest is painstaking. Flowers open for only a few hours each morning, and workers carefully extract the stigmas, often with tweezers. The amount of hand labor helps explain both saffron’s price and the challenge of turning it into a profitable crop.
The rooftop of the Terra building at CSU Spur is home to a rooftop garden filled with a variety of native plants. It overlooks the Rocky Mountains and downtown Denver. Credit: Colorado State University
“It’s certainly not the easiest crop to grow or the easiest crop to work with, but the investment can be well worth it,” Bailey said.
The Colorado Department of Agriculture has committed $80,000 through its
Specialty Crop Block Grant Program
to investigate that possibility, particularly as a source of supplemental income late in the season and during dry years.
A Potential Boost for Farm Income
“For a lot of farmers, the price for their goods isn’t keeping up with the price of inputs, so what we’re really trying to do is find new crops that will work with Colorado’s climate and for our producers’ bottom line,” said Sam Hahn, the department’s next generation and specialty crops program manager. “Saffron has a high labor input, but it could really be a boon for our farmers.”
Successfully growing the flowers would answer only part of the business question. Farmers would still need to assess startup costs, bulb suppliers, equipment, labor availability, and buyers. A valuable spice does not automatically translate into a profitable harvest.
Its labor demands could nevertheless create another benefit. Hahn said the November bloom might provide agricultural jobs during a period when many farmworkers are typically unemployed, while helping farms adapt to a changing climate.
“It’s so important that we experiment with these high-value crops to see if it can supplement the market in our state and keep us competitive,” Hahn said.
Saffron Thrives Beneath Solar Panels
Some of the most promising results are emerging 75 feet (23 meters) above the ground. Bailey’s plots occupy the roofs of two CSU Spur buildings, with Denver’s skyline and the Rocky Mountains in view. One grows among native Colorado plants, including sunflowers. Another sits beneath solar panels in an agrivoltaic system, where the same space supports crops and electricity production.
Reece Bailey is studying how saffron fares in Colorado’s arid, high-elevation environment. Credit: Colorado State University
“I’m always curious about how different plants evolve and how they adapt to green roofs, and lately, I’ve come to realize that saffron is almost the ideal plant for these environments,” said Jennifer Bousselot, Bailey’s faculty adviser and an associate professor of horticulture and landscape architecture at CSU.
Spur’s rooftop gardens have carefully selected soil characteristics and are designed to use water efficiently. Saffron also tolerates some shade, and Bailey’s research so far has found that
yields nearly double beneath the partial shade of solar arrays
“This could provide cash flow value for farmers who want to use solar as an energy source, or who happen to be in an urban agriculture setting,” Bailey said.
Testing a Crop for Dry Years
Water use offers another reason to keep testing. Bailey said saffron requires roughly half as much water as corn and could potentially survive on rainfall alone, making it an appealing candidate for a region where irrigation water is under pressure.
“This crop is incredibly drought resistant,” Bailey said.
The experiments extend beyond Spur’s rooftops to CSU’s Foothills Campus and Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms, at the base of the mountains south of Denver. At Chatfield Farms, Lauren Hazlett, one of the head growers working at the solar array, has welcomed the sight of flowers appearing as other plants fade.
“I never thought I’d ever be able to see saffron growing, especially in Colorado—it’s something I always associated with the other side of the world,” she said.
Bousselot and Bailey have also sent bulbs to farmers in Paonia, Pueblo, and Montrose. Their reports will help show how saffron performs in working farm operations and whether its potential benefits carry beyond the research plots.
There is already a long history of finding uses for the spice. Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to help heal battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed it for bubonic plague, and Cleopatra used its fragrance to attract potential suitors. Today, it flavors dishes such as paella and risotto and is increasingly sought after in perfumes.
Modern research is also exploring its medicinal properties. Some studies suggest saffron may support mental health and help alleviate depression, while others have investigated its possible
anti-inflammatory effects
. Those research areas could add to its commercial appeal, although Colorado’s trials are focused on whether farmers can grow and sell it successfully.
“Up until now, we haven’t really been able to study saffron in Colorado at a deeper level, but the demand is there, and I only think we’ll be talking about it more and more,” Bailey said.

title: More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why
content:
More than a billion years of Earth’s geological history have mysteriously vanished from rock formations across several continents. New research suggests that slow, deep-seated movements within the planet may explain how these enormous gaps formed and why they remain visible today. Credit: Stock
Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.
A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in
, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.
Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.
“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.
Regions for which a mantle flow model predicts a dynamic topography history conducive (orange) or non-conducive (grey) to Great Unconformity formation and preservation. Laurentia (‘LAU’), Baltica (‘BAL’), and North China (‘NCH’) are three regions where the Great Unconformity is well documented. Credit: Associate Professor Nicolas Flament and Santosh Dhungana
The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.
Tracing Earth’s Missing History
Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.
To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can
gently lift enormous stretches of land
or allow them to sink.
Santosh Dhungana and Associate Professor Nicolas Flament. Credit: Michael Gray/University of Wollongong
The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.
How Sinking Continents Preserved The Gap
The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.
Top: The Great Unconformity was formed by continental-scale erosion of ancient crystalline basement during Neoproterozoic times, followed by continental-scale sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times. Bottom: Mantle flow models predict Neoproterozoic dynamic uplift followed by Phanerozoic dynamic subsidence for Laurentia (‘LAU’), Baltica (‘BAL’), and North China (‘NCH’). Credit: Associate Professor Nicolas Flament and Santosh Dhungana
The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.
“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.
“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”
Reference: “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity” by Santosh Dhungana, and Nicolas Flament, 4 November 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5
This study was funded by the Australian Research Council.

title: Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It
content:
Immunotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that harnesses the body’s immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. Unlike traditional treatments that directly target tumors, immunotherapy strengthens or redirects the immune response, offering promising results for many cancers. However, it can sometimes cause the immune system to attack healthy tissues, leading to potentially serious side effects. Credit: Shutterstock
Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.
Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.
Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.
“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.
Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in
that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.
Diet helps recreate immunotherapy side effects
Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.
“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”
Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe. Credit: University of Pittsburgh
Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence
cancer patient outcomes
responses to immunotherapy
. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.
The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.
Gut microbes can worsen or ease inflammation
Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.
The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.
Stabilizing immune cells reverses inflammation in mice
Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.
Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.
“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”
The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.
“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

title: Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top
content:
Tofu is a versatile, plant-based protein made from soybeans that provides all nine essential amino acids. Credit: Shutterstock
Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.
Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.
Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.
Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.
Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.
Two bar charts comparing greenhouse gas emissions and water pollution produced by plant-based and animal-based protein sources per 100 g of protein. Credit: Chris Macdonald
Looking Beyond A Single Food Label
The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.
As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.
Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”
The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.
Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026,
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems

title: Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain
content:
GLP-1 medications, such as semaglutide, mimic a naturally occurring hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and digestion. Commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, these drugs can promote weight loss by reducing hunger and slowing stomach emptying. Credit: Shutterstock
Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.
Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.
In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the
University of Gothenburg
University of Copenhagen
have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in
, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.
Why Weight-Loss Drugs Could Affect Memory
GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.
The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.
Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.
Stina Börchers, Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg, and University of Copenhagen. Credit: Josefin Bergenholtz
“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.
Understanding How Metabolic Treatments Influence the Brain
A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.
Christoffer Clemmensen, Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen. Credit: University of Copenhagen
Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.
“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.
The Next Step Toward Protecting Cognitive Health
The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.
They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.
Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026,

title: Why Did Polynesians Suddenly Sail Across the Pacific After 1,700 Years? Scientists May Have Found the Answer
content:
A traditional Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe on display. Population pressures and advances in sailing technology may have helped transform Polynesian migration. Credit: Shutterstock
The real history behind Moana may be tied to a devastating drought that pushed Polynesian voyagers toward wetter islands and helped reshape human settlement across the Pacific.
In Disney’s Moana, a young Polynesian girl sails beyond her island’s barrier reef to save her threatened home. Scientists have now uncovered evidence that a real environmental crisis may have helped drive one of history’s greatest ocean migrations, pushing Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific after centuries without expanding farther east.
The findings offer a fascinating connection to the story behind Moana, which recently returned to theaters in a live-action adaptation.
A 1,700-year pause in Pacific expansion
Around 3,000 years ago, the ancestors of modern Polynesians arrived in Samoa and Tonga. For approximately 1,700 years, their eastward expansion appeared to stop. This mysterious period became known as the “Long Pause.”
Then, between AD 900 and 1050, everything changed. Within roughly 250 years, Polynesian voyagers had reached and settled islands across the Pacific, including Tahiti and Hawai’i, with their expansion extending to the continental Americas.
Swamp and lake sediments are found across the Pacific islands often in remote volcanic crater lakes or mountain rain forests like here on Tahiti. Credit: University of Southampton
Researchers from the University of Southampton and the University of East Anglia believe a prolonged drought helped trigger this extraordinary movement.
David Sear, Professor of Physical Geography at the University of Southampton and lead author of the study, said, “We have confirmed the theory that the end of the Long Pause coincided with a period of mega drought in the homeland islands of Samoa and Tonga – and also a period of increasing rainfall in the receiving islands. As they headed east, they found wetter islands with nobody on them.”
Ancient mud reveals a devastating drought
To uncover what happened, the team examined ancient mud buried beneath swamps and lakes in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, and the Cook Islands.
Dr. Mark Peaple, a paleoclimate research fellow at the University of Southampton, conducted the geochemical analysis. He studied chemical traces left by freshwater algae and leaves, focusing on different forms of hydrogen called isotopes. Their proportions change depending on rainfall, allowing scientists to reconstruct how wet or dry the islands were thousands of years ago.
Prof David Sear (l) and Dr Mark Peaple (r) coring a swamp in Polynesia to collect mud samples that contain records of rainfall over thousands of years. Credit: University of Southampton
The evidence revealed a severe drought beginning shortly before the migration and continuing during it. When the Long Pause ended, Samoa and Tonga were experiencing their driest conditions in the last 2,000 years. Meanwhile, islands farther east were becoming wetter.
Climate modeling led by Manoj Joshi, Professor of Climate Dynamics at the University of East Anglia, helped explain why. Changes in Pacific Ocean surface temperatures over several decades had shifted a vast tropical rain belt eastward, leaving Samoa and Tonga with less rainfall.
“The climate changes we identified would have transformed daily life on these islands. Reduced rainfall would have affected freshwater availability, food production and the resilience of communities, creating powerful incentives for people to seek opportunities elsewhere,” Joshi said.
Dan Skinner, a research fellow at the University of East Anglia who conducted climate modeling experiments, identified prolonged drought lasting years or even decades as a definite factor behind the migration.
Professor David Sear with mud extracted from swampland in French Polynesia. Credit: University of Southampton
More people and better sailing technology
But worsening conditions were probably not the only influence. Sear explained that growing populations would have placed additional pressure on limited resources. At the same time, Polynesian sailors may have improved their voyaging canoes, moving from U-shaped to V-shaped hulls and developing better rigging. These advances could have helped them sail against the prevailing winds, which generally blow from east to west across the South Pacific.
Together, environmental pressure and improved sailing technology may help explain how Polynesian communities undertook such remarkable journeys.
“There was a huge explosion of migration, and within 250 years they had landed and settled every little dot in the South Pacific, from tiny coral atoll islands to larger lands. It was a very rapid process,” Sear said.
Reference: “How Did changing climate in the tropical South Pacific contribute to the eastward migration and settlement of Polynesia?” by David Sear, Mark Peaple, Peter Langdon, Daniel Skinner, Manoj Joshi, Adrian Matthews, Charlotte Hipkiss, Tim Osborn, Gordon Inglis and Justin Sheffield, 5 May 2026,
Journal of Pacific Archaeology

title: A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived
content:
New analysis reveals that these cave drawings are partially covered by calcite mineral, which has kept them safe for tens of thousands of years. Credit: Adapted from ACS Omega 2026, DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.
About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.
Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.
Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”
Due to the presence of prehistoric soil and footprints immediately in front of the cave walls, researchers had to set up their analysis instruments nearly 8 feet away. Credit: Adapted from ACS Omega 2026, DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
Studying cave art without touching it
In a study reported in
ACS Omega
, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.
To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.
Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to
reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye
. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.
Natural varnish and possible torch marks
Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:
Thin layers of calcite glowed blue under a blacklight. These mineral layers had been left behind by water flowing over the limestone surface, forming a natural varnish that covered parts of the artwork.
Some areas fluoresced orange. That glow could come from hot charcoal or other burning materials, such as a lit torch, rubbed against the wall to create the drawings.
“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.
The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.
Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026,
ACS Omega
DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.
Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

title: Scientists Just Found a Key Ingredient for Superconductivity at Room Temperature
content:
Superconductors are materials that allow electricity to flow without electrical resistance, eliminating energy losses caused by heat. They could transform technologies ranging from power grids and magnetic levitation trains to quantum computers. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers have discovered that a key requirement for superconductivity can persist even at room temperature.
Scientists searching for a superconductor that works at room temperature have identified a potential way forward. New research from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich shows that electrons can form the pairs needed for superconductivity even at room temperature. The findings, published in
, suggest that a different requirement may be preventing these materials from conducting electricity without resistance.
The key appears to be how paired electrons behave collectively. Although the pairs can survive at much higher temperatures than previously understood, they must also act in a coordinated way for superconductivity to emerge.
Why Superconductivity Remains So Difficult to Achieve
Electrical resistance causes energy to be lost as heat whenever current passes through an ordinary conductor. This is useful in a toaster, where resistance heats a metal wire until it glows, but undesirable in power transmission and electronic devices. Superconductors eliminate electrical resistance, potentially enabling more efficient energy storage, levitating trains, and advanced quantum computers.
First authors Maialen Ortego Larrazabal and Jiasen Niu with the measuring equipment Credit: LMU, Faculty of Physics
The obstacle is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C (-436°F), often using expensive liquid helium. Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911, and researchers made major progress in the mid-1980s when they identified materials that could become superconducting at temperatures around -173°C (-279°F). Yet these higher-temperature superconductors presented a mystery: the established theory explaining conventional superconductivity could not account for their behavior.
“We don’t understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all,” says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. “And if you don’t understand it, you can’t systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.”
Electron Pairs Can Survive at Room Temperature
Superconductivity requires two essential conditions. First, electrons must form partnerships known as Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated quantum state called phase coherence. Without both conditions, a material cannot sustain superconductivity.
In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and phase coherence emerge together as the material cools below a critical temperature. The new research shows that these processes can occur separately in high-temperature superconductors. Electron pairs can form and remain stable at temperatures far above the point where electrical resistance disappears, including at room temperature.
“This is really good news,” says Swart. “We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren’t possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.”
The Remaining Barrier to Room-Temperature Superconductivity
The findings indicate that the interaction binding electrons into pairs can remain sufficiently strong at room temperature. This shifts attention toward phase coherence, which may be the limiting factor preventing superconductivity at higher temperatures.
“The ‘glue’ that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature,” says Swart. “This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.”
The researchers have not demonstrated room-temperature superconductivity, but their results help narrow the search for what is missing. Swart plans to investigate how phase coherence develops and what prevents electron pairs from achieving it at higher temperatures.
“If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.”
Reference: “Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor” by Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Genda Gu, Ingmar Swart and Milan P. Allan, 5 November 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in One of the Deadliest Cancers
content:
Fox Chase researchers identified ANO6 as a potential pancreatic cancer target that may slow tumor growth and reduce immune suppression. Credit: Fox Chase Cancer Center
Researchers have identified another potential approach to treating pancreatic cancer, with early experiments suggesting that blocking a protein could slow tumor growth and strengthen immune defenses.
Pancreatic tumors can be surrounded by tissue so dense that it compresses blood vessels, making it difficult for nutrients to reach cancer cells. Even under these conditions, the cells continue growing. How they obtain the materials needed to survive has remained an important question.
Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified one way pancreatic cancer cells obtain cholesterol and other fats, known as lipids. Their study, published in
Nature Cancer
, also identified a protein that helps control this process and could offer a potential target for cancer treatment.
The research focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These tumors contain large numbers of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), cells that produce and organize connective tissue. As CAFs and their collagen fibers expand, they can compress nearby blood vessels, restricting the tumor’s blood supply.
Cells that restrict blood flow also feed tumors
Despite contributing to this nutrient shortage, CAFs also help cancer cells overcome it.
“We found that CAFs can act as a source of these nutrients,” said Edna Cukierman, PhD, a professor and co-leader of the Cancer Signaling and Microenvironment Program at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Using laboratory and animal models, we discovered that CAF units acquire cholesterol from the bloodstream and transfer it to nearby pancreatic cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis”
Trogocytosis occurs when one cell takes small pieces of another cell’s membrane during direct contact. In this case, pancreatic cancer cells acquire pieces of CAF membranes containing cholesterol and other lipids that support their survival and growth.
The researchers discovered that this transfer depends on a protein called anoctamin 6 (ANO6), which helps prepare the CAF membrane for the exchange.
“These findings help explain how pancreatic cancer cells obtain essential nutrients despite the unusual structure of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment,” said Igor Astsaturov, MD, PhD, a professor at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Cancer-associated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders. They actively support tumor growth by transferring lipids to cancer cells.”
When researchers reduced or eliminated ANO6 in CAFs, the cells became less effective at supporting pancreatic cancer cell survival. In mouse models, tumors supported by CAFs with functional ANO6 grew substantially faster than those without functional ANO6.
Cholesterol may exhaust cancer-fighting T cells
The same nutrient transfer process also appeared to interfere with the immune system.
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are immune cells that recognize and kill cancer cells. When these T cells come into contact with CAFs, they can acquire membrane material containing cholesterol. Excess cholesterol in the tumor environment can contribute to T-cell exhaustion, making these immune cells less effective at fighting cancer.
“With Serge Fuchs, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and co-author on the paper, we were surprised to find that the same cellular mechanism can benefit the tumor in two ways – by supplying cancer cells with lipids while also weakening cancer-fighting T cells,” said Astsaturov. “Targeting ANO6 could potentially disrupt both of these tumor-supporting functions at the same time.”
In mouse models, blocking ANO6 reduced cholesterol accumulation in T cells within tumors and improved markers of their activity. Laboratory experiments also showed that T cells exposed to CAFs with reduced ANO6 were better able to kill cancer cells.
Two drugs reduce tumor weight in mice
The researchers then tested whether drugs that interfere with ANO6-dependent activity could slow tumor growth. In mouse models, treatment with niclosamide or clofazimine significantly reduced tumor weight. Niclosamide also reduced cholesterol delivery to pancreatic cancer cells.
These findings suggest that targeting ANO6 could both restrict a nutrient source for pancreatic tumors and improve the immune response against them. However, the results remain preclinical, and further research is needed to determine whether selectively blocking ANO6 would work as a treatment in patients.
Trogocytosis is also only one of several ways pancreatic cancer cells may obtain lipids. The researchers suggest that the drugs tested could potentially help treat other difficult cancers, although that possibility requires further investigation.
“We believe our findings identify ANO6 as a potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt the nutrient supply supporting pancreatic cancer cells and reduce the immune-suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment,” said Astsaturov.
The findings also build on nearly a decade of research into how the tissue surrounding pancreatic tumors supports cancer growth.
“Excitingly, reducing ANO6 expression also disrupted the stromal synapse-mimicry circuit we previously identified, which coordinates tumor nutritional support, CAF-unit metabolism, and immune suppression. These findings position ANO6 as the missing mechanistic link that unifies nearly a decade of discoveries by our team,” said Cukierman.

title: Could Vitamin B12 Hold the Key to Treating a Rare Genetic Disorder?
content:
Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that helps the body produce healthy red blood cells, maintain nerve function, and synthesize DNA. Credit: Stock
A search for genes linked to lifespan uncovered an unexpected connection between RNA splicing, metabolism, and developmental disorders.
A mutation linked to a rare developmental disorder appears to interfere with more than the way cells process genetic instructions. Researchers discovered that it also disrupts vitamin B12-dependent metabolism in tiny roundworms. Supplying the vitamin restored key metabolic processes and corrected developmental abnormalities in the animals, raising questions about whether a similar approach could eventually help people.
The findings concern Verheij syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that causes developmental delays, growth problems, and short stature in children. The condition is associated with changes in a gene involved in RNA splicing, an essential process that prepares messenger RNA for protein production. During splicing, cells remove unnecessary sections of RNA and join the remaining pieces to form instructions that can be used to build proteins.
A Genetic Mutation Reveals a Metabolic Problem
The discovery emerged from experiments with the roundworm
C. elegans
, a widely used model organism in biological research. Scientists were initially searching for genes that influence lifespan when they identified a mutation in a splicing-related gene associated with Verheij syndrome in humans. Worms carrying the mutation grew more slowly and remained unusually small, resembling some of the developmental problems seen in affected children.
Further genetic screening and metabolic analysis showed that the mutation altered biochemical pathways that depend on vitamin B12. These pathways support normal growth and cellular function. When researchers administered vitamin B12 to the affected worms, the disrupted metabolic processes returned to normal, and the animals’ developmental defects were corrected.
In the disease model shown on the left, C. elegans worms exhibit a stress response, which is visible in green. Administration of vitamin B12 counteracts this effect, as can be seen on the right. Credit: W. Huang / Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing
“We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism,” says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. “Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.”
Could the Findings Apply to Human Patients?
To investigate whether similar metabolic disruptions occur in humans, the researchers examined publicly available data from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at University Hospital Cologne, to obtain blood samples from patients with Verheij syndrome. The analyses provided evidence that metabolic pathways affected in the worms may also be altered in people with the condition.
However, the results do not establish that vitamin B12 supplementation can treat Verheij syndrome in humans. Additional research is needed to determine whether the metabolic changes contribute directly to patients’ symptoms and whether correcting them could provide clinical benefits. The findings also suggest that metabolic dysfunction may deserve greater attention in other genetic disorders involving defective RNA splicing.
“Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases,” says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. “A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.”
Reference: “Vitamin B12 alleviates spliceosomopathy via phospholipid remodeling” by Jonathan Kölschbach, Hormos S. Dafsari, Emily Baum, Anna Löhrke, Chun Kew, Ivan Dikic, Wenming Huang and Adam Antebi, 7 August 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76295-9

title: Scientists Discover That Male and Female Hearts Age in Surprisingly Different Ways
content:
Scientists have discovered that the heart does not age uniformly, with inflammation and tissue scarring concentrated in unexpected locations. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals surprising differences in how male and female hearts age at the cellular level.
The heart may age very differently from one region to another. A detailed study of mouse hearts found that molecular signs associated with chronic inflammation and tissue scarring were concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root, rather than being distributed evenly throughout the organ.
Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) identified these hotspots by mapping thousands of cells from young and aged mice. Published in
Aging Cell
, the findings suggest that structures often overlooked in cardiac aging research may play a central role in how the heart changes over time.
Why the Heart’s Valves May Be Aging Hotspots
Previous studies of cardiac aging have largely concentrated on heart muscle, particularly the left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and throughout the body. Because mammalian heart muscle cells have very limited capacity for regeneration, understanding how they deteriorate with age has been a major research priority. The JAX team instead examined the entire heart, using single-cell and spatial genomics technologies to identify both the molecular activity of individual cells and their locations within the organ.
“The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine,” said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. “It turns out they’re home to many of the cells we’re interested in, and that’s where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated.”
“Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue,” Rosenthal said. “We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don’t age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don’t age at the same rate either, even within one individual.”
Maps of young (top) and aged (bottom) mouse hearts showing where immune cells called macrophages (left) and fibroblasts (right) are most abundant. Blue indicates fewer cells and red indicates more cells. The highest concentrations of both cell types appear around the aorta and heart valves, regions identified as hotspots of age-related change. Credit: The Rosenthal Lab, The Jackson Laboratory
How Immune Cells and Fibroblasts Influence Cardiac Aging
Aging is associated with persistent, low-grade inflammation, sometimes called “inflammaging.” The researchers focused on two cell populations involved in this process: immune cells that help regulate inflammation (macrophages) and structural cells responsible for maintaining connective tissue and producing scar tissue (fibroblasts). In older mouse hearts, macrophages showed increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and tissue remodeling, while fibroblasts exhibited molecular patterns linked to fibrosis (or scarring).
“To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life,” Rosenthal said. “What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.”
The team also detected increased activity in two genes within the identified hotspots.
produces an inflammatory signaling molecule, while
(also known as p21) helps regulate the cell cycle and is commonly associated with cellular senescence. Their activity points to changes in signaling between neighboring cells, not simply isolated changes within individual cell types. “We’re not talking about single genes. We’re talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts,” Rosenthal said.
A Surprising Discovery in Young Hearts
Some molecular markers traditionally associated with senescent cells were already present in young mouse hearts. Cellular senescence occurs when cells permanently stop dividing, often following stress or damage. Senescent cells can contribute to inflammation and tissue deterioration, but the researchers found that the presence of commonly used senescence markers does not necessarily establish that a cell has entered this state.
“What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren’t where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us,” Rosenthal said. “That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don’t mean a cell is senescent. There’s nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.”
Male and Female Hearts Show Different Molecular Changes
The study also identified differences in how fibroblasts responded to aging in male and female mice. In males, older fibroblasts showed greater involvement in molecular pathways associated with fibrosis. In females, aging was linked more closely to pathways involved in heart development and protein production. These findings describe differences in gene activity, not demonstrated differences in cardiac function or disease risk.
Rosenthal noted that cardiovascular disease patterns also differ between men and women, with disease risk generally increasing after menopause in women. However, the mouse findings do not establish a mechanism for those human differences. Comparisons with previously published human heart data did identify several shared molecular programs associated with aging, including pathways involved in cellular stress responses.
“Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process,” said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.
What the Findings Could Mean for Cardiovascular Health
Age is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but separating changes caused by aging itself from those associated with lifestyle, environmental exposures, and disease remains difficult. Although the study did not establish whether the identified cellular changes directly impair heart function, the controlled conditions in which the mice lived helped researchers examine the biological effects of aging.
“Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself,” said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. “Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.”
The researchers are now investigating how exercise, diet, and disease influence the interactions between immune cells and fibroblasts. Their goal is to distinguish changes that occur during normal aging from those that may increase the heart’s susceptibility to disease. Although the current findings do not immediately suggest new treatments, the cellular map provides a foundation for studying how inflammation and fibrosis develop in specific regions of the aging heart.

Clark, Leon Frommer, Sikander Hayat, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, J. Matthew Mahoney and Nadia A. Rosenthal, 5 November 2026,
Aging Cell
DOI: 10.1111/acel.70768

title: Perovskite Connect 2026 in review: 30% growth, top keynotes and what our attendees said
content:
Perovskite Connect 2026 in review: 30% growth, top keynotes and what our attendees said
Last month we held
Perovskite Connect 2026
at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED. It was only the second edition of the event, and attendance grew by about 30% over last year. Since then we have asked attendees, speakers and exhibitors what they thought, and the feedback was great. Here is a short look back, and a look ahead to 2027.
A full room for the opening keynotes at Perovskite Connect 2026
The keynotes
The conference opened with keynotes from Oxford PV, CubicPV, GCL and Microquanta, and the second day opened with Qcells, Caelux, Tandem PV and SolarEdge. Together, these talks gave a clear picture of where perovskite tandems stand on their way to the market:
Oxford PV
spoke about the era of perovskite-on-silicon, and what it takes to bring tandem solar modules to market.
discussed how accelerated testing and energy yield analysis can establish the bankability of perovskite products.
Microquanta
both presented their four-terminal tandem strategies, an approach that avoids the current-matching constraints of two-terminal devices.
described scaling perovskite-silicon tandems from lab records to production on industrial M10 wafers, and
shared the wins and the remaining challenges of producing and deploying 1x2 meter perovskite products.
Tandem PV
talked about its path to bankability for perovskite/silicon tandem panels, and
SolarEdge
showed how module-level power electronics can protect the gains of tandem modules from mismatch losses.
The exhibition area at the Estrel
Beyond the keynotes, the program had many more strong talks. Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin presented its Solar TAP approach to turning perovskite innovation into impact, imec/EnergyVille covered structures and processes for upscaling perovskite modules and tandems, and ZSW presented a recycling procedure for perovskite minimodules. The day before the conference was dedicated to masterclasses and tours, including a tour of HZB.
The main topics
The talks covered the whole perovskite value chain, and a few themes came up again and again:
Tandems move to the fab
: perovskite-silicon tandems were the clear focus, with both two-terminal and four-terminal approaches on show, and many talks on the path from lab cells to full-size wafers and modules.
Bankability and reliability
: accelerated stress testing, energy yield, encapsulation and LED-based stability testing, with talks from CubicPV, Tandem PV, Eternal Sun, Everlight and H.B. Fuller.
Production tools and processes
: roll-to-roll production (Energy Materials Corporation, nextCoatema, ROWO Coating), inkjet printing (UniJet, Dracula Technologies), spatial ALD (Kalpana), laser processing (Bergfeld Lasertech) and contactless metallization (HighLine Technology).
Materials and inks
: metal oxide transport layers (Sofab Inks, TU Dortmund), interface materials (Nano-C), printable ITO inks (PINA Creation), organic transport materials (LinXole) and the high-purity materials needed for reproducible manufacturing (Noctiluca).
New module designs and sustainability
: Power Roll's ITO-free micro-groove modules, Homerun Energy's vertically integrated value chain, and ZSW's work on recycling.
Overall, the message from Berlin was that perovskites are moving from lab records to production lines, and that the focus now is on bankability, reliability and cost at scale.
What attendees said
We received a lot of great feedback. Here are some of our favorites:
"The event was truly excellent, striking the perfect balance between scientific and technological insights and industrial perspectives. The presentations provided a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art and the progress being made towards the industrialization of various technologies. The exhibition area was also a great opportunity to connect and exchange ideas with leading companies in the field."
- Luigi Vesce, University of Rome Tor Vergata
"I found the Perovskite Connect event to be excellent. The agenda was very relevant and everyone stayed on time and on topic. Having several of the leaders in this industry (Oxford, GCL, Tandem, Cubic, etc) made the networking extremely valuable."
- David McDougall, H.B. Fuller
"I thought the event was very well organised, with a really high quality of companies attending and some excellent presentations. The overall energy and networking were very good too."
- Neil Spann, Power Roll
"Thank you for a fantastic event. It was extremely useful for us as an early-stage start-up. The masterclass and talks were high quality and very practical, the HZB tour was a highlight, and the networking drinks led to several valuable new connections."
- Nathaniel Davis, TwoPhold
"The event was very well organized and a lot of interesting contributions were given."
- Immo Koetschau, Oxford PV
If you attended and missed a talk, all the presentations were recorded and are available to attendees on TechBlick's event platform.
Join us in 2027: speak, exhibit, sponsor
We're already working on
Perovskite Connect 2027
, which will be held on October 20-21, 2027 at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, with masterclasses and tours on October 19. Perovskite Connect will again be co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED, a major gathering for the printed, flexible and roll-to-roll electronics industries.
We expect the event to keep growing. Tandem production lines are coming online, and more perovskite companies are moving from pilot lines to products. If your company works on perovskite materials, equipment, cells, modules or testing, this is the place to show your work to the people who matter.
If you would like to present, exhibit or sponsor in 2027, please
contact us now
. Early conversations get the best speaking slots, booth locations and sponsorship options. You can also
register to attend here
. See you in Berlin!

title: Perovskite nanocrystal LEDs reach four times higher efficiency without a ligand-exchange step
content:
Perovskite nanocrystal LEDs reach four times higher efficiency without a ligand-exchange step
Researchers at Kookmin University, Sungkyunkwan University and Hanyang University have developed perovskite nanocrystal LEDs that need no separate post-synthetic ligand-exchange process, reaching a maximum external quantum efficiency of 11.4%, around four times the 2.7% obtained from conventionally synthesized nanocrystals.
Perovskite nanocrystals are attractive for display LEDs for their high luminescence efficiency, color purity and solution processability, but nanocrystals from conventional synthesis come coated in large quantities of organic ligands with long hydrocarbon chains. Those chains impede charge transport between neighboring nanocrystals, so building a high-performance device has generally required a post-synthetic step to swap the long-chain ligands for shorter ones. Much recent work has approached the problem through ligand design instead, including
an “all-in-one” organic ligand for emissive nanocrystals
a strategy that reached 31.7% EQE
Rather than treating the surfaces after synthesis, the team controlled the nanocrystals’ surface chemistry from the synthesis stage, using a heat-up method based on a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction. The resulting films showed lower energetic disorder and more ordered crystalline structures than films made from conventionally synthesized nanocrystals, along with significantly improved charge transport between nanocrystals. These nanocrystals were then incorporated directly into the emissive layer of the devices.

title: i-Components says a customer will test its perovskite barrier film in space this year
content:
i-Components says a customer will test its perovskite barrier film in space this year
Korea-based barrier film maker
i-Components
says it has supplied samples of a space-grade barrier film for perovskite solar cells to global space companies. The company says one customer plans to test a flexible perovskite solar cell in space within the year.
Barrier films protect perovskite cells from moisture and oxygen, and the company says durability is critical for space-grade cells that must keep their performance in extreme conditions. i-Components says it is working with perovskite solar cell makers in Japan and China to validate film quality and improve its specifications, and that it has the quality and mass-production capability to supply products to customer requirements.
The company says it has invested a total of 25.5 billion won (about US$19 million) to add production lines for barrier films for displays and solar cells, and plans to expand beyond displays into solar. “We will prepare for development and mass production of barrier films in step with the commercialization pace of perovskite solar cells, from ground applications to space,” a company official said.

title: 机制搭台 场景拓展——浙江省整县光伏试点（钱塘区）建设经验-索比光伏网
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 规划目标
政策分类依据: 三年行动方案设定整县光伏新增装机、总量翻番等定量目标与时间表
content:
浙江省发展改革委深入贯彻党中央、国务院关于碳达峰碳中和的决策部署，落实国家能源局整县屋顶
开发试点部署，制定《浙江省光伏发电高质量发展三年行动方案(2026—2028年)》，将杭州市钱塘区等11个县(市、区)列为整县示范，加强调度指导，推动试点地区先行探索、形成经验。在浙江省发展改革委指导下，杭州市钱塘区把整县光伏试点建设作为全域低碳建设的重要抓手，坚持机制搭台、资源挖潜、场景拓展、效益转化一体推进，试点建设取得阶段性成效。目前，该地光伏装机已达200万千瓦，成为浙江省首个集中式光伏装机超百万千瓦的区县，有力支撑区内2个省级零碳园区创建。
一、强化“三端协同”，夯实试点落地支撑
一是高位统筹建机制。钱塘区将整县光伏试点作为区委、区政府重点工作，成立由主要负责同志任双组长的工作专班，系统构建“134X”工作体系，即锚定三年新增装机不低于200万千瓦、总量翻番的总目标，聚焦工业、地面、机构3个特色领域，打造园区、建筑、交通、农旅4个“光伏+”融合应用场景，因地制宜培育X个创新示范场景。二是全域排摸绘底图。地毯式摸排光伏资源，形成255万平方米工业园区屋顶、15万平方米公共机构屋顶、1.5万余亩坑塘水面3张资源清单，绘制全域开发“一张图”，全部建成后光伏装机可突破350万千瓦。三是流程重塑提效率。建立新型光伏项目备案管理机制，出台区级
项目开发建设管理办法，探索容缺办理机制，推动项目从立项到并网审批周期压缩60%以上。
二、强化“四维发力”，拓展光伏应用场景
一是推动“光伏+园区”全面铺开。综合采用“自投自建”“屋顶租赁”等开发模式，推动存量工业园区屋顶“能建尽建”，到2028年形成碳排替代空间17万吨。二是推广“光伏+建筑”一体集成。大力推广BIPV光伏建筑一体化应用，加快推进党政机关、高校等公共机构15万平方米屋顶空间光伏建设。三是打造“光伏+交通”共建共享。统筹利用园区道路、交通主干道和农田机耕路等闲置资源，推动辖区内高速收费站、港区光伏建设全覆盖，实现清洁能源100%消纳。四是深化“光伏+农旅”一地两用。迭代升级“渔光互补”复合开发模式，形成全省首个超百万千瓦级“渔光互补”集群，年发电量预计超12亿度。
三、强化“三链联动”，放大试点综合效益
一是做优惠企链。坚持“以光伏降成本、以绿电增效益”，推动工商业光伏“应上尽上”，降低企业用能成本，同步探索绿电直连。以全省首个绿电直连项目为例，项目实现绿电精准溯源和产品碳足迹核算，投运后每年可减少碳关税支出近千万元。二是做实富民链。坚持发展成果全民共享，推广“企业投资+村集体出租”发展模式，让农户屋顶、机耕路等闲置资源变成可持续的增收资产。临江街道东庄村利用7万平方米闲置空间打造的光伏项目年内投用，预计每年为村集体增收50万元。三是做强产业链。把丰沛绿电资源作为牵引产业转型、强链补链的重要抓手，今年以来已招引落地绿色能源产业项目7个、总投资近百亿元。目前全区共集聚绿色能源产业规上企业79家，其中国家级绿色工厂14家。
下一步，省发展改革委将围绕碳达峰碳中和目标，持续强化全省整县光伏试点统筹，进一步加强规划衔接、政策指导和跟踪调度，及时总结提炼试点地区在机制搭台、场景拓展、绿电直连等方面的经验做法，通过政策解读、案例推广等方式推动在全省复制应用，为全省新型能源体系建设提供有力支撑。

title: 广期所：调整多晶硅期货相关合约交易手续费标准-索比光伏网
content:
广期所11月11日发布公告，调整多晶硅、碳酸锂期货相关合约交易手续费标准。
关于多晶硅期货PS2711合约、碳酸锂期LC2711合约有关事项的公告
经研究决定，现将多晶硅期货PS2711、碳酸锂期货LC2711合约有关事项公告如下：
多晶硅期货PS2711合约交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之一、日内平今仓交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之二点五，交易指令每次最小下单数量中的每次最小开仓下单数量为5手、每次最小平仓下单数量为1手，非期货公司会员或者客户单日开仓量不得超过200手。
碳酸锂期货LC2711合约交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之零点八、日内平今仓交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之零点八，交易指令每次最小下单数量中的每次最小开仓下单数量为2手、每次最小平仓下单数量为1手，非期货公司会员或者客户单日开仓量不得超过800手。
单日开仓量是指非期货公司会员或者客户当日在单个合约上的买开仓数量与卖开仓数量之和。套期保值交易、做市交易的单日开仓数量不受上述标准限制。具有实际控制关系的账户按照一个账户管理。

content:
为进一步健全陕西省电力市场矛盾纠纷多元化解机制，妥善处置电力市场化交易中的各类争议，依法保护各类经营主体合法权益，维护公平有序的电力市场秩序，近日，陕西省发改委、西北能源监管局联合印发通知，组建陕西省电力市场纠纷调解委员会（以下简称“调委会”）。
调委会将聚焦纠纷受理与调解处置、调解员队伍建设、制度规则建设、纠纷研判与风险预警、政策宣贯与咨询服务、协同联动与闭环管理等方面履行职责，受理发电企业、售电公司、电力用户、电力交易机构、电力调度机构以及虚拟电厂、独立储能、分布式电源聚合商等新型经营主体在电力中长期交易、现货交易、合同履约、电量计量与结算、电价执行、绿电绿证交易、辅助服务与需求侧响应等业务中产生的民事商事争议。
下一步，西北能源监管局将与陕西省发改委一道，加强业务指导和监督，推动调委会公平公正开展调解，促进电力市场矛盾源头化解、就地化解，为全省电力市场健康有序发展提供有力保障。

title: EGL3 secures marine infrastructure licence for Scottish waters
content:
A marine infrastructure licence has been granted for Eastern Green Link
3 (EGL3), a joint venture between SSEN Transmission and National Grid Electricity
Transmission (NGET). The licence permits the installation and operation
of the project's infrastructure in Scottish waters.
The approval follows years of project development, marine surveys, public
engagement and environmental assessments, providing greater insight into
the habitats and species along the planned cable route.
This process has helped shape the planning and design of the project, ensuring
environmental impacts are minimised.
EGL3 will deliver a high-voltage subsea electricity link capable of transporting
renewable energy between Scotland and England, helping to meet growing
electricity demand.
James Johnson, Joint Venture Programme Director at SSEN Transmission, said:
"This marks a really significant moment for the project and reflects
many years of design development and marine survey activities that have
underpinned this successful outcome."
"Throughout the development process, we have worked closely with local
communities, marine stakeholders, offshore developers and asset owners,
whose feedback has helped shape our plans and minimise potential impacts
wherever possible."

title: Taean Wind Power signs major supply chain deals for 504 MW offshore wind project
content:
Taean Wind Power has reached a key milestone after securing multiple domestic
supply chain partnerships for the 504 MW Taean
offshore wind farm.
The agreements include a design, supply, transport, installation and commissioning
contract with HD Hyundai Heavy Industries.
The company has also signed a Capacity Reservation Agreement with LS Cable
& System and LS Marine Solution for the supply and installation of
subsea cables, alongside a monopile supply agreement with GS Entec.
The partnerships with these leading suppliers reinforce the growing capabilities
of Korea's offshore wind supply chain and manufacturing sector.
This announcement marks another step towards the project's scheduled completion
in 2029.

title: Wergeland CEO discusses Norway’s offshore wind opportunities
content:
In the latest episode of Offshore Wind Leaders, host Ivar Slengesol spoke
with Margunn Bjørnestad, CEO of Wergeland Group, about leadership, industrial
development and the challenges of building a competitive offshore wind
industry.
Drawing on a career spanning finance, infrastructure and offshore energy,
the conversation examined how offshore wind can benefit from lessons learned
in oil and gas, while recognising the need for a simpler, lower-cost approach.
The conversation explored Wergeland Group's involvement in projects such
as Hywind Tampen, Hywind
Scotland
and Culzean,
and how experience gained through offshore project delivery has helped
shape the company's approach to floating wind.
The episode also examined the challenge of reducing costs, with the view
that floating wind must move beyond demonstration projects and adopt a
more industrialised approach if it is to become more competitive.
Another theme was the need for greater project certainty. Without a steady
pipeline of projects, the industry risks losing talent and investment to
more active markets.
The conversation also highlighted the role of a strong domestic market
in helping Norway build expertise, strengthen its supply chain and compete
internationally.
Workforce development was another area of focus, with discussions over
the need to support the industry's long-term growth, highlighting the importance
of attracting young people to offshore wind and ensuring the sector develops
the leadership required for growth.
The full conversation is available in the fourth episode of Offshore Wind
Leaders, a PowerPod series exploring the people, strategies and decisions
shaping the future of offshore wind.

title: Nexans completes testing milestone for Orkney Link subsea cable
content:
Nexans has reached a milestone for the Orkney Link Project by completing
the Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) of the 220 kV subsea cable connection
between Orkney and mainland Scotland.
The testing concludes more than a year of manufacturing work at the company's
cable facility in Halden, Norway. Successful completion of the FAT confirms
the cable is ready to move into the next stages of project delivery.
The Orkney Link, being developed by SSEN Transmission, it plans to connect
Finstown in Orkney with Dounreay in Caithness through a 220 kV HVAC link.
The project includes approximately 53km of subsea cable and will provide
transmission capacity of up to 220MW.
The new connection is expected to strengthen the electricity network and
support the integration of renewable energy generated in Orkney.
Onshore cable installation and jointing works are expected to continue,
while preparations are advancing for the offshore installation campaign
planned for 2027.
