title: Jensen Huang Is Out; Are Inference Providers Screwed?
content: What a week. Jensen Huang , the CEO and cofounder of the world’s second-most-valuable company, resigned, Nvidia said Thursday morning , after reports of extramarital affairs both with a woman alleged to have spied for Beijing as well as a woman who reported to him at Nvidia . Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress will become interim CEO, the company said, while it searches for a permanent successor. Much remains uncertain, including implications for Nvidia’s business of selling advanced AI chips and for Nvidia’s aggressive investments in AI model developers and infrastructure startups that are holding up the AI economy. I’m sure we’ll be getting into all of it in the upcoming days. Meanwhile… It’s not only a tough week to be Huang, but it’s also a tough week to be an inference provider , a well-funded category of startups that help developers use open-source models at high speeds across Nvidia servers. Most recently, Fireworks , one of the most heavily-funded startups in this category, suffered a security breach that exposed customer data to hackers and has also prompted some large customers to consider ditching the service. (In a note to customers, Notion , one of Fireworks’ customers, suggested that, although the inference provider promised it was using zero data retention , meaning that it wouldn’t store any data from Notion after processing a request, Notion later learned that data was actually being retained.) While that incident was bad enough on its own, it exposes a potential systemic vulnerability for the rest of the inference market: the cloud firms that inference providers lease capacity from And that makes me wonder whether it will have a chilling effect beyond Fireworks. The breach was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud provider that Fireworks uses, we reported Wednesday . And increasingly, inference providers are turning to these smaller cloud providers because they can’t rent enough servers from the major cloud providers, such as Microsoft , Amazon and Google , Cathy and I reported in the same article. Capacity shortages have gotten so dire that inference providers like Modal have started using more than 30 different small clouds to access servers they can turn around and rent to their own customers. Many of these cloud providers are young startups themselves and don’t have the security expertise of a major cloud provider. So you can imagine that the sort of breach Fireworks suffered might not be out of the realm of possibility for its competitors, including Baseten , Modal and Fal . Already, I’ve heard of at least one customer of these inference providers that is considering moving its business off these startups. If it did that, it would run open-source models either in its own data centers or with the hyperscalers because its leaders are so spooked about what happened with Fireworks. I’d imagine that other developers, especially those that were affected by the Fireworks breach, would be wary of using alternative inference providers that are sourcing their compute from the same small neoclouds as well. These security concerns could further accelerate the trend Cathy and I wrote about on Wednesday where inference providers buy their own Nvidia servers and stand them up in data centers themselves, rather than renting such servers from other clouds. In building their own data centers, the inference firms could get more control of the security of the cloud services they provide and also improve their gross profit margins, since they’re not paying to rent servers from cloud providers that themselves need to hit certain profit margins. (Margins have been a hurdle for inference providers since they first emerged on the scene three years ago.) This buy-versus-rent approach has its own downsides, though. Finding the power, land and chips to build a data center or even just leasing an existing data center requires a lot of specialized expertise that most companies don’t have. That could explain why inference providers like Fal have job postings for staff to help with data center efforts. And it’s not clear whether the inference providers can do a better job at sourcing chips and managing data centers than the dozens of other cloud providers that are already doing so. Plus doing so requires billions of dollars at a time when the capital markets are seizing up for smaller borrowers (see: the recent neocloud crisis). That’s why Fireworks, for example, has explicitly told investors that it believes acquiring chips and building data centers is a commodity and that its true defensible moat lies in developing software that can run models quickly. Of course, dozens of other firms are trying to do the same thing. Here’s what else is going on… People On The Move Meta Platforms is changing the leadership of its massive data-center operation, with longtime executive Santosh Janardhan telling employees that he is stepping down as head of global infrastructure and will leave the company early next year. Dave Brown , a veteran of Amazon Web Services whom Meta hired in July, will take over as infrastructure head. title: Alice Huang’s Companies Invested in DeepSeek, Promising Nvidia Chips
content: The network of companies tied to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy in a romantic relationship with Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, recently invested in Chinese AI star DeepSeek, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. The investments were meant to forge closer ties with DeepSeek so Alice Huang’s companies could supply a steady stream of Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips, which are banned from sale to China, according to one of the three people. The investments, which haven’t previously been reported, illustrate the hidden yet important role Alice Huang and her companies have played in China’s AI industry. DeepSeek shot to global stardom in early 2025, after its R1 model showed capabilities comparable to those of OpenAI’s latest model at the time but was trained at a fraction of the cost. Nvidia’s Huang, whose resignation as CEO was announced on Thursday morning, had been one of DeepSeek’s most prominent admirers. In his keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in January, he said DeepSeek’s R1 was “really, really exciting work.” “We’re so happy with it,” he added. But DeepSeek, like other Chinese AI firms, has been held back by a persistent AI chip shortage, resulting from U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips in place since late 2022. While DeepSeek has been at the forefront of adapting to Huawei chips, it is still trying to gain access to more Blackwell chips, which can be used for research, and as a fallback in case Huawei chips don’t work. During DeepSeek’s second funding round between July and October, DeepSeek employees introduced companies connected to Alice Huang and her family, Century Litong and its parent company, Shanghai-listed Jiangsu Lettall Electronics, to several investors, the people said. The DeepSeek employees made clear that Century Litong and Lettall, collectively referred to as “Litong Inc” in the industry, were a substantial supplier of blackmarket Nvidia AI chips, and therefore deserved allocation in the hotly contested funding round, the people added. Litong Inc. ended up participating in the funding round, which raised 105.5 billion yuan ($15.8 billion) in October, the people said. The companies invested through special purpose vehicles set up by DeepSeek’s investors for the funding round. As a result, no entity from Litong Inc appears directly on DeepSeek’s shareholder list . One of the investments went through a special purpose vehicle set up by Beijing-based venture capital firm Monolith Management, according to stock exchange filings and Chinese corporate records. Lettall invested 95 million yuan ($14 million) in the entity, the records show. Monolith, founded by former Sequoia Capital China partner Cao Xi, is the third-largest investor in DeepSeek after two rounds of funding. It couldn’t be learned how much money in total Litong Inc put in DeepSeek, but a person with direct knowledge of DeepSeek’s second funding round said the group of companies invested through multiple vehicles. Century Litong has priority access to Nvidia’s chips thanks to its status as one of the chip designer’s preferred cloud partners, which it attained just four months after it was founded in 2023. The company operates data centers and rents out AI chips including Nvidia’s graphics processing units. Litong imported 240,000 Nvidia chips worth at least $7.5 billion into China since 2023, despite tightening U.S. export controls, The Information reported earlier this week. The close ties between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang made the imports possible, The Information reported. Century Litong has managed to import Blackwell chips despite a U.S. crackdown on chip smuggling since late last year, according to two other people with direct knowledge of the situation. Alice Huang never held a stake or an executive position at Century Litong or Lettall (whose name in Mandarin is also Litong). The Information mapped out her relationship with these companies through a myriad of former ownerships and corporate transactions that involved her sister Huang Yu and her husband Kang Wei. DeepSeek’s second funding round drew nearly 30 investors, many of them Chinese tech giants and state-affiliated firms. It was the biggest Chinese AI company fundraising so far. The round valued DeepSeek at about 615.5 billion yuan ($92 billion). Tencent and battery giant CATL were the biggest backers.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns, Creating Uncertainty for the AI Sector
content: Nvidia CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resigned in a stunning turn of events that upends the world’s second-most-valuable company and rattles one of the foundations of the AI economy. Finance chief Colette Kress will become interim CEO, Nvidia said in a statement on Thursday morning. The move came three days after the board announced an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly concluded earlier this year that Huang had developed a close relationship with a woman they believed was spying for Beijing. Huang on Sunday also apologized to Nvidia employees for having an extramarital affair. The company said it was initiating a search for a permanent CEO “and will consider internal and external candidates.” Huang has internally and externally pushed back on the need for a succession plan, according to employees and Huang’s public commentary. He has dozens of direct reports but no clear No. 2. Nvidia’s shares were trading down 12% in early trading on Thursday. In its statement, Nvidia said thanked Huang for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” It did not elaborate on the reasons for Huang’s departure. Nvidia said one of its directors, Harvey Jones, would become the company’s “first-ever chair of the board.” In a securities filing, Nvidia said the board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. His departure appeared to come quickly. As of Tuesday, Huang was operating normally within Nvidia, including preparing for next week’s quarterly earnings call, according to a person familiar with the situation. A Tuesday meeting with Nvidia’s executive staff—a group of 50 or so executives who mostly report directly to Huang—proceeded normally, other than Huang’s delivery of a short apology to his colleagues at the start of the meeting, that person said. But Huang faced other revelations that added to precariousness of his position at Nvidia. Several former employees told The Information that Huang was widely believed to have been in a separate relationship with Kimberly Powell, a vice president who ran healthcare technology-related initiatives at the company and reported directly to Huang. The alleged relationship was widely discussed by employees for years, these people said. Earlier Wednesday, The New York Times earlier reported that video evidence of the affair between the two executives had surfaced internally earlier this year. Huang and Powell, along with representatives for Nvidia and Huang, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Earlier in the week, Nvidia had hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the investigation into Huang’s conduct, and President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang. The Information reported Tuesday that Alice Huang worked at a Chinese firm that distributed hundreds of thousands of advanced Nvidia AI chips despite a U.S. ban on their sale to China. Huang’s firing is a major blow to a company that he has become synonymous with since he co-founded it in 1993. Nvidia has soared to Olympian heights during the current AI boom, in part through Huang’s relentless style of leadership and aggressive efforts to stay ahead of its competition. Nvidia’s graphics processing units are the dominant chips for training and running AI models, turning the company into a business juggernaut that reported $216 billion in revenue last year. In recent years, Huang told some senior colleagues that he planned to run Nvidia until he is 120 years old, according to a former Nvidia manager who heard the comments (Huang is currently 63). “This company was built around him for 30 years,” this person said. “This is unimaginable.” Huang’s ouster also creates uncertainty for the broader AI sector. He has been one of the most high-profile public advocates for AI, rebutting concerns about its safety even as others in the industry have raised them. And he has aggressively pumped Nvidia’s cash into a new crop of cloud companies that rent out its server chips to AI developers, as well as into AI developers such as OpenAI. Nvidia is planning to invest $10 billion in Anthropic’s initial public offering next week and has discussed providing credit guarantees related to a proposed data center in West Virginia that Anthropic plans to lease. As of earlier in the fall, Nvidia had $100 billion in equity investments in other companies. Huang’s ouster is likely to rattle stock market investors who have already been skittish about some of the smaller firms that depend on Nvidia server chips and capital to run their businesses. Huang’s successor will likely face questions about whether they plan to continue Nvidia’s practice of investing so freely in its customers. It also remains unclear whether any successor to Huang will have the clout to continue the tactics that helped make Nvidia so dominant—for example, its muscling of key partners like the chip manufacturer TSMC for capacity. The company is facing an array of competitors eager to chip away at its power. Google, AMD and Amazon offer competing server chips, and more potential competition is coming from Anthropic and OpenAI. “Jensen is so singular,” says an executive at a company that is a major customer of Nvidia’s chips. The fallout from Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang could spread beyond him. In recent days, The Information and other media organizations have reported on the reluctance of leaders in the Commerce Department in the past to impose export controls on AI chips and related technologies that would prevent China from getting access to them. Nvidia has lobbied aggressively against such rules in the past. (Late Wednesday, The Information reported that the Commerce Department is finalizing a new rule that would close a loophole that has allowed Chinese AI firms to remotely access advanced AI chips.) Lawmakers from both parties have begun calling for tougher export controls on Nvidia’s chips and related products, which Congress could pass in the coming weeks as part of a collection of legislation called the National Defense Authorization Act. A House subcommittee has also asked Huang to testify behind closed doors at a hearing in Washington next week about his relationship with Alice Huang. The outcome of that and other related probes could lead to further departures from Nvidia. Huang’s ouster could also be awkward for members of his family: His daughter and son, Madison and Spencer Huang , both work at Nvidia, along with Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez .

title: Exclusive: SES AI CEO Says Drone Sales Could Lead to Profit
content: In 2021, SES AI CEO Qichao Hu proudly appeared in a company video brandishing a technological breakthrough: a full-size next-generation lithium-metal battery ready to power an electric vehicle, produced in the company’s new factory in South Korea. But in the five years since then, Hu has found no EV maker prepared to deploy that battery in a commercial car, putting millions of dollars of SES’ investment at risk. So this year, Hu threw in the towel and completely rebuilt the South Korean manufacturing line. Now it’s configured to make batteries one-tenth the size of the EV battery—the perfect scale to power drones. And though SES lost $73 million last year, Hu thinks drone battery sales could eventually allow the company to turn a profit. The pivot reflects the impact of the drone boom on the next-generation battery industry after a roughly four-year-long industry slump. In recent months, startups that had earned either very little or no revenue ever have started to see some real money flow in. Virtually all of the next-gen startups, like SES, continue to lose money. But Hu said the early drone revenue received so far means SES is finally earning some money back on the more than $55 million in accumulated equipment and other capital costs incurred since he founded the company in 2012. “All the technology that we’ve developed the last 14, 15 years, now we are monetizing all that technology,” he told me. It’s the latest abrupt strategic turn for SES, which Hu founded out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he was a postdoctoral researcher. The original idea was to develop a battery that used lithium metal as the anode. The industry as a whole had been seeking to develop such a battery since the 1970s because pure lithium metal delivers exceptional energy density, which would translate into extraordinary EV driving range. But no one could manage that feat because lithium metal can explode or catch fire when it comes into contact with air or moisture. Over the subsequent years, Hu developed various working versions of the battery. In 2016, his lab produced a design known as anodeless, because it created its own lithium-metal anode internally on the first charging cycle, thus not requiring some costly equipment. It delivered energy density exceeding 500 watt-hours per kilogram, well over twice that of conventional lithium-ion batteries. But it would sustain only 10 or so charge-discharge cycles. “We were like, ‘OK, who’s going to want these things?’ No car company would want that. So we just basically filed a patent and then shelved it,” Hu said. Hu went on with development until his big 2021 unveiling of the full-size battery. Honda, Hyundai and General Motors all invested in the company, with loose plans to use the battery in future EVs. Then came the downturn in U.S. EV sales. Suddenly, expensive next-gen batteries no longer interested major car companies, which instead began looking to power their EVs with cheaper “good enough” conventional batteries. All three carmakers ended their battery development projects with SES. To survive, Hu repeatedly changed his plans: He moved SES into stationary storage batteries; he developed a materials discovery system using AI; he added silicon and lithium-iron-phosphate batteries to SES’ repertoire. Those gave SES some cash—last year, the company generated $21 million in revenue, and it projects $30 million to $35 million in revenue this year, most of it from stationary storage batteries. But Hu is now focusing on the drone boom, triggered by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which has taken that anodeless battery off the shelf and into use for interceptor drones. “Drones have thrown a lifeline to a lot of the battery startups in the U.S.,” he said. Last month, SES finished the first stage of reconfiguring the drone battery production line in its Chungju, South Korea, factory. It has the capacity to produce 1 million battery cells per year, enough to power approximately 150,000 small quadcopters. Hu said the company will triple the capacity in the second quarter of next year to 3 million battery cells. He said he is responding to a “flood of orders,” but these are still only from countries and companies validating the performance of SES’ batteries. He said he is on the verge of getting commercial production orders that will take up most or all of the planned production. Compared with the EV market, selling drone batteries is easy, Hu suggested. Car companies spend five or more years putting new batteries through tests before making any commercial production commitment—and so far, virtually no next-gen battery startup has gotten past this gauntlet. “Drones are way faster. It’s maybe nine months of validation,” he said. “For some of the smaller drone companies, it could be like three months or just a week.” Most battery startups I speak with have also pivoted to supplying the drone industry, and I asked Hu whether the market for drone batteries is getting saturated. He said it isn’t. “The drone market is still quite early and still evolving, whether it’s defense or civilian commercial applications,” he said. “I do think battery companies need to move quickly and establish some level of scale to actually matter in the space.”

title: Commerce Department Finalizing Long-Awaited AI Remote Access Rule

content: The Commerce Department is finalizing a long-awaited rule that will prevent Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to two people familiar with the process. The move could help the department push back on criticism that it has acted too slowly to create policies to limit China’s access to advanced AI technologies—rules that have been opposed by influential companies such as Nvidia. The rule, which could be announced as soon as this month, will expand existing semiconductor-related controls from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and extend them to seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to prevent remote access and chip smuggling into China, the people said. Commerce is currently consulting with other government agencies on the rule before it can be finalized, they added. The change will implement a policy that Nvidia has pushed against in previous lobbying efforts, as it would put more stringent requirements on data centers abroad that are major buyers of its chips. Commerce’s decision to finalize the rule could, in part, reflect Nvidia’s waning influence in Washington. Nvidia’s board has been investigating CEO Jensen Huang for an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and is reportedly considering whether to remove Huang from his position. The Bureau of Industry and Security has faced growing criticism that it has moved too slowly in implementing new export control policies at a time of heightened AI competition with China. The remote access loophole, in particular, meant restrictions on chip exports to China could be easily circumvented, allowing Chinese AI companies to train their models using the most advanced U.S. chips. That criticism of the Bureau of Industry and Security and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler has heightened in recent days after news reports that the Commerce Department halted an investigation into Megaspeed, a Singaporean company embroiled in a scandal involving its former top executive and Huang, after Nvidia intervened . Several prominent Republican lawmakers have called for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to explain why the agency has not moved to block Megaspeed from buying advanced chips. The so-called remote access loophole has long been a focus area for export control policy experts, who argue that it allows Chinese AI companies to gain access, through data centers largely in Southeast Asia, to advanced chips that would otherwise be restricted. There have been previous efforts under the Trump administration to address the loophole through Commerce rules, The Information has reported . And the White House recently provided feedback to Congressional staff requesting a provision be added to export control measures currently being debated in a must-pass defense bill that would have required the Commerce Department to create a rule preventing remote access to certain chips, The Information reported Monday. If finalized, the new Commerce rule could allay some of these concerns by taking action on an issue at the top of the wish list for many China hawks. Remote Access Under the current Commerce Department regime, certain countries such as Saudi Arabia and Vietnam need licenses to receive exports of advanced AI chips. The licenses include controls and conditions such as restricting remote access to companies, as well as different security measures that prevent chip smuggling. Along with Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, the new countries that will now be subject to those licensing requirements include Brazil, Indonesia, Norway and South Africa, said the two people familiar with the rule, which extends to Nvidia Blackwell chips and above. One of the people said that in addition to preventing remote access to advanced AI chips, bringing those new countries under the licensing regime could also combat smuggling. That’s because the rule will now require customers seeking chip exports to tell the Commerce Department who is receiving the chips and what they’re going to be used for, and will subject them to ongoing monitoring. The rule will likely face pushback from governments in those countries, as well as U.S. companies who operate there. Under the new rule, however, U.S. company-run data centers in those countries will not require licenses to receive exports of chips, as long as they restrict remote access of AI chips of a certain capability to countries where the U.S. has arms embargos, such as China, Russia and Venezuela. Those U.S. companies will instead be subject to new reporting requirements, including informing the Commerce Department if they have any customers from arms-controlled countries. The companies will also have to report who the customers in those countries are and how much compute they have, one of the people said. While the new rule is restricted to seven additional countries for now, it could expand, according to one of the people, who said the rule is designed to put other countries on notice that chip smuggling and remote access in a way that is contrary to U.S. interests will not be tolerated. The Commerce Department is also planning to formally rescind the Biden-era AI licensing framework known as the diffusion rule, one of the people said. In May 2025, the Trump administration announced its intention to rescind the rule and issue a replacement, though it never formally scrapped it.

title: Nvidia CEO’s Exit Looms
content: Well, that didn’t take long. Jensen Huang’s time as CEO of Nvidia appears to be coming to an end, according to multiple reports that the board was meeting Wednesday night to consider his future. Just three days ago, it announced an inquiry into whether he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” but at the time the board said it had “confidence in Jensen.” It seems likely that confidence was undermined by a New York Times story on Wednesday that said Huang had had an affair with a company executive in addition to an industry executive who may also be a Chinese spy. If the board dumps Huang, it will demonstrate that no CEO is indispensable, no matter how vital their role is. Many observers had insisted the opposite in recent days, perhaps understandably. After all, Huang co-founded the company and still owned 3.6% of the stock, making him one of the biggest shareholders. As we wrote in this piece , he “has a hand in nearly every aspect of the company’s day-to-day operations.” Along with Sam Altman, he’s been probably the most articulate advocate for AI. Most importantly, his vision of the future has positioned Nvidia to benefit more than any other company from the AI boom, driving its market capitalization to a high of $5.8 trillion in early October, according to Koyfin. Not surprisingly, investors have freaked out about the possibility of his exit. After falling 10% in the first two days of this week, Nvidia was trading down 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday to around $160, giving the company a market capitalization of around $3.85 trillion. The question now is who will replace him. There are no obvious internal candidates, although Nvidia could appoint an executive as interim chief. That suggests the board will have to go outside Nvidia. Earlier this week we suggested that either AMD CEO Lisa Su or Arm CEO Rene Haas could succeed Huang. On TITV on Tuesday , D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria suggested Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan. This is a big job. Who can do it? Anthropic’s Not-So-Powerful Trust Anthropic executives are meeting with investors this week, ahead of next week’s expected IPO. Here’s one thing investors should ask: How concerned should they be about the Long-Term Benefit Trust, a secretive group that has the power to appoint and remove a majority of Anthropic’s board? Their job is to ensure the company is run in a way that balances the financial interests of shareholders with Anthropic’s mission to develop advanced AI “for the long-term benefit of humanity.” What a balancing act! And who controls the trust? It turns out that the trustees—who include a former Fed chair, a health policy wonk, and a physics professor at Harvard University—pick future trustees. (There’s a vacancy for a fifth trustee, by the way, and it pays $400,000 a year!) In other words, it’s a closed club, which seems to give those four an extraordinary amount of power. But things are not exactly what they seem. A big restriction on the trust’s power essentially defangs it. The trust appoints and can in theory remove four of Anthropic’s seven directors. In reality, it can only remove three of those four unilaterally. A committee of Anthropic’s board, which includes Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, has to approve the trust’s removal of the fourth board member. If the board committee opposes the director’s removal, Anthropic’s employees get involved and have to approve it. As Amodei and other company co-founders essentially pick three of the seven board members, the co-founders could counter any effort by the trust to replace a majority of the board. The board committee also has a role if the trustees want to remove one of their members. Anthropic says in its filing that “these procedural requirements are intended to promote collaboration between the Trustees and our leadership in identifying and sourcing candidates” for the board and the trust. The rules “do not give our board of directors the substantive ability to limit the LTBT’s freedom to elect directors of its choosing.” It’s hard to take that statement seriously, given that it’s precisely what the requirements do. The point is that it’s the founders rather than the LTBT who control the company. For investors, that’s probably good news, given how aggressively Anthropic competes—see here and here —and given its success in overtaking OpenAI. Of course, as AI models become more sophisticated and more powerful, a clash over its risks to society seems likely. Don’t be surprised if one day a huge fight breaks out between the trust and the board reminiscent of OpenAI’s 2023 brawl over the short-lived removal of CEO Sam Altman. When that happens, expect the founders to prevail. The Information’s Top 50 If there’s one field every parent should encourage their child to go into, it’s cybersecurity. The spread of AI, with the ability to uncover holes in software that hackers can exploit, is becoming a huge deal. NBC News reported this week that cybersecurity firms were “turning away new clients” because they were overwhelmed! It shouldn’t be surprising, then, that cybersecurity is a hot sector for startups. In our latest installment of The Information 50—our annual list of the most promising startups out there—three of the four most highly valued companies are security startups. Here’s the list. title: Sequoia Capital to Invest in AI Holding Co. Sequence
content: Sequoia Capital is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Sequence Holding, a one-year-old business that just announced a $7.7 billion insurance acquisition co-led by Michael Dell’s family office, say people familiar with the matter. This will be Sequoia’s second known investment in a new category of holding companies. These aim to buy businesses in established industries such as accounting, insurance and HOA management and then replace or complement some human work with AI. The new money raised from Sequoia is likely to allow Sequence, which has been scouting for targets, to make more acquisitions, according to people familiar with the matter. Previously Sequoia invested in its partner Ravi Gupta’s Ithaca Holdings, which announced a $1.3 billion deal to buy dating app Bumble . The planned investment in Sequence, which hasn’t been reported, comes amid an overhaul at Sequoia since partners Alfred Lin and Pat Grady took the leadership reins at the storied venture firm in November. In recent weeks, the firm has merged its early and growth-stage investing team, shut down its London office to focus on U.S. investments and reworked its so-called evergreen fund that its former leader Roelof Botha created to hold shares in startups after they go public for longer than the firm normally does. Under Lin and Grady, the firm has aggressively pursued AI deals this year after Sequoia sat out some major AI investments during Botha’s leadership. The firm co-led Anthropic’s May funding round at a $965 billion valuation and made dozens of AI-related investments since last November. Representatives for Sequoia and Sequence Holdings declined to comment. Dell Partnership Founded in 2025, Sequence Holdings has raised at least $75 million from 8VC, Lux Capital and Conviction. Last month, it took insurance broker Baldwin Group private in a cash and debt deal co-led by Dell’s family office DFO Management. In recent years, venture capitalists have been pouring money into such permanent holding companies, with the goal that they can help modernize these services or traditional businesses with AI tools. Such investments are likely to generate returns more like private equity, say four times the investments, paling besides venture’s targeted 10X returns. But investors say they should be more predictable and generate another way for VC firms to return cash to their backers. These VC-backed AI holdings companies have all done large acquisitions the past year. Josh Kushner’s Thrive Capital last year set up Thrive Holdings, which raised more than $2 billion in funding from investors including Altimeter, D1 Capital Partners and SoftBank. Last month, that firm agreed to buy 152-year-old home security firm ADT in an all-cash deal worth $15.3 billion including debt. Meanwhile, General Catalyst invested in holding company Long Lake in 2024. Earlier this year, Long Lake took American Express Global Business Travel private for $6.3 billion. Sequence Holding has already made a minority investment in privately held community lender BankSouth. Sequence’s CEO Michael Lee said in a podcast interview with Conviction partner Sarah Guo that AI reduced consumer loan underwriting turnaround times by 94% since March and cut commercial loan underwriting from 30 days to 11 days. Lee also said Sequence is taking a different approach than traditional private equity firms, by focusing on doing one deal per year instead of multiple ones, and allowing its engineers to take part in important decision-making.

title: New Startup Voya Energy Proposes Replacement for Loud Diesel Generators in Data Centers
content: In 2023, Shayle Kann, a venture capitalist with Energy Impact Partners, was mulling a longstanding fixation—how to get rid of the loud and polluting diesel generators used to provide backup power for most AI data centers. He put the question to the head of his technology team: Isn’t there some material rivaling the enormous energy density of hydrocarbons that could do the same job cleanly and quietly? The result was Voya Energy, a Hayward, Calif., startup that promises to replace diesel generators with a novel electrochemical process that converts scrap aluminum into electricity without emissions, toxic waste or noise. In August, Kann’s firm led a $35 million Series A round for Voya at a $113 million valuation. Voya leads a lineup of three energy technology companies that made the 2026 edition of The Information 50 , our list of the most promising tech startups, published Wednesday. The other two are Critical Loop, a Long Beach, Calif., startup that offers fast backup power generation, which we profiled last month after it landed a big deal to power an aerospace facility for Anduril Industries; and Parallax, a San Francisco startup that makes natural gas turbines using 3D-printed technology. All three startups fit neatly into the biggest technology boom in decades, offering ways to power AI data centers. Richard Wang, a battery expert whom Kann recruited to be Voya’s CEO, said he expects to deploy pilot versions of the aluminum generator in 2028 and to deliver commercial models to AI data centers and other customers in 2029. But for now, the idea is little more than a concept: No one appears to have ever used metals as fuel to power a commercial industrial facility, and Voya has made only a rudimentary version of the equipment necessary to do so. The idea is that a machine turns scrap aluminum like soda cans into small pellets. A mechanical system loads those pellets into a generator and combines them with an electrolyte, which releases electricity held electrochemically inside the aluminum. The generator delivers that electricity to the data center, and the spent aluminum converts to aluminum trihydrate, which can be used to remake pellets, according to Wang. Voya’s origins start with Kann and his Energy Impact colleague. By early 2024, they had stumbled across a concept that had been around awhile—that the electricity stored in some metals could efficiently deliver a lot of power, just as fossil fuels do. They decided to try to fund a startup to see if they could make that idea work as a business. In 2024, a friend introduced Kann to Wang, a next-generation battery expert. Wang attracted attention in 2021 when he sold Cuberg, a lithium-metal battery startup he co-founded a few years earlier while a graduate student at Stanford University, to Northvolt for an undisclosed amount. Early in 2024, Northvolt shut down Cuberg (and a few months later Northvolt declared bankruptcy). Wang was now out of work. A friend introduced him to Kann, who told him about his idea of how to replace diesel generators. Wang wasn’t impressed. “This looks half-baked,” Wang recalled responding. “I don’t think this is ready to be a company yet, honestly, and I don’t know if I’m the right person to do this right now.” But Wang agreed to join Energy Impact as a technology fellow and explore the concept. After four or so months, he had warmed to the idea. “You look at the ease of producing the metal, the ease of consuming the metal to make electricity, how easy it is to convert it back and forth between metal and metal oxide,” he told me. Wang had started with the periodic table and narrowed down the metals that would be best as electricity generators to magnesium, zinc, iron and aluminum. Aluminum quickly won the bake-off. “Aluminum stands out naturally as having the highest energy density, being an incredibly abundant, very available commodity resource,” he said. Wang told Kann he had changed his mind. “He came to us and he was like, ‘I think this should be a company and I would like to run it,’” Kann said. In April 2025, Energy Impact led a $13 million seed round for Voya. The standard system Wang has in mind would involve two storage containers, one a standard 20-foot-long container with a 2-megawatt aluminum generator, and the other a 10-foot one containing enough aluminum pellets to produce 100 megawatt-hours of energy. Wang said the advantages of such a system include that aluminum rivals hydrocarbons in terms of energy density and can be stored at an industrial site in a much more compact space than diesel because it’s not flammable and releases no emissions. Voya claims the system converts 57% of the pellets into electricity, higher than diesel’s average 35% conversion efficiency. The one ultrapolluting aspect of using aluminum is the smelting stage. By relying on scrap aluminum, Voya is initially avoiding dealing with the smelting question. But Wang said there are ways to sharply reduce the amount of energy used to smelt the metal and the emissions released in the process. “Our ultimate ambition is to really think about designing our own smelting cells and systems and ultimately plants that are of our own creation, because we think that’s the pathway to get to the lowest-cost-possible aluminum,” Wang said.

title: AI Inference Startups Are Quietly Buying Their Own Chips
content: The fast-growing crop of startups that lease computing capacity from cloud firms and then resell it, without spending a nickel on their own AI chips, are at a crossroads. Finding it harder to line up enough computing capacity to serve their customers, some are starting to buy their own chips, which is likely to drastically change the economics of their business. The difficulty in getting enough compute also has pushed some of these startups to look for computational resources from dozens of smaller neoclouds, which tend to have more available capacity than larger hyperscalers such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. News this week of a hack of Fireworks, one of the best known of these startups, highlights the risk of that approach. The hack was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud used by Fireworks, according to a person with knowledge of the situation. The hack has prompted some of Fireworks’ customers to consider switching to alternative providers. Startups like Fireworks are known as inference providers—because they cater to customers who need chips to run AI models, a process known as inference. They don’t own chips or data centers, instead devoting their efforts to building software that can help customers better optimize running AI models. These firms have grown quickly. Fireworks, for instance, passed $1 billion in annualized revenue in July, the company said, up five times from what it was generating a year earlier, while others like Fal have doubled their revenue pace in a matter of months, The Information reported in September. Fireworks was most recently valued at $17.5 billion, the highest of the group. But the growing difficulty of securing compute could jeopardize the sector’s rapid growth. In some cases, cloud firms are becoming less willing to lease capacity to rivals. CoreWeave earlier this year decided to stop selling compute to Baseten, according to someone with knowledge of the strategy. CoreWeave launched its own inference service in March this year and didn’t want to devote computing resources to a rival, the person said. Someone close to Baseten disputed the idea that Coreweave had reduced the compute it provides to Baseten. A spokesperson for CoreWeave said: “We have good relationships with inference providers and many of them are our partners, consuming CoreWeave services where it makes sense for their business model, which we are happy to support.” Paddy Srinivasan, CEO of cloud firm DigitalOcean, said he prioritizes “customers that have real-end user demand…versus those reselling our capacity…honestly, because we have so much demand from companies that are actually building software on our stack.” DigitalOcean operates its own data center space. Some inference providers have responded by striking deals with a wide range of smaller cloud firms. Modal, for example, went from working with all the major hyperscalers as cloud partners and a few neoclouds in its first four years as a company to signing up to 30 additional neocloud partners in the past year, when it couldn’t get Nvidia Blackwell chips at the prices and quantity it wanted from larger cloud firms, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson in an interview. Modal still works with hyperscalers, though it tends to rent other chips from them, Bernhardsson said. Some cloud industry executives said inference providers that don’t own their own hardware could be left high and dry if demand for computing capacity disappears or bigger firms decide to cut them off. Inference companies are “like the WeWork of the [graphics processing unit] world, where WeWork went out and signed these long-term leases over office space and then turned around and tried to sell it on a short-term basis. It works well while it works, until either demand or financing dries up,” said Kent Draper, chief commercial officer for Iren, which has built its own data centers. “People are seeing the benefits of vertical integration.” No Choice Some inference providers have decided they have no choice but to invest in their own hardware. Fal, which focuses on hosting video and image AI models, has recently started buying its own Nvidia chips to place in leased data centers, said Raghu Rao, who joined Fal in July to help build out its data center strategy. Fal will use the $1.65 billion in venture capital funding it raised earlier this month to help pay for extra compute capacity, including GPU purchases and renting cloud space from AWS. Fal is also hiring staff to help with the data center effort, Rao said. Fal’s plans to buy hardware haven’t previously been reported. “As we’ve grown tremendously, there’s been a need to both lease as well as own our own hardware,” Rao said. Fal has also expressed interest to investors in borrowing money to help it finance hardware purchases, according to a person with knowledge of the plans. Rao declined to comment on the possibility of debt financing. In recent months, inference providers have been talking to lenders and intermediaries about borrowing money to pay for compute contracts with neoclouds, according to someone involved in the deals. The providers are seeking ways to use borrowed money rather than the equity they have raised from venture capitalists to secure the compute they need, the person said. Together, meanwhile, started buying its own hardware last year and was planning to have 250 megawatts of its own data center capacity by the end of 2026, The Information reported in March. Baseten is also looking to buy Nvidia GPUs to place in data centers that Baseten intends to manage, according to people with knowledge of the plans. CoreWeave itself has made a similar transition. Until now, it has mostly operated data centers owned by other companies. But it revealed last year that it is building its own campus, believing that is the best way to control its hardware. Not all inference companies think they need to own hardware, though. Fireworks leaders have told investors the company believes acquiring the physical chips and building and operating data centers is a commodity, and Fireworks has a more defensible moat in building software that can run models quickly, according to ae person familiar with its strategy. It does not currently have plans to buy hardware, another person with knowledge of Fireworks said. Modal has also told investors it’s interested in purchasing more of its own hardware for data centers, a person with knowledge of those plans said. In an interview, Modal CEO Bernhardsson said the company will do whatever it needs to do to get capacity it needs, but he doesn’t think differentiation comes from owning hardware, echoing a critique hardware owners like Iren have lobbed at inference providers such as Modal. “The hardware layer…is not…where I feel like a lot of value is created. At the end of the day, you’re just buying chips and reselling them,” Bernhardsson said. “So we focus on the software layer. That’s where we’re always going to add the most value.”

title: Anthropic’s PE-Backed Venture, Ode, Pushes to Get Paid for AI Results
content: Private equity firms and AI labs are sorting out how to charge clients and hire enough engineers for joint ventures they’ve launched to build custom AI tools for businesses. That comes as private equity firms are looking to the technology to boost profits, including at companies they’ve struggled to sell. One such team-up is Ode with Anthropic , which launched in July with $1.5 billion in capital commitments from investors including Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman. Ode currently charges most of the several dozen businesses it works with a fixed fee to develop and launch custom AI products, people familiar with the partnership say. The company lets clients retain ownership of the AI software it builds, the people said, allowing them to keep using or even sell the tools once completed without paying Ode ongoing fees. Those terms help Ode attract customers that balked at the terms offered by the team of engineers at Anthropic that embeds with enterprises, which seeks to retain ownership of the custom software it builds and license it back to customers, one of the people said. But Ode has been looking at other ways to earn more on AI projects. Some Ode executives initially proposed coinvesting in companies that were also its customers, but Blackstone’s team pushed back on the idea, one of the people said. Instead, Ode decided to charge performance-based bonus fees on top of the fixed project fees, allowing it to earn more if clients hit specific financial targets. Less than 10% of Ode’s clients are paying those performance-based fees, one of the people said, though Ode is aiming to grow that share. Setting the fees can be difficult because the company and its customers both need to agree on how to measure any AI-driven gains, including setting a baseline and financial or product-related goals. The fees may be negotiated once a contract is signed and Ode then does some early exploratory work and collects data, giving both sides enough information to set terms before moving on to the building phase, the people said. Ode inherited some of its business from Fractional AI, a startup founded in 2024 that the venture acquired in May for an undisclosed sum. Fractional already worked mostly with private equity–backed companies to automate tasks and build custom AI software, and Fractional co-founders Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel became Ode’s CEO and chief technology officer, respectively. One of those clients, risk and compliance software company LogicGate, paid a fixed fee in the low seven figures for a project that began under Fractional last summer and finished this fall, said LogicGate CEO Diego Panama. (LogicGate’s backers include growth equity firm PSG, which led the company’s $113 million funding round in 2021.) Ode engineers built a custom agent that shortened LogicGate’s client onboarding from 120 days to 90 days or less. LogicGate received full intellectual property ownership and training to run the tool independently, Panama said, and it subsequently began selling the agent to other businesses and has signed several deals. The agent is set to launch publicly at the end of the month. Around half of Ode’s clients are software or business services companies, while the rest come from industrial and other sectors. Its client base is split roughly equally between portfolio companies of Ode’s backers, including at least six Blackstone companies, and other businesses. All of the Blackstone portfolio companies working with Ode currently pay fixed fees, including accounting firm Citrin Cooperman, where Ode engineers built a new onboarding system, similar to the work they did at LogicGate. Blackstone typically sets targets to improve earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in a specific division when evaluating how an AI project is working. Other AI services firms are experimenting with similar fee structures. Hyde , backed by Bain Capital Ventures and General Catalyst, launched last year and helps businesses build custom AI models using their own data. Clients then own the customer models and can run them themselves or pay Hyde to host them. Hyde typically assigns two engineers to work with clients for around four weeks per project, charging for that work plus a recurring fee for using its software platform. (Clients also pay for compute based on usage.) Around half its contracted revenue includes a portion of fees tied to results—its fee for an automotive client, for example, is tied to whether agents meet certain car sales goals. Hyde CEO Anirudh Sanga said demand for Hyde’s services has roughly doubled monthly for the past three months. At the same time, a shortage of engineers is limiting how much business AI services firms can take on. Anthropic itself has sought to address the shortage, announcing a $100 million effort last month to train 10,000 deployment engineers at customer and partner companies by the end of next year. Upstart AI services firms are also competing with major tech firms for talent. Microsoft in July committed $2.5 billion to its Microsoft Frontier Co. with the aim of placing 6,000 engineers inside enterprise customers, partnering with consultancies like Accenture and EY . As of November 2025, Fractional had an annual revenue run rate of over $12 million. At the time of the May acquisition, it was generating around $30 million in ARR, which has since nearly tripled, according to people familiar with the matter. But Ode is being selective about the clients it takes on because it doesn’t have enough engineers to handle all potential business, one of the people said, though it has enough demand for at least two to three times its current workload. OpenAI Deployment Co. has faced similar constraints. The venture, backed by TPG and other investment firms including Brookfield Asset Management and Bain Capital, has sought to hire more engineers to expand available capacity. Ode has made several acquihires and acquisitions since launching, including one of Casper Studios , which designed specialized AI products using Claude. Ode remains open to exploring more deals, a person familiar with the venture said, but is looking to expand its services or geographic reach instead of simply adding more people. Hyde, for its part, isn’t currently seeking acquisitions, but it has declined several takeover offers, Sanga said, mostly from large companies looking to quickly establish their own AI deployment team. Fintech and Crypto Startups to Watch Each year, The Information picks 50 startups that have the potential to be breakout stars. This time around, our fintech and crypto category featured new twists on trading and betting and startups positioned to benefit from growth in emerging areas like agentic payments . There’s Fomo, a viral trading app that plans to branch out from memecoins to tokenized stocks, and Catalyst, a startup offering agents that help people trade across venues like prediction markets and crypto exchanges. On the payments side, Natural is offering bank accounts for AI agents, while stablecoin-backed card provider Kast is expanding beyond retail customers by courting merchants. What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.
Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.

Fahrwerke zählen zu den am stärksten belasteten Baugruppen eines Flugzeugs. Beim Start, bei der Landung und beim Rollen wirken hohe Kräfte auf Radachsen, Kolben, Bolzen und weitere sicherheitskritische Komponenten. An Funktionsflächen berühren Lager, Buchsen oder Dichtungen die Bauteiloberfläche. Reibung, lokale Druckspitzen und wiederkehrende Lasten erzeugen dort Verschleiß. Gleichzeitig greifen Kälte, Hitze, Feuchte, Kerosin, Reinigungs- und Enteisungsmittel sowie Eis, Sand und Staub die Oberflächen an und begünstigen Korrosion.
Bei einer Wartung eines Fahrwerks bauen Fachleute Komponenten aus, reinigen, prüfen und vermessen sie. Kleinere Schäden schleifen sie aus, solange die Reparaturgrenzen dies erlauben. Bei zu großem Materialverlust bleibt häufig nur der Austausch. Das verursacht Kosten, verlängert Standzeiten und bindet Ressourcen.
Üblicherweise schützt Hartchrom die Funktionsflächen vor Verschleiß und Korrosion. Strengere Anforderungen an Umwelt- und Arbeitsschutz erhöhen jedoch den Bedarf an Alternativen. Bei beschädigten Bereichen reicht Schutz allein nicht aus: Hier zählt eine zweite Fähigkeit, nämlich verlorenes Material gezielt wieder aufzubauen, ohne die Eigenschaften des hochfesten Grundwerkstoffs zu beeinträchtigen.
Klassische Schweißverfahren eignen sich dafür nur bedingt. Zu viel Wärme verändert bei hochfesten Luftfahrtstählen das Gefüge, beeinflusst die mechanischen Eigenschaften und kann durch Verzug zu geometrischen Abweichungen führen. Besonders kritisch ist die Wärmeeinflusszone. Eine geeignete Reparaturtechnologie muss deshalb zwei Anforderungen zugleich erfüllen: Sie erzeugt eine sichere metallische Verbindung und begrenzt den Wärmeeintrag.
LEGATO entwickelt eine neue Reparaturkette
An dieser Herausforderung setzt das Forschungsprojekt LEGATO an. Das Gesamtvorhaben untersucht verschiedene Aspekte künftiger Fahrwerke und bündelt dafür Kompetenzen aus Forschung und Industrie. In einem Teilvorhaben entwickelt das Fraunhofer-Institut für Lasertechnik ILT eine laserbasierte Reparaturkette für hochbelastete Fahrwerkskomponenten.
»Im Mittelpunkt unserer Forschung stehen drei Schritte«, verrät Kim Julia Kallies, Projektleiterin am Fraunhofer ILT. »Material lokal wieder aufbauen, die Randzone mechanisch einstellen und die erzeugte Schicht zuverlässig prüfen.«
Die Liebherr-Aerospace in Lindenberg bringt als Industriepartner Anforderungen aus Fertigung, Wartung und Instandhaltung ein: reale Bauteile und Schadensbilder ebenso wie Vor-gaben zu Werkstoffen, Härte, Oberflächenqualität und geringem Wärmeeintrag. Der assoziierte Partner Hegenscheidt-MFD unterstützt das Teilvorhaben mit Erfahrung in Rollier- und Festwalzprozessen.
»Für uns zählt am Ende nicht nur, ob eine Schicht im Labor funktioniert«, erklärt Harald Betsch von Liebherr-Aerospace. Er ist Senior Expert Thermal Spraying/Welding im Bereich Materials and Processes. »Entscheidend ist, ob der Prozess zu realen, belasteten Fahrwerkskomponenten, ihren Werkstoffen, Schadensbildern und Reparaturgrenzen passt. Genau diese Anforderungen bringen wir aus Entwicklung, Fertigung und Instandhaltung in LEGATO ein.«
Den Materialauftrag übernimmt EHLA, eine Hochgeschwindigkeitsvariante des Laser Metal Deposition (LMD). Ein Laser schmilzt metallisches Pulver auf und trägt es lokal auf die Bauteiloberfläche auf. Die hohe Prozessgeschwindigkeit und der vergleichsweise geringe Wärmeeintrag machen EHLA besonders interessant für wärmeempfindliche und hochfeste Werkstoffe.
Kim Kallies und ihre Forschungsgruppe untersuchen im Projekt mehrere Werkstoffkombinationen aus der Anwendung. 300M repariert das Team mit artgleichem Material. Für korrosionsbeständige Schichten prüft es unter anderem einen martensitischen Edelstahl, einen speziell für EHLA entwickelten Werkstoff. Auch 15-5PH, ein hochfester, korrosionsbeständiger Stahl für Fahrwerksstrukturen, gehört zu den untersuchten Werkstoffen.
Eine Besonderheit von EHLA führt zum nächsten Schritt: Die Prozessgeschwindigkeiten liegen deutlich näher an mechanischen Bearbeitungsverfahren als beim konventionellen LMD. Dadurch koppelt das Team den Materialauftrag direkt mit einem mechanischen Bearbeitungsschritt. Genau diesen Ansatz verfolgt SCaRB.
EHLA und Rollieren in einem Prozess
SCaRB steht für Simultaneous Coating and Roller Burnishing. Der Ansatz verbindet den EHLA-Materialauftrag mit einem direkt nachlaufenden Rollierprozess. Während der Laser metallisches Pulver auf die Bauteiloberfläche aufträgt, folgt das Rollierwerkzeug mit definiertem Abstand und bearbeitet die frisch erzeugte Schicht noch während des Beschichtungsprozesses.
Die hohe Prozessgeschwindigkeit von EHLA schafft dafür die Grundlage: Materialauftrag und Rollieren laufen in einem gemeinsamen Prozessablauf. Das Team spannt das Bauteil zwischen Beschichten und mechanischer Bearbeitung nicht neu ein, spart Rüstzeit und nutzt den kurzen zeitlichen Abstand zwischen beiden Prozessschritten.
SCaRB nutzt nicht nur die Geschwindigkeit des EHLA-Prozesses, sondern auch dessen Rest-wärme. Die frisch aufgetragene Schicht ist kurz nach dem Materialauftrag noch warm und verformt sich dadurch leichter plastisch. Der Abstand zwischen Laser und Rollierwerkzeug bestimmt, wie warm und verformbar die Schicht beim Rollieren noch ist. Damit steuert dieser Abstand Oberfläche, Härte und Eigenspannungen mit.
Für die Umsetzung entwickelte Hegenscheidt-MFD ein Rollierwerkzeug, welches das Fraunhofer ILT in die Maschinenumgebung integrierte. Über die Zustellung des Werkzeugs stellt das Team die Rollierkraft ein. Mit wechselbaren Rollen passt es Rollenradius und Rollenhärte an die jeweilige Anwendung an.
»Für uns ist entscheidend, dass wir die EHLA-Schicht nicht erst nachträglich bearbeiten, sondern den warmen Zustand direkt im Prozess nutzen«, erklärt die Projektleiterin. »Das Rollieren glättet die Oberfläche, beeinflusst aber zugleich Härte und Eigenspannungen. Damit macht SCaRB aus dem Materialauftrag einen Prozess, mit dem wir die Reparaturstelle gezielt funktional einstellen können.«
Materialeigenschaften gezielt einstellen
Für die spätere Funktion einer reparierten Fahrwerkskomponente reicht die ursprüngliche Geometrie allein nicht aus. Oberfläche und Wärmeeinflusszone brauchen die passenden Eigenschaften für den späteren Lastfall. Dies ist der entscheidende Vorteil von SCaRB: Die Rolle glättet die aufgetragene Schicht, erhöht die oberflächennahe Härte und beeinflusst die Eigenspannungen.
Der Materialauftrag erzeugt je nach Prozess Zugeigenspannungen. Unter zyklischer Belastung begünstigen sie Ermüdungsrisse. Das Rollieren reduziert diese Spannungen und wandelt sie unter geeigneten Bedingungen in Druckeigenspannungen um. Damit wird eine Reparaturstelle nicht nur geometrisch, sondern auch funktional an den späteren Lastfall angepasst.
Die gewünschten Eigenschaften der Reparaturstelle lassen sich über das Prozessfenster steuern. Laserparameter, Pulverparameter, Abstand zwischen Laser und Rollierwerkzeug, Rollierkraft, Rollenradius und Rollenhärte beeinflussen Oberfläche, Härte und Eigenspannungszustand unterschiedlich stark. Im Anschluss werden Schichthaftung, Gefüge, Härte, Eigenspannungen, Oberflächenqualität und vor allem das Ermüdungsverhalten unter realen Lasten überprüft.
Gerade die Ermüdungsfestigkeit spielt bei Fahrwerkskomponenten eine zentrale Rolle, weil sie im Betrieb wiederholt hohen mechanischen Belastungen ausgesetzt sind. Die nächsten Untersuchungen klären deshalb, wie die durch SCaRB eingestellten Eigenspannungen mit der Lebensdauer reparierter Komponenten zusammenhängen. Die Komponente braucht über ihre Einsatzdauer zuverlässig die geforderten Eigenschaften.
Zur Reparaturkette gehört damit auch ein geeignetes Prüfverfahren. Das Fraunhofer IWS bringt dafür LAwave ein, die Laser-induced Surface Acoustic Wave Spectroscopy. Hier regt ein Laser akustische Oberflächenwellen an; das Verfahren wertet deren Verhalten aus und liefert präzise Informationen über die oberflächennahen Eigenschaften der Beschichtung und des darunterliegenden Bereichs, ohne das Bauteil zu beschädigen.
Damit ergänzt LAwave die Prozesskette an einer ausschlaggebenden Stelle: EHLA baut Material lokal wieder auf oder erzeugt eine Schutzschicht, SCaRB stellt Oberfläche und Randzone mechanisch ein, LAwave liefert zerstörungsfreie Daten über die behandelten Bereiche. So rücken Reparatur, Funktion und Prüfung eng zusammen.
Vor einem standardisierten Reparaturverfahren in der Luftfahrt stehen aber noch weitere Entwicklungs- und Qualifizierungsschritte. Das Team überträgt die Ergebnisse aktuell auf reale Bauteilgeometrien und repräsentative Belastungen und erbringt die Nachweise für eine mögliche spätere Anwendung.
Ausblick auf eine automatisierte Reparaturkette
Langfristig zielt LEGATO auf eine durchgängige digitale Reparaturkette. Am Anfang steht ein automatisierter Scan der beschädigten Komponente. Aus den erfassten Geometriedaten bestimmt das System Schadensgröße und Materialverlust und leitet daraus die Bahn für den anschließenden Materialauftrag ab.
Die Reparatur erfolgt lokal mit EHLA. Direkt dahinter bearbeitet das SCaRB-Werkzeug die frisch aufgetragene Schicht und stellt Oberfläche und Randzone ein. Je nach Funktionsfläche folgt ein gezielter Polier- oder Schleifschritt. Den Abschluss bildet eine zerstörungsfreie Prüfung.
Im Zielbild laufen alle Schritte in einem gemeinsamen Aufbau ab, ohne dass das Team das Bauteil zwischen den einzelnen Schritten neu einspannt. Scan, Materialauftrag, mechanische Bearbeitung und Prüfung bilden dann keine getrennten Arbeitsschritte mehr, sondern Teile einer vernetzten Prozesskette.

Hohe EU-Förderung für innovativen 3D-Druck

Bastian Rapp (links) und Jürgen Rühe (rechts) wollen mit neuartigen und nachhaltigen 3D-Druckverfahren das Gebiet der Kunststoffverarbeitung verändern.
| Copyright:
Silvia Wolf / Universität Freiburg
Download
• Zwei Forscher der Universität Freiburg erhalten einen hoch dotierten Synergy Grant des Europäischen Forschungsrates (ERC).
• In ihrem geförderten Projekt entwickeln sie neuartige und nachhaltige 3D-Druckverfahren, die das Gebiet der Kunststoffverarbeitung grundlegend verändern könnten.
• Die Förderung läuft über sechs Jahre und beträgt rund zehn Millionen Euro.
Prof. Dr. Bastian Rapp und Prof. Dr. Jürgen Rühe erhalten einen Synergy Grant des Europäischen Forschungsrats (ERC). Damit fördert die Europäische Union (EU) ihr gemeinsames Forschungsprojekt „CHiC2PRINT“, das innovative, nachhaltige 3D-Ducktechnologie mit leistungsfähigen und kostengünstigen Kunststoffen der industriellen Fertigung verbindet. Rapp ist Professor für Prozesstechnologie und Rühe Professor für Chemie und Physik von Grenzflächen an der Technischen Fakultät der Universität Freiburg.
Die Förderung läuft über sechs Jahre und beträgt rund zehn Millionen Euro. Mit Synergy Grants fördert der ERC interdisziplinäre Forschungsteams, deren Arbeiten die Kriterien wissenschaftlicher Exzellenz erfüllen und Ergebnisse mit einem hohen Innovationsgrad erwarten lassen. In diesem Jahr wurden von mehr als 950 eingereichten Anträgen 48 für eine Förderung ausgewählt.
Nahezu beliebige Geometrien
„Wir freuen uns riesig über diese Förderung“, sagt Rapp. „Wir sind dabei, ein neues Kapitel der 3D-Drucktechnologie zu schreiben: Bald wird es möglich sein, Objekte in etablierten Kunststoffsystemen sehr viel schneller herzustellen, als es aktuell mit Spritzguss möglich ist.“ Bisher ermöglicht klassischer Spritzguss zwar die kostengünstige Herstellung robuster Kunststoffprodukte, ist aber bei komplexen Formen eingeschränkt. 3D-Druck erlaubt dagegen nahezu beliebige Geometrien, benötigt aber oft spezielle Materialien oder aufwendige Fertigungsverfahren. Diese Grenzen wollen Rapp, Rühe und ihr internationales Forschungsteam überwinden.
Materialtechnologischer Trick
Die Forschenden entwickeln dafür eine Technologie, mit der sich handelsübliche Kunststoffe durch gezielte Belichtung dreidimensional strukturieren lassen. Dabei wird das Material nicht wie beim herkömmlichen 3D-Druck Schicht für Schicht aufgebaut. Stattdessen entstehen durch den Einsatz von Licht komplexe Strukturen direkt im Inneren eines bereits vorhandenen Kunststoffkörpers. Grundlage hierfür ist das sogenannte volumetric printing (Volumendruck). Dieses Verfahren wird gepaart mit einem materialtechnologischen Trick aus der Photochemie, der es ermöglicht, kommerzielle Kunststoffe lichtempfindlich zu machen – so werden sie für den 3D-Druck zugänglich. Langfristig könnten so Bauteile entstehen, deren Form und Eigenschaften sich präzise einstellen lassen, beispielsweise mit gezielt unterschiedlichen Festigkeiten innerhalb eines einzigen Werkstücks.
Vollständig neuartige Wege
Ein weiterer wichtiger Aspekt ist hierbei die Nachhaltigkeit der eingesetzten Materialien. 3D-gedruckte Objekte sind bisher meistens nicht recyclingfähig und müssen verbrannt oder deponiert werden, was sie aus umwelttechnischer Sicht problematisch macht. In dem geförderten Projekt sollen die hergestellten Objekte am Ende ihrer Lebenszeit wieder komplett in einzelne Komponenten zerlegt werden („Enthaftung“). Die einzelnen Komponenten werden so gespalten, dass die ursprünglichen Kunststoffe wiedererhalten und erneut verarbeitet werden können. „Die Förderung des ERC ist für uns ein großer Ansporn, innovative und nachhaltige 3D-Druckverfahren zu entwickeln“, sagt Rühe. „Die Verbindung von neuartiger, fast nach Science Fiction klingender Drucktechnologie und vollständig neuartigen Wegen, ein breites Spektrum an Materialien 3D-druckbar und sehr viel nachhaltiger zu machen, könnte das gesamte Gebiet der Kunststoffverarbeitung revolutionieren.“
ZUR PERSON
Prof. Dr. Bastian Rapp ist Professor für Prozesstechnologie am Institut für Mikrosystemtechnik (IMTEK) der Universität Freiburg. Zu seinen Forschungsschwerpunkten zählen Additive Fertigung, die Entwicklung neuer Materialsysteme wie funktionale Gläser, sowie die Komponentenminiaturisierung und die Mikrosystemtechnik. Er ist Geschäftsführender Direktor des Freiburger Materialforschungszentrums (FMF) und Mitgründer des Spin-offs Glassomer GmbH, das 3D-Druckverfahren der nächsten Generation für Glas anbietet. 2019 erhielt er einen ERC Consolidator Grant für seine Arbeit an taktilen Displays für Menschen mit Sehbehinderung.
Prof. Dr. Jürgen Rühe ist Professor für Chemie und Physik von Grenzflächen am Institut für Mikrosystemtechnik (IMTEK) der Universität Freiburg. Zu seinen Forschungsschwerpunkten zählen neue Wege zur Beschichtung von Oberflächen, wobei die Kombination von Oberflächenchemie und Mikrostrukturierung vollständig neuartige Materialien ergibt. Rühe ist Geschäftsführender Direktor des Freiburger Zentrum für Interaktive Werkstoffe und Bioinspirierte Technologien (FIT). Er ist Sprecher des Exzellenzclusters livMatS, das sich mit adaptiven Materialsystemen befasst, sowie Co-Sprecher des DFG-Graduiertenkollegs BioBuild, das neue Materialien für adaptive Architektur entwickelt. Für eine Arbeit auf dem Gebiet der Oberflächenmodifizierung erhielt er unter anderem den DECHEMA-Preis der Max-Buchner-Forschungsstiftung.

title: KI soll neue Materialien nach Maß entwickeln
content:
KI soll neue Materialien nach Maß entwickeln

Gemeinsam mit Forschenden aus Oxford und Jülich erhält Professor Pascal Friederich den ERC Synergy Grant.
| Quelle:
Amadeus Bramsiepe, KIT
| Copyright:
Amadeus Bramsiepe, KIT
Download
Der Europäische Forschungsrat (ERC) fördert das Projekt ODDITY – ein Forschungsvorhaben, das Professor Pascal Friederich vom Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT) gemeinsam mit Partnern am Forschungszentrum Jülich und der Universität Oxford eingeworben hat. Die Forschenden kombinieren Künstliche Intelligenz (KI), Molekülchemie und autonome Labore, um gezielt Molekülstrukturen zu entwickeln. Das soll die Suche nach neuen Materialien für Anwendungen wie die Photovoltaik wesentlich beschleunigen. Der ERC fördert das Projekt über sechs Jahre mit 9,7 Millionen Euro.
Technischer Fortschritt hängt wesentlich davon ab, welche Materialien zur Verfügung stehen. Die Entwicklung von Photovoltaik, Lichtsensoren und elektronischen Bauteilen benötigt Stoffe, die mehrere Anforderungen gleichzeitig erfüllen: Sie müssen unter anderem bestimmte optische und elektrische Eigenschaften besitzen sowie stabil und leicht zu verarbeiten sein. Ein Beispiel sind hauchdünne Schichten in Solarzellen, die Licht absorbieren und elektrische Ladungen transportieren.
Baukastensystem für Moleküle
Was ein Material leisten kann, bestimmt vor allem sein molekularer Aufbau. Das Projekt ODDITY (On-Demand Discovery by Molecular Ingenuity) verfolgt einen systematischen Ansatz, um aus mehr als einer Billion möglicher Molekülstrukturen gezielt diejenigen zu finden, die bestimmte Anforderungen erfüllen. Der Europäische Forschungsrat fördert dieses Vorhaben nun mit einem Synergy Grant. „Mit dem ERC Synergy Grant wird ein Forschungsansatz ausgezeichnet, der das Potenzial hat, die Entwicklung neuer Materialien grundlegend zu verändern. Das Projekt ODDITY vereint wissenschaftliche Exzellenz in den Bereichen Künstliche Intelligenz, Chemie und Materialforschung und zeigt eindrucksvoll die Stärke internationaler Zusammenarbeit“, sagt Professor Oliver Kraft, Vizepräsident Forschung, Lehre und Akademische Angelegenheiten des KIT.
„Wir verbinden mithilfe von KI eine beschleunigte chemische Synthese mit reversiblen Reaktionen“, sagt Professor Pascal Friederich vom Institut für Nanotechnologie (INT) des KIT. Wie in einem Baukastensystem sollen sich Moleküle innerhalb weniger Sekunden oder Minuten aus chemischen Bausteinen zusammensetzen, anschließend wieder zerlegen und neu kombinieren lassen. Auch ihre Eigenschaften sollen in diesem Tempo untersucht werden. „Wir wollen mit einem hohen experimentellen Durchsatz die Suche nach geeigneten Materialien von Jahren auf Wochen verkürzen“, sagt Friederich.
KI steuert Experimente
Friederich entwickelt dafür mit einer Arbeitsgruppe KI-Modelle, die ausgehend von den gewünschten Materialeigenschaften geeignete Molekülstrukturen finden sollen, die sich auch tatsächlich chemisch herstellen lassen. „Geplant ist, Daten aus Computersimulationen, Labormessungen und Tests an Bauteilen zusammenzuführen. Unser Ziel ist es, mithilfe von maschinellem Lernen zu erfahren, welche Bausteine wir auswählen und wie wir sie zusammensetzen müssen, um ein Molekül mit bestimmten Eigenschaften zu erhalten“, erklärt der Forscher. Generative KI soll zudem neue chemische Bausteine vorschlagen und damit die Auswahl möglicher Materialien erweitern. „Die KI-Modelle helfen uns, vielversprechende Moleküle zu finden, ohne jede mögliche Kombination einzeln untersuchen zu müssen. Sie unterstützen uns auch bei der Entscheidung, welcher Versuch als Nächstes sinnvoll ist. Die Ergebnisse fließen anschließend wieder in die Modelle ein.“
Enge Zusammenarbeit mit Oxford und Jülich
Den ERC Synergy Grant hat Friederich am KIT gemeinsam mit Teams in Oxford und Jülich eingeworben. Jülich hat dabei eng mit der Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg am Helmholtz-Institut Erlangen-Nürnberg für Erneuerbare Energien (HI ERN) zusammengearbeitet.
Die Forschenden steuern ihre jeweilige Expertise in der Molekülchemie und der automatisierten Materialuntersuchung bei. Das Team um Professor Iain McCulloch an der Universität Oxford entwickelt die chemischen Verfahren, mit denen sich Moleküle zusammensetzen und verändern lassen – einschließlich reversibler Reaktionen, die es ermöglichen, Bausteine zurückzugewinnen und wiederzuverwenden. Das Team von Professor Christoph Brabec am Forschungszentrum Jülich steuert autonome Laborplattformen bei. Diese dienen dazu, Dünnschichten herzustellen und zu charakterisieren sowie Bauteile in einem Ultra-Hochdurchsatz-Verfahren zu testen.
ERC Synergy Grant
Der Europäische Forschungsrat (ERC) fördert mit Synergy Grants vielversprechende Forschungsteams. Die geförderten Projekte sollen nur in Zusammenarbeit der beteiligten Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler möglich sein und zu Entdeckungen an den Schnittstellen zwischen etablierten Disziplinen sowie zu wesentlichen Fortschritten an den Grenzen des Wissens führen. Für die Ausschreibung 2026 stellt der ERC insgesamt 500 Millionen Euro bereit. Es gingen insgesamt 957 Anträge ein, von denen 48 gefördert werden. (cka)
Im Dialog mit der Gesellschaft entwickelt das KIT Lösungen für große Herausforderungen – von Klimawandel, Energiewende und nachhaltigem Umgang mit natürlichen Ressourcen bis hin zu Künstlicher Intelligenz, technologischer Souveränität und demografischem Wandel. Als Die Universität in der Helmholtz-Gemeinschaft vereint das KIT wissenschaftliche Exzellenz vom Erkenntnisgewinn bis zur Anwendungsorientierung unter einem Dach – und ist damit in einer einzigartigen Position, diese Transformation voranzutreiben. Damit bietet das KIT als Exzellenzuniversität seinen mehr als 10 000 Mitarbeitenden sowie seinen 23 000 Studierenden herausragende Möglichkeiten, eine nachhaltige und resiliente Zukunft zu gestalten. KIT – Science for Impact.
